children.text: tattvacintāmaṇau śabdāprāmāṇyavādaḥ
children.translated_text: The discourse on the non-validity of verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>) in the <s>Tattvacintāmaṇi</s>

children.text:
atha śabdo nirūpyate /
prayogahetubhūtārthatattvajñānajanyaḥ śabdaḥ pramāṇam /
karaṇañca tat yasmin sati kriyā bhavatyeva /
children.translated_text: Now verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>) is examined. <s>Śabda</s> is a means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>), being produced by knowledge of the true nature of the object that is the cause of the utterance. And the instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>) is that in the presence of which the action certainly occurs.

children.text:
na ca śabde sati pramā bhavatyeveti nāyaṃ śabdaḥ prāmaṇam /
na ca śabdo na pramāṇamiti vākyasya prāmāṇyāpramāṇyayorvyāghātaḥ , asyāprāmāṇye 'pi etadutthāpyamānāvisaṃvādāditi cet na, ākāṅkṣādimataḥ padārthasmaraṇādivyāpāravataḥ pramāṇatvena tathābhūtāt pramotpatterāvaśyakatvāt atathābhūtatve ca phalājanakatvasya karaṇāntarasāmyāt /
tathāpi śabdo na pramāṇāntaraṃ padārthasaṃsargasyānumānādeva siddheḥ /
tathāpi gāmābhyāja daṇḍeti padāni vaidikapadāni vā tātparyyaviṣayasmāritapadārthasaṃsargajñānapūrvakāṇi ākāṅkṣādimatpadakadambatvāt ghaṭamānayetivat /
yogyatāsattimattve sati saṃsṛṣṭārthaparatvāt tatparasannimattvāddeti na hetuḥ, saṃsṛṣṭohi yor'thastatparatvaṃ tatparasannidhimattvaṃ vā asiddhaṃ saṃsarṅgasya prāgapratīteḥ /
saṃsṛṃṣṭatvaprakārakapratītiparatvaṃ tatprakārakapratītiparasannidhimattvaṃ vā anāptokte nirākāṅkṣe ca vyabhicāri /
saṃsargasya bahuprakārakatve 'pi nānābhimatasaṃsargasiddhistasya tātparyyāviṣayatvāt /
anyathā śabdādapyabhimatānvayabodho na syāt /
ata eva viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāvavadarthakāni tadbodhapūrvakāṇi veti na sādhyam /
children.translated_text: But since valid cognition (<s>pramā</s>) does not certainly occur in the presence of verbal testimony, this verbal testimony is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>. Nor is there a contradiction between the validity and non-validity of the sentence 'verbal testimony is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>,' since even if this [statement] is non-valid, the content conveyed by it is non-deceptive—if so objected, no; because from words possessing <s>ākāṅkṣā</s> (expectancy) and other [conditions], which have the function of recollecting word-meanings, valid cognition necessarily arises when [the words] are in that state [i.e., a <s>pramāṇa</s>], and in the absence of that state, failure to produce the result is analogous to [the failure of] other instruments. Even so, verbal testimony is not a separate <s>pramāṇa</s>, since the connection of word-meanings can be established through inference alone. Even so, the words 'drive the cow with a stick,' or Vedic words, are preceded by the cognition of the connection of word-meanings recollected as the object of purport (<s>tātparya</s>), because they are a collection of words possessing <s>ākāṅkṣā</s> (expectancy) and other [conditions], like 'bring the pot.' [The reason] 'because of being directed toward a connected meaning when possessing <s>yogyatā</s> (fitness) and <s>āsatti</s> (contiguity), or because of the proximity of words directed toward that'—is not [valid], because the directedness toward the connected meaning or the proximity of words so directed is unestablished, since the connection has not yet been cognized. Or, directedness toward cognition having the mode of connectedness, or the proximity of a word directed toward cognition having that mode—this deviates in utterances by a non-trustworthy speaker and in sentences that leave no expectancy. Even though the connection has many modes, the establishment of only the intended connection [is needed], since [the other connections] are not the object of purport. Otherwise, even from verbal testimony, the desired connected meaning would not be cognized. For this very reason, [the claim that] the words 'mean [things] in the qualifier-qualificand relation and are preceded by cognition thereof' is not what needs to be proved.

children.text:
yattu smāritārthasaṃsargavantoti sādhyaṃ, matvarthaśca liṅgatayā jñāpakatvaṃ /
na cānyonyāśrayaḥ, pūrvapūrvānumitihetutvena anāditvāt /
tanna /
jñāpakatvamātreṇārthāsiddheḥ /
pramāpakatve tenaiva vyabhicārāt /
jñānāvacchedakatayā ca saṃsargasiddhiḥ jñānajñānasya tadviṣayaviṣayakatvaniyamāt /
children.translated_text: As for the [amended] probandum 'they possess the connection of the recollected meanings'—the suffix '-mat' has the function of indicating by way of a logical mark (<s>liṅga</s>). Nor is there mutual dependence, since [the process] is beginningless, each prior inference being the cause of each subsequent one. That is not so, because the purpose is not achieved by mere indication. If [it is claimed to have] the capacity to produce valid cognition, there is deviation by that very [reason]. And the establishment of the connection is through [its being] the delimitor of cognition, since there is the invariable rule that the cognition of a cognition has as its object the object [of that cognition].

children.text: (Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,1, p. 39)
children.translated_text: (Bibliotheca Indica 98, IV,1, p. 39)

children.text:
saṃsarge ca sambandhina eva viśeṣakatvāt /
pakṣadharmatābalāt vyapakatvenāgṛhītasyāpi saṃsargaviśeṣasya siddhiḥ /
athaivaṃ bhrāntijñānamapi bhramaḥ syāt /
na ceṣṭāpattiḥ., īśvarasyāpi srabhrāntatvāpatteḥ /
idaṃ rajatamiti bhramādiva śuktau rajatajñānavānayamiti bhramasya jñānāt bhrāntijñapravṛttyāpatteśca /
yattu bhramaviṣayakatvena na pramatvaṃ bhramaviṣayāṇāṃ siddhyasiddhiparāhatatvāt iti, tacca vakṣyāmaḥ /
maivaṃ, asadviṣayakatvena na bhramatvaṃ bhramaviṣayāṇāṃ sattvāt kintu vyadhikaraṇaprakārakatatvena /
na ca bhramasya jñāne vyadhikaraṇaṃ prakāraḥ, rajatatvaprakārakatva bhrame 'pi sattvāt anyathā bhrāntyucchedaḥ pramāṇābhāvāt /
nanu prakārakavākye vyabhicāraḥ viśeṣadarśanena tacca saṃsargajñānābhāvāt /
na ca saṃsargamapratītya vākyaracanā na sambhavatītyāhāryyaṃ tasya saṃsargajñānaṃ sambhavatīti vācyam /
tāvatpadajñānādeva ekasyeva vākyaracanopapatteḥ /
anyaccāpi tasyaiva tantratvāditi cet , na, etadvākyametasya padārthasaṃsargaṃ bodhayiṣyatītyāśayena vākyaprayogāt tasyāpi saṃsargajñānāt yogyatāvirahācca /
ata eva visambādivākye ekavaduccarite na vyabhicāraḥ /
śabdāt saṃsargapratyayastu yogyatābhramāt /
atha saṃsargajñānaṃ vinā ekasyānyasya vā sambādivākye bhrāntaprakārakavākye ca vyabhicāraḥ kathaṃ vā tacca saṃsargapramā vaktṛjñānānumānāsambhavāditi cet na /
yadi tacca saṃsargapramā tadā vedatulyatetyuktam /
ākāṅkṣā - yogyatāsattiśca jñātopayujyate, anyathā śābdabhramānupapatteriti /
children.translated_text: And in the connection, it is the relata themselves that are the differentiators. By the force of the property-of-the-subject (<s>pakṣadharmatā</s>), even a particular connection not grasped as such is established. Now then, even erroneous cognition would be an error-cognition [i.e., a valid cognition of error]. Nor is there the undesired consequence [of this]—because there would follow the consequence that even <s>Īśvara</s> (God) is erroneous. Just as from the error 'this is silver' [regarding nacre], from the cognition of the error—'this person has the cognition of silver regarding nacre'—there would follow the consequence of activity based on erroneous cognition. As for [the claim that] 'being directed toward the object of error does not constitute valid cognition, because the objects of error are undermined by the question of their being established or not established'—we shall address that. It should not be so; being directed toward a non-existent object does not make something erroneous, because the objects of error do exist; rather, [error consists in] having a mode that occurs in a different locus (<s>vyadhikaraṇa</s>). Nor is the mode in the cognition of error occurring in a different locus, since silver-ness as a mode exists even in error; otherwise there would be the destruction of error, due to the absence of a <s>pramāṇa</s> [to establish it]. But there is deviation in sentences with a qualified mode, through the perception of a particular [counterexample], and that is because of the absence of cognition of the connection. Nor should it be said 'since composing a sentence is not possible without having cognized the connection, the cognition of the connection by the speaker is inferable'—because the composition of a sentence by a single person is possible from the mere cognition of so many word-meanings. And if [it is objected that] the other [cognition] too depends on that very [speaker], no—because the utterance of the sentence is with the intention 'this sentence will convey to this [hearer] the connection of word-meanings,' and because that [speaker] too has the cognition of the connection, and because of the absence of fitness. For this very reason, in sentences [uttered] by a credible speaker like the 'saṃbā' sentence, when uttered by one person, there is no deviation. The cognition of the connection from verbal testimony is due to the error regarding fitness. Now, if [one asks] how, without the cognition of the connection, there is deviation in 'saṃbā' sentences by one or another person, and in sentences with erroneous modes, and how that cognition of the connection can be valid when inference from the speaker's knowledge is impossible—no. If that [cognition] is a valid cognition of the connection, then it is said to be equivalent to the Vedas. And <s>ākāṅkṣā</s> (expectancy), <s>yogyatā</s> (fitness), and <s>āsatti</s> (contiguity) are useful only when known; otherwise, the impossibility of verbal error [would follow].

children.text: (Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,1, p. 50)
children.translated_text: (Bibliotheca Indica 98, IV,1, p. 50)

children.text:
ucyate /
arthajñānaṃ pravarttakaṃ na tu tajjñānajñānaṃ gauravāt vyabhicārācca, ato rajataviṣayakamiti cet satyaṃ, na tu rajatatvaprakārakaṃ pravarttakañca tathā, tadubhayasaṅkarāpattiśca /
etena lakṣaṇādyanurodhāttātparyyagraho vākyarthadhīhetuḥ tātparyañca padārthasaṃsargaviśeṣapratītyuddheśyakatvaṃ, tathāca tadgrāhakānumānādeva tātparyajñānāvacchedakatayā saṃsargasiddhirityapāstam /
kiñca vyāpakatāvacchedakaprakārikānumitirataḥ smāripadārthasaṃsargajñānapūrvakāṇīti tasmāt pravarttakaṃ jñānaṃ śabdādeva /
ata eva pravṛttyarthamanuvādakatā śabdasyetyapāstaṃ /
śābdānumityorbhinnaprakārakatvāt ekaviṣayatvābhāvena stātparyaviṣayamithaḥsaṃsargavantaḥ ākāṅkṣādimatpadasmāritatvāt yogyatāsattimattve sati sasarṅgaparapadasmāritatvādvā, anāptokte yogyatāvirahāt na vyabhicāraḥ, tacca bādhakasattvāt, tajjanyajñānasya bhramatvāt ekākāravākyasyāpi bādhakasattvāsattvābhyāṃ yogyāyogyatvāt /
children.translated_text: It is said: Knowledge of the object is what prompts activity, not the knowledge of that knowledge, due to cumbersomeness and deviation. Therefore, if [it is claimed] that [the cognition] has silver as its object—true, but it is not the case that [a cognition] having silver-ness as its mode is what prompts activity; otherwise there would follow the conflation of both. By this, [the view that] 'the apprehension of purport, based on conformity with definition and other [considerations], is the cause of sentential cognition, and purport is the intended-ness for the cognition of a particular connection of word-meanings, and thus the establishment of the connection is through [its being] the delimitor of the inferential cognition that apprehends the purport'—is refuted. Moreover, the inference has a mode that is the delimitor of the pervasion-relation; therefore [the words] are preceded by the cognition of the connection of the recollected word-meanings. Therefore, the cognition that prompts activity comes from verbal testimony itself. For this very reason, [the claim that] verbal testimony has a merely reiterative function regarding the object of activity is refuted. Since verbal cognition and inferential cognition have different modes, and due to the absence of a single object, the [word-meanings] that are the object of purport possess mutual connection, because they are recollected by words possessing <s>ākāṅkṣā</s> (expectancy) and other [conditions], or because they are recollected by words directed toward the connected [meaning] when possessing <s>yogyatā</s> (fitness) and <s>āsatti</s> (contiguity). In utterances by a non-trustworthy speaker, there is no deviation due to the absence of fitness; and that [absence of fitness] is due to the presence of a sublating cognition (<s>bādhaka</s>); because the cognition produced by it is erroneous; and because even a sentence of one form has fitness or unfitness depending on the presence or absence of a sublating cognition.

children.text: (Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,1, p. 64)
children.translated_text: (Bibliotheca Indica 98, IV,1, p. 64)

children.text:
atha pratipatturjijñāsāṃ prati yogyatā sā ca śrotari tadutpādyasaṃsargāvagamaprāgabhāvarūpākāṅkā bādhakapramāvirahā yogyatā avyavahitasaṃsargapratiyogijñānamāsattiḥ tāśca svarūpasatyo hetavo /
na tu jñātāḥ gauravāt tadbodhaṃ vinānvayānubhave vilambābhāvāt saṃsarganirūpyatvena prathamaṃ duravadhāraṇatvācceti na tāni liṅgaviśeṣaṇāneti cet, na, yogyatādiśūnyatve 'pi tadabhimānena saṃsargapratyayādanyathā śābdabhāsocchedaprasaṅgaḥ /
rājā putramākāṅkṣati puruṣaṃ veti saṃśaye viparyaye ca
children.translated_text: Now, fitness (<s>yogyatā</s>) is with respect to the desire to know of the cognizer; and that is: in the hearer, expectancy (<s>ākāṅkṣā</s>) has the form of the prior absence of the apprehension of the connection to be generated by that [utterance]; fitness (<s>yogyatā</s>) is the absence of a sublating valid cognition; contiguity (<s>āsatti</s>) is the cognition of the counterpositive of the immediate connection; and these are causes that are real in their own nature. But they are not [required to be] known, due to cumbersomeness, and because there is no delay in the experience of the connected meaning without the cognition thereof, and because [the connection] is difficult to ascertain initially since it is to be determined with reference to the connection—therefore these are not qualifications of the logical mark—if so objected, no; because even in the absence of <s>yogyatā</s> and other [conditions], due to the belief [that they are present], a cognition of the connection arises [from verbal testimony]; otherwise there would follow the destruction of verbal error.

children.text:
vākyārthadhīpratibandhācca, yogyatāyāśca saṃśayasādhāraṇaṃ jñānamātraṃ hetuḥ, sva- parabādhakapramāvirahaḥ kvacit niścīyate 'pi yatheha ghaṭo nastītyacca svayogyānupalabdhā ghaṭābhāvaniścayenānyasasyāpi ghaṭapramāviraho niścīyate /
kvacidbādhakapramāmātravirahasaṃśaye 'pyanvayabodhaḥ bādhasaṃśayasyādūṣaṇatvāt /
children.translated_text: And because of the obstruction of sentential cognition in the case of doubt and contrary cognition, as in 'The king desires a son [or] a man'; and because for <s>yogyatā</s>, mere cognition common to doubt is the cause; the absence of a sublating valid cognition by oneself or another is sometimes ascertained, as in 'there is no pot here,' where through one's own valid non-apprehension of the appropriate [object], the ascertainment of the absence of the pot also ascertains the absence of another's valid cognition of the pot. Sometimes even when there is doubt about the mere absence of a sublating cognition, the cognition of the connected meaning arises, because doubt about sublation is not a vitiating factor.

children.text: (Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,1, p. 68)
children.translated_text: (Bibliotheca Indica 98, IV,1, p. 68)

children.text:
kiñca tavāpi yogyatādikaṃ pramāṇye prayojakaṃ āptoktatvasya tathātve gauravāt anāpto 'kte 'pi saṃvādena pramāṇyācca /
evañca jñāyamānakaraṇe pramāṇyaprayojanakatayā jñānamāvaśyakamiti tāsāṃ jñānaṃ hetuḥ, tacca samabhivyāhāraviśeṣādineti /
maivaṃ /
yatra vimalaṃ jalaṃ ityaśrutvaiva nadyāḥ kacche mahiṣaścaratīti śṛṇoti tatrākāṅkādikamasti /
na ca nadau-kacchayoḥ saṃsarga iti, vyabhicārāt /
ata eva tanmātraṃ prayojakaṃ pramāṇye /
atha yāvātsamabhivyāhṛtetyapi liṅgaviśeṣaṇaṃ katipayapadasmāriṇastu saṃsargapratyayoliṅgābhimānāditi cet /
na /
tatsandehe 'pi vākyārthāvagamāt /
tatra saṃsargabhrāntiriti cet na /
anyakāraṇābhāvena padameva bhrāntijanakaṃ tathācāduṣṭaṃ sattadevābhrāntiṃ janayat kena vāraṇīyam /
asaṃsargāgrahastaceti cet /
na /
saṃsarge bādhakābhāvāt /
athāptoktatvaṃ liṅgaviśeṣaṇaṃ tadeva vā liṅgam /
na ca nadī- kacchayoḥ saṃsarge āptoktatvaṃ, āptoktatvañca pramāṇye tantramiti taddhattayā jñāyamānasya hetutvena tatra jñānamāvaśayakaṃ vyāptimattayā jñātasyeva liṅgasya, tadavagamaśca loke bhramādyamūlakatayā mahājanaparigraheṇa vede smṛtau ceti cet /
na /
yatra kutracidāptatvamanāptasyāpi sarvacāptamapramitaṃ, bhrānteḥ puruṣadharmatvāt prakṛtavākyārthayathārthajñānavattvañcāptatvaṃ prathamaṃ durgrahaṃ, bhramādyamūlakatvasya pravṛttisaṃvādādeśca tadgrāhasyājñānāt pravṛttiśca sandehādapi /
children.translated_text: Moreover, even for you, <s>yogyatā</s> (fitness) and the like are the operative factors in validity (<s>prāmāṇya</s>). If the property of being uttered by a trustworthy person (<s>āptoktatva</s>) is to be similarly [operative], there is superfluity (<s>gaurava</s>), and since even in an utterance by a non-trustworthy person there is validity due to concordance (<s>saṃvāda</s>). Thus —

children.text: (Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,1, p. 77)
children.translated_text: (Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,1, p. 77)

children.text:
kiñca pakṛtasaṃsarge ayamābhrānto yathārthajñānavānveti saṃsargamapratītya jñātumaśakyaṃ vākyārthasyāpūrvatvāt /
vayantu būmaḥ bādhakapramāṇābhāvo yogyatā
children.translated_text: Moreover, [the claim that] 'this person is undeluded and possesses veridical cognition in regard to the referent in question (<s>prakṛtasaṃsarga</s>)' — without apprehending the connection, this cannot be known, since the meaning of the sentence (<s>vākyārtha</s>) is unprecedented (<s>apūrva</s>). We, however, [hold that] —

children.text: sā ca na liṅgaviśeṣaṇaṃ bādhakapramāṇamātravirahasya sarvatra niścātumaśakyatvāt , tatsaṃśaye 'pi śabdādanvayabodhācca, śabdaprāmāṇye tu yogyatāyāḥ saṃśaya-niścayasādhāraṇaṃ jñānamātraṃ prayojakamiti śabdaḥ pramāṇamiti /
children.translated_text: And that [condition] is not a qualifier of the inferential mark (<s>liṅgaviśeṣaṇa</s>), because the mere absence of a defeating <s>pramāṇa</s> (<s>bādhakapramāṇa</s>) cannot be ascertained in all cases, and because even when there is doubt about it, verbal cognition of the connection (<s>anvayabodha</s>) arises from the word (<s>śabda</s>).

children.text: (Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,1, p. 83)
children.translated_text: (Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,1, p. 83)

children.text:
jaranmīmāṃsakāstu loke vaktṛjñānānumānāttadupajīvasaṃsargānumānādvā vākyarthasiddhau śabdasyānuvādakatvaṃ vede tu tadabhāvāt svātantreṇa prāmāṇyamiti vadanti /
tanna /
vede kḷptasāmagrīto loke 'pi saṃsargapratyayādanyathānuvādakatāpi na syāt liṅgasya pūrvatve 'pi vyāptismṛtivilambena tadvilambāt /
anāptoktau vyabhicārāt vedatulyāpi sāmagrau na niścāyiketi cet /
na /
cakṣurādestathātvena tacchaṅkāyāmapi pramāpakatvāt /
jñāyamānaṃ karaṇaṃ sandehe na niścāyakaṃ liṅgavaditi cet /
na /
saṃśayo hi na vākye tasya niścayāt, na tajjanayajñānapramāṇye tasya taduttarakālīnatvāt , nāptoktatve tanniścayasyānaṅgatvāt /
nanu loke āptoktatvasandehe vākyārthadhīrneti tanniścayohetuḥ tathā ca vākyārtagocarayathārthajñānajanyatvagrāhakāt /
tadupajīvino 'numānāt vākyarthadhīriti cet /
na /
vedetadrahitasyāpi sāmarthyāvadhāraṇāt tadaniścaye 'pi vedānukāreṇa paṭhyamānamanvādivākye 'pauruṣeyatvābhimāni nogauḍamīmāṃsakasyārthaniścayāt /
na cāsau bhrāntiḥ, bādhakābhāvāt pauruṣeyatvaniścayadaśāyāmapi tasya tathātvāt /
children.translated_text: The ancient <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s>, however, [hold that] in the everyday world, since the meaning of a sentence is established through inference of the speaker's cognition or through inference of the connection based on that, verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>) is merely reiterative (<s>anuvādaka</s>); but in the case of the <s>Veda</s>, in the absence of that [speaker's cognition] —

children.text: (Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,1, p. 89)
children.translated_text: (Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,1, p. 89)

children.text:
na cāsaṃsargāgrahamātraṃ tat arthasya tathābhāve 'pi asaṃsargāhatve saṃsargocchedāpatteḥ /
na cāptoktatvanniścayarūpakāraṇābādhāt saṃsargajñānabādhaḥ, vyabhicāreṇa hetutāyāmeva bādhāt laukikatvena jñāte tadaṅgamiti cet /
na /
mānābhāvāt vākyārthasyāpūrvatvena liṅgābhāvena tadgrahāsambhāt / yadi cāpauruṣeyatvaniścaye satyeva vedādarthapratyayaḥ tadā doṣavatpuruṣāpraṇītatve satyākāṅkṣādimatpadasmāritatvena vede padārthasaṃsargasiddhirastviti vede 'pyunuvādakaḥ syāt /
taduktaṃ, ``vyastapundūṣaṇāśaṅkaiḥ smāritatatvāt padairamī /
anvitā iti nirṇīte vedasyāpi na tat kutaḥ'' /
na caivaṃ śabdasya pramāṇatvamapi, anumānādeva vākyarthapramotpatteriti /
children.translated_text: And it is not the case that the mere non-apprehension of the connection is that [defeating condition], because even when the referent is as such, if the connection were defeated by non-apprehension, the absurd consequence of total annihilation of connections would follow. Nor is certitude in the form of [cognition arising from] trustworthy utterance (<s>āptoktatva</s>) —

children.text:
prābhākarāstu vyabhicāriśabdavyāvṛttamavyabhicāryanugatapramāprayojakamupeyaṃ yadabhāvādanāptoktavākyādapramā anyathā kāryavaicitryaṃ na syāt, tacca jñātamupayujyate jñāmānakaraṇe jñanopayogivyabhicārivailakṣaṇyatvāt pramāhetutvādvā vyāptivacchabdaśaktivacceti, anyathā śabdābhāsocchedaprasaṅgaḥ /
na cāptoktatvaṃ tathā, saṃvādāt pramāṇe śukodīrite bhrāntapratārakasaṃvādivākye vede ca tadabhāvādāptoktatvānumāne vyabhicārivyāvṛttaliṅgābhāvācca /
bhāve vā tadvata eva śabdasya pratyāyakatvāt /
children.translated_text: The <s>Prābhākaras</s>, however, [hold that] what is to be accepted (<s>upeya</s>) is that which, distinguished from deviant words (<s>vyabhicāriśabda</s>), invariably accompanies non-deviant [words] and is productive of valid cognition (<s>pramā</s>), in the absence of which even from a sentence not uttered by a trustworthy person there would be no valid cognition — otherwise, what —

etenāpramāhetutvaṃ na bhrama-pamāda-vipralipsā-karaṇāpaṭavānāṃ parasparaṃ vyabhicārāt militasyāvyāpakatvāt /
kintvāptoktatvābhāvasyāpramāhetutvaṃ tadabhāvaścāptoktatvaṃ pramāheturityapāstaṃ /
āptoktatvasya prathamaṃ liṅgābhāvena jñātumaśakyatvāt /
ata eva vyabhicāraśaṅkāviraho hetuḥ sā ca loke bhramādimūletyāptoktatvānumānāducchidyate, vede ca pauruṣeyatvaniścayeneti nirastaṃ /
abhimatavākyārthasyāpūrvatvena sādhyāprasiddheḥ vede sadoṣapuruṣāpraṇītapadasmāritatvena saṃsargasiddheranuvādakatāpatteśca /
nāpi doṣābhāvaḥ bhrāntapratārakavākyajanyajñāne pratyakṣeṇāgṛhītasaṃvāde tadabhāvāt /
doṣabhāvasya hetutvāt tatra vākyaṃ mūkameva vyavahārastu pratyakṣāditi cet /
na /
anubhavāpalāpāpāt taddhetutve vivādāt vede 'pyanuvādakatāpatteśca /
kiñca doṣābhāvasya pramāhetutve 'pramāyāṃ doṣaḥ kāraṇaṃ tasya ca pratyekaṃ hetutve vyabhicāraḥ militasya tattve ekasmādapramā na syāt bhramādīnāṃ pratyekaṃ doṣatve 'nanugamaḥ militasya tu tattve ekasmādapramānudayaprasaṅgaḥ /
tasmāt lāghavāt yathārthatātparyakatvaṃ śābdapramāprayojakaṃ tacca yathārthavākyarthavākyarthapratītiprayojanakatvaṃ loka-vedasādhāraṇaṃ tadabhāvādapramā sa eva doṣaḥ, na hi jātyaiva kaściddoṣaḥ, tadvighātakatvācca bhramādīnāṃ doṣatvaṃ /
ata eva bhrāntapratārakavāṅkyaṃ śukādivākyañca pramāṇaṃ saṃvādāt /
ata evānyaghaṭābhiprāyeṇa gehe ghaṭo 'stītyukte yatra dhaṭāntaraṃ dṛṣṭvā tamānayati tatrānyaparatvācchabdo na pramāṇaṃ vyavārastu pratyakṣādeva yaṣṭīḥ praveśayeti ca mukhyārthabodhe tacca tātparyaṃ jñātamupayujyate jñāyamānakaraṇe jñānopayogivyabhicārivailakṣaṇyādvyāptivacchaktivacca, anyathā anyaparādanyānvayabodhona syāt iti śabdābhāsocchedaprasaṅgaḥ, tadabhramācca śābdabhramaḥ /
ata eva yaṣṭīḥ praveśayetyaca lakṣaṇā nānārthe vinigamanā ca tayostātparyagrahamūlakatvāt /
yadi ca yatra vāstavaṃ tātparyaṃ taṃ śābdobodhayati tadā lakṣaṇānāṃ mukhyārthānvayānupapattyupayogo na syāt /
(Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,1, p. 111)
ata eva pacatītyukte 'yoktena svayaṃ smṛtena vā kalāyapadenopasthite kalāyaṃ pacatītyanvayabodho na bhavati tātparyāniścayāt /
na ca tātparyagrāhakasya prakaraṇādeḥ prāthamyādāvaśyakatvācca śabdasahakāritā na tu tātparyagrahasyeti vācyam /
teṣāmananugatatvena parasparavyabhicārādahetutvāt tātparyagrāhakatātvananugatānāmapi vyāpyatvāt dhūmādīnāmiva /
tacca tātparya vede nyāyagamyaṃ, yatra nyāyāt tātparyamavadhāryate sa eva vedārthaḥ, loke ca na kevalaṃ nyāyānusāri tātparyaṃ iti na nyāyagamyaṃ kintu pumabhiprāyaniyantritaṃ, nyāyāviṣaye 'pi puruṣecchāviṣaye pratītijanakatvāt puṃvacasāṃ /
vaktā ca parakīyavākyārthajñānotpādanecchāyā vākyamuccārayati /
sā cecchā yadi vaktruryathārthavākyārthajñānapūrvikā bhavati tadaiva paraṃ taduccāraṇasya tadaiva paraṃ taduccāraṇasya pumabhipretayathārthavākyārthajñānaparatvaṃ yathārthajñānecchāvyāpyaṃ nirvahatīti vakturyathārthavākyārthajñānavattāmavijñāya yathārthapratītiparatvaṃ jñātuṃ na śakyata iti prathamamāptavākyādvaktṛjñānānumānapūrvakamarthatathātvamanusandhāya yathārthapratītiparatvaṃ jñātuṃ na śakyata iti prathamamāptavākyādvaktṛjñānānumānapūrvakamarthatathātvamanusandhāya yathārthatātparyaniścayaḥ /
anumānaccedaṃ vākyaṃ bhramādi-viśiṣṭajñānayoranyatarajanyaṃ vākyatvāditi /
tato bhramādinirāse sati pariśeṣādvākyārthajñānānumānaṃ ayaṃ svaprayuktavākyārtharyathārthajñānavān bhramādyajanyavākyaprayoktutvāt ahamiva, na tvāptatvāt sādhyaviśeṣāt /
tata ete padārthā yathocitasaṃsargavantaḥ yathārthajñānaviṣayatvāt āptoktapadasmāritatvādvā manduktapadārthavaditi /
nanu vakturjñānaviśeṣo 'numeyaḥ jñāne cārtha eva viśeṣaḥ na tvarthādhīno 'nyaḥ arthenaiva viśeṣaḥ ityaupacāriko tṛtīyā tathāca vākyārthajñānaviśeṣo 'numeyaḥ tasya cāprasiddhyā na vyāptigrahaḥ /
ata evāsmin vākyarthe ayamabhrānta āpto veti jñātumaśakyamiti śabda eva tamaryaṃ bodhayediti cet, na, tātparyāvadhāraṇārthaṃ tvayāpyaśābdā eva saṃsargaviśeṣapratīteravaśyābhyupeyatvāt anyathā kva tātparyanirūpaṇaṃ / ata eva āptotkatvabhramādyanyatvanirūpaṇamapi sukaraṃ /
śābdantu saṃsargajñānaṃ prathamaṃ na bhavati jñānāntarantu bhavatyeva /
na caivaṃ śabdo na pramāṇaṃ tadarthasya prāgeva siddheriti vācyam /
tavāpi tulyatvāt /
nanu tathāpi kathamarthaviśeṣasiddhiḥ viśeṣeṇa vyāptyagrahāditi cet /
na /
yathā yo yatra pravarttate sa tajjñānātīti sāmānyatovyāptijñāne pākādau pravṛttidarśanāt pākaviṣayakāryatājñānānumānaṃ, yathā ceṣṭāviśeṣadarśanāt daśasaṃkhyābhiprāyamātrajñāne ghaṭe tacceṣṭādarśanāt ghaṭe daśatvajñānaṃ tathā sāmānyatovyāptyāvāpi viśeṣasiddhiḥ /
children.translated_text:
By this, the status of being a cause of invalid cognition (<s>apramā</s>) does not belong to error (<s>bhrama</s>), negligence (<s>pramāda</s>), desire to deceive (<s>vipralipsā</s>), and deficiency of the instrument (<s>karaṇāpaṭava</s>), since they mutually deviate [from each other], and since their combination is not a universal concomitant.
However, [the opponent argues:] the absence of being stated by a trustworthy person (<s>āptoktatvābhāva</s>) is the cause of invalid cognition, and the absence of that [i.e., its presence] is <s>āptoktatva</s> (being stated by a trustworthy person), which is the cause of valid cognition — this is refuted,
since <s>āptoktatva</s> cannot be known initially in the absence of an inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>).
Therefore, the absence of suspicion of deviation is the [real] reason [for validity]; and that [suspicion] is rooted in error and so forth in ordinary life — hence it is cut off through inference from trustworthy statement; and in the <s>Veda</s>, through the ascertainment of its being of personal authorship — this is rejected,
since the desired meaning of the sentence, being unprecedented (<s>apūrva</s>), is an unestablished <s>sādhya</s> (what is to be proven); and in the <s>Veda</s>, since the connection is established through the words being remembered as not composed by a defective person, the consequence of redundancy (<s>anuvādakatā</s>) follows.
Nor is the absence of defect [a cause of validity], because in cognition generated by the statement of a deluded or deceptive person, where non-contradiction has not been grasped by perception, that [absence of defect] does not exist.
If [the opponent says:] the presence of defect is the cause [of invalidity]; there the statement is simply mute [regarding validity], while practical activity is based on perception —
No, because that would be a denial of experience; because there is dispute about its being the cause [of invalidity]; and because even in the <s>Veda</s>, the consequence of redundancy would follow.
Moreover, if the absence of defect is the cause of valid cognition, then in invalid cognition, defect would be the cause; and if each [defect individually] were the cause, there would be deviation; if their combination were the cause, then invalid cognition would not arise from a single [defect]; if error and so forth were each individually a defect, there would be no common property; and if their combination were the cause, there would be the undesirable consequence that invalid cognition would not arise from a single one.
Therefore, by parsimony (<s>lāghava</s>), the having of purport regarding the true meaning (<s>yathārthatātparyakatva</s>) is what makes verbal testimony a valid means of knowledge; and that is the capacity to produce cognition of the true meaning of the sentence — common to both ordinary usage and the <s>Veda</s>; from the absence of that, invalid cognition [arises]; that itself is the defect. For no defect exists by its mere genus (<s>jāti</s>); rather, error and so forth have the status of defect because they obstruct that [capacity].
Therefore, even the statement of a deluded or deceptive person, and even the speech of a parrot, is a valid means of knowledge, because of [occasional] non-contradiction.
Therefore, when someone says 'There is a pot in the house' with the intention of a different pot, and where another pot is seen and one brings that, there the word is not a valid means of knowledge because it has a different purport; practical activity, however, is based on perception alone. And in the case of '[bring] the staffs (<s>yaṣṭīḥ</s>), [make them] enter,' when the primary meaning is understood, that purport (<s>tātparya</s>) is known and is useful. In the case of the instrument of known [meaning], the knowledge being useful [and yet] deviating, it is distinguished from <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion) and <s>śakti</s> (capacity) — otherwise, from a statement having a different purport, the understanding of a different connection would not arise, and there would be the undesirable consequence of the destruction of verbal fallacy (<s>śabdābhāsa</s>); and from the non-erroneousness of that, verbal error would [also be refuted].
Therefore, in 'make the staffs enter' also, secondary meaning (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>) and determination in a different sense — both of these are rooted in the apprehension of purport.
And if, wherever the actual purport exists, the word conveys that, then secondary meanings would have no use in the inapplicability of the primary meaning.
(Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,1, p. 111)
Therefore, when one says 'he cooks' (<s>pacati</s>), the understanding of the connection 'he cooks pulses' does not arise when the word 'pulse' is presented either by a conjunct [word] or by one's own memory, because of the uncertainty of purport.
Nor should it be said that the context and so forth, being the apprehenders of purport, because of their priority and necessity, are co-operators of the word, but not [that they are co-operators] of the apprehension of purport —
because those [contextual factors], not having a common property and mutually deviating, are not causes [of validity]; because even those that are not pervaded by the property of apprehending purport are [nonetheless] pervaded [by it], just like smoke and so forth.
And that purport, in the <s>Veda</s>, is ascertainable through reasoning (<s>nyāya</s>). Where purport is determined through reasoning, that alone is the meaning of the <s>Veda</s>. In ordinary usage, however, purport does not merely follow reasoning, and so is not ascertainable through reasoning alone; rather, it is governed by the speaker's intention, because the words of a person produce cognition even in the domain of the person's will, which is beyond reasoning.
And the speaker utters the sentence out of the desire to produce in another the cognition of the sentence-meaning.
If that desire is preceded by the speaker's cognition of the true sentence-meaning, then and only then does the utterance have the capacity for producing in the other a cognition of the true sentence-meaning intended by the speaker — [a capacity] pervaded by the desire for true cognition. Therefore, without knowing the speaker's possession of cognition of the true sentence-meaning, the capacity for producing true cognition cannot be known. Therefore, first from the trustworthy person's statement, through inference preceded by the inference of the speaker's cognition, having ascertained the correspondence of the object, the determination of purport regarding the true [meaning] is made.
If [one asks:] from inference — 'this sentence is produced by one of two cognitions, either one qualified by error and so forth, or [a valid one], because it is a sentence' —
then, upon the removal of error and so forth, by the method of residues (<s>pariśeṣa</s>), the inference of the speaker's cognition of the sentence-meaning [follows]: 'This [speaker] possesses cognition of the true meaning of the sentence he has uttered, because he is the utterer of a sentence not produced by error and so forth, like myself.' But [this is] not through <s>āptatva</s> (trustworthiness), because that is a specific form of the <s>sādhya</s> (what is to be proved).
Then [one infers:] these word-meanings are connected with the appropriate relations, because they are the objects of true cognition, or because they are remembered from words spoken by a trustworthy person, like the word-meanings spoken by me — and thus [verbal cognition follows].
Objection: The specific cognition of the speaker is to be inferred. And in cognition, the specific qualification is nothing but the object itself, not something else dependent on the object. The qualification is by the object itself — thus the third [case ending] is figurative. Accordingly, the specific sentence-meaning cognition is to be inferred, and since that is not established, there can be no apprehension of <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion).
Therefore, regarding this sentence-meaning, it is impossible to know whether this [speaker] is non-deluded or trustworthy — hence the word itself should convey that meaning — if so, No, because even you must necessarily accept non-verbal cognition of a specific connection for the purpose of determining purport; otherwise, where would purport be ascertained? Therefore, the determination of <s>āptoktatva</s> (trustworthiness) or the determination of being other than error and so forth is also easy.
However, verbal cognition of the connection does not arise initially; but another cognition [of the connection] does arise.
Nor should it be said that thus the word is not a valid means of knowledge because the object is already established previously —
because the same applies to you as well.
Objection: Even so, how is the specific object established, since <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion) with the specific [object] has not been apprehended?
No. Just as, when the general <s>vyāpti</s> is known — 'whoever engages in something possesses cognition of that' — from seeing engagement in cooking and so forth, there is the inference of cognition whose content is cooking; and just as, from seeing a specific gesture, when the cognition of merely the intention of the number ten is [known], from seeing that gesture in respect of a pot, there is the cognition of the number ten in respect of the pot — so too, even with a general <s>vyāpti</s>, the specific [object] is established.

yadvā idaṃ vākyaṃ sākāṅkṣaivatadarthaviṣayakaikajñānahetukaṃ āptoktatve sati etadarthapratipādakatvāt madvākyavat, tata ete padārthāḥ parasparasaṃsargavantaḥ sākāṅkatve satyekajñānaviṣayatvāt satyarajatajñānaviṣayavat, evaṃ vakturyathārthavākyārthajñāne 'numite prakaraṇādinā vaktrabhipretayathārthavākyārthajñāne 'numite prakaraṇādinā vaktrabhipretayathārthapratītiparatvajñānaṃ tato vedatulyatayā śabdādarthapratyaya ityanuvādaka śabdaḥ vaktṛjñānāvacchedakatayā saṃsargajñānānumānāt tadupajīvisaṃsargānumānādvā vākyārthasya prāgeva siddheḥ /
yattu saṃsargāgraho bhramaḥ tadabhāvaśca saṃsargagraha eveti bhamābhāve 'numīyamāne saṃsargajñānamevānumitaṃ ityāptatvānumānāntargatameva vaktṛjñānānumānaṃ na tu vaktṛjñānānumāne taliṅgaṃ iti /
tanna, bhramohi jñānadvayaṃ agṛhītabhedaṃ tadabhāvaśca gṛhītabhedajñānaṃ, na hi jñānābhāve suṣuptau bhramavyavahāraḥ, tato bhramābhāvaniścayānantaraṃ vaktṛjñānānumānaṃ, tarhi yādṛśaṃ liṅgaṃ tādṛśameva gamakamastviti /
children.translated_text:
Alternatively, this sentence, being syntactically expectant (<s>sākāṅkṣa</s>), is the cause of a single cognition whose content is the meaning of that [sentence], when it is spoken by a trustworthy person (<s>āptokta</s>), because it conveys that meaning — like my sentence. Then, these word-meanings possess mutual connection, because, being syntactically expectant, they are the content of a single cognition — like the contents of cognition of true silver. Thus, when the speaker's cognition of the true sentence-meaning is inferred through context and so forth, the cognition of the speaker's intended true sentence-meaning is produced; hence, by analogy with the <s>Veda</s>, the understanding of the object from the word follows — thus the word is redundant (<s>anuvādaka</s>), since the sentence-meaning is already established previously through the inference of [the speaker's] cognition as delimited by the speaker's cognition, or through the inference of connection dependent on that.
As for the objection that the non-apprehension of connection is error, and its absence is the apprehension of connection, so that when the absence of error is inferred, the cognition of connection itself is inferred — hence the inference of the speaker's cognition is included within the inference of trustworthiness and is not a separate inferential mark for the inference of the speaker's cognition —
that is not so, because error is a cognition of two [things] whose difference is not apprehended, and the absence of that is a cognition whose difference is apprehended. For in the absence of cognition, as in deep sleep, there is no application of the term 'error.' Therefore, subsequent to the ascertainment of the absence of error, the inference of the speaker's cognition [follows]. Well then, let whatever is the inferential mark be itself the indicator —

children.text:
atrocyate /
yathārthavākyarthadīparatvaṃ na jñātaṃ pramotpādakaṃ gauravāt vākyarthanirūpyatvena prathamaṃ jñātamaśakyatvācca tasyāpūrvatvāt /
children.translated_text:
Here it is stated:
The having of purport regarding the true sentence-meaning, when not known, does not produce valid cognition, because of its greater complexity (<s>gaurava</s>), since it must be ascertained through the sentence-meaning [first], and since it cannot be known initially, due to its unprecedented nature (<s>apūrvatva</s>).

yacca loke bhramādi nirāsānantaraṃ vaktṛjñānācchedakatayā tadagre svātantreṇa vā pumabhipretavākyārthajñāne tatpratītiparatvaṃ prakaraṇādinā jñāyata ityuktaṃ, tanna, vākyārthamajñātvā atrāyabhrānta iti jñātuṃ puruṣatvādvakturbhrama - pramādasambhavena prathamaṃ bhramādyajanyatvasya grahītumaśakyatvāt pravṛttisaṃvādāderjñānottarakālīnatvāt bhramādijanyavilakṣaṇatvena ca śabdasyājñānāt jñāne vā yādṛśoliṅgatvaṃ tasyaiva pratyāyakatvaṃ avyabhicārāt vede 'pi vākyārthamavijñāya tadyathārthapratītiparatvaṃ nyāyenāpi jñātumaśakyaṃ viṣayanirūpyatvāt pratīteḥ loke tātparyanirūpaṇārthamaśābdavākyārthapratīteḥ prathamaṃ tvayāpi svīkārāt /
anyathā vaktṛjñānānumānaṃ na syāt /
na ca lokavatmānāntarāttadavagamaḥ, vedārthasya tadaviṣayatvāt vedasya prathamaṃ mūkatvat, na ca nyāyasiddhe vedārthe mānāntarātātparyagrahaḥ, vedasyānuvādakatāpatteḥ śabdasyāpramāṇatvāpattervā /
ajñāte vākyarthe tarka - saṃśayayorapyabhāvāt ayaṃ padārtho 'parapadārthasaṃsṛṣṭo na veti saṃśaye tarke vā ekakoṭau saṃsarga upasthita iti cet, na, aniścite tātparyāniścayāt tayoragṛhītatāsaṃsargaviṣatvenāsadarthaviṣayakatvena vā vākyarthāviṣayatvācca /
anyathā lāke 'pi tābhyāmevopasthitiriti kiṃ vaktṛjñānānumānena /
vastutastu yadi yathārthatātparyakatvaṃ jñānaṃ śabdapramotpādakaṃ tadā loka-vedayāstādṛśapadasmāritatvena padārthasaṃsargānumitisambhavāt na śabdaḥ pramāṇaṃ syāt /
api ca puṃvākyasya doṣa-viśiṣṭajñānānyatarajanyatve 'numite pariśeṣāddoṣājanyatvaniścayadaśāyāṃ vedatulyā sāmāgrī puṃvākye 'pi vṛtteti tata evārthaniścayāt vedavattasyāpi prāmāṇyaṃ, anumitānumānasya vyāptismṛtyādivilambitatvāt /
etenābādhitārthaparatvaṃ loke vede ca pramāpakaṃ loke vākyartho bādhito 'pi dṛṣṭa iti śrotuḥ pramāṇāvatāraṃ vinā na bādhābhāvaniścayaḥ sa ca kvacicchṛturindriyeṇa kvacidvakturāptatvānumānena vede tu nyāyāttanniścayaḥ tadarthasya pramāṇāntarāviṣayatvāt na tatra śaṅketi sāmāgrībheda iti nirastaṃ /
prathamabhramādyabhāvasyāptasya vā niścetumaśakyatvāt vedasyānuvādakatāpatteśca /
children.translated_text:
And what has been said — that in ordinary usage, after the removal of error and the like, through the cessation of the speaker's cognition or independently thereafter, in the cognition of the sentence-meaning intended by the person, the orientation [of the sentence] toward that cognition is known through context and the like — that is not correct. Because without knowing the sentence-meaning, one cannot know "this person has erred here," since due to the person-nature of the speaker there is the possibility of error and carelessness, and thus the quality of not being produced by error and the like cannot be grasped first. Because [knowledge of] conformity with successful activity and the like arises only after the cognition. And because verbal testimony is not known as being of a different character from what is produced by error and the like. Or [if you say that] whatever quality serves as a mark (<s>liṅga</s>) in the cognition, that very quality is what produces the inferential knowledge — [we respond:] because of non-deviation. In the <s>Vedas</s> too, without knowing the sentence-meaning, its orientation toward true cognition cannot be known even through reasoning, because cognition is determined by its object. Because even you accept that in ordinary usage, for determining the purport, the cognition of the sentence-meaning is non-verbal and comes first.
Otherwise the inference of the speaker's cognition would not be possible.
Nor is the understanding of that [Vedic meaning] from another means of knowledge, as in ordinary usage, because the meaning of the <s>Vedas</s> is not the object of that [other means of knowledge], since the <s>Veda</s> is initially "mute" [i.e., not yet understood]. Nor is the purport grasped from another means of knowledge when the Vedic meaning is established through reasoning, because that would reduce the <s>Veda</s> to being merely repetitive, or because verbal testimony would cease to be a valid means of knowledge.
Because when the sentence-meaning is not known, there is no basis even for reasoning or doubt. If [it is argued that] in the doubt or reasoning "this word-meaning is combined with that other word-meaning or not," the connection is presented with respect to one alternative — no, because when [the purport] is not ascertained, the purport is not ascertained either, since those [reasoning and doubt] have as their object a connection that is not grasped, or have a non-existent object, and [in any case] do not have the sentence-meaning as their object.
Otherwise, even in ordinary usage the presentation would be just through those two [reasoning and doubt], so what need for the inference of the speaker's cognition?
In truth, if the cognition of correct purport is what produces valid verbal knowledge, then in both ordinary and Vedic usage, since the inference of the connection of word-meanings is possible through the recollection of such words, verbal testimony would not be an independent means of knowledge.
Moreover, when it is inferred that a human statement is produced either by a defect-possessing cognition or by [a veridical one], then by elimination, at the stage of ascertaining that it is not produced by a defect, the same causal complex that exists in the <s>Veda</s> is also present in human statements, and from that alone the meaning would be ascertained; hence like the <s>Veda</s>, human statements too would have validity, since the inference of inferred [validity] is delayed by dependence on the recollection of pervasion and the like.
By this, [the view that] "the orientation toward an un-sublated meaning is what validates, in ordinary and Vedic usage alike; in ordinary usage the sentence-meaning is also seen to be sublated; hence for the hearer, without the operation of another means of knowledge, there is no ascertainment of non-sublation; and that [ascertainment] is sometimes through the hearer's sense-perception, sometimes through inference of the speaker's trustworthiness, but in the <s>Veda</s> it is through reasoning — since the Vedic meaning is not the object of other means of knowledge, there is no doubt there — thus there is a difference in the causal complex" — is refuted.
Because first establishing the absence of error and the like, or the trustworthiness [of the speaker], cannot be done; and because of the consequence that the <s>Veda</s> becomes merely repetitive.

children.text:
tasmāt bhramādyajanyatvaṃ āptokatvaṃ abādhitārthakatvaṃ yathārthatātparyakatvaṃ nirastavyabhicāraśaṅkatvaṃ anyadvā vyabhicārivyāvṛttaṃ yatpramotpādakaṃ tat svarūpasat na jñātaṃ /
anyathā tādṛśasya vākyārthāvyabhicāritayā tādṛśapadasmāritatvāt liṅgādeva saṃsargasiddhiḥ syāditi jitaṃ vaiśiṣikaiḥ /
atha vyavahārānumitavyavaharttṛkāryānvitajñāne upasthitatvena padānāṃ hetutvagrahādanvitābhidhāyakatvaṃ tadānīṃ śabdasya liṅgatvenonupasthiteriti cet /
na /
liṅgābhāvenaiva śabdādanvitajñānopapatternākāṅkṣādimacchabdena kāraṇatā gauravāt / śabdasya liṅgatvaṃ sambhavadapi bālena na jñātamiti cet, so 'yaṃ bālasya doṣo na vastuna ityādi vakṣyate /
kiñcaivaṃ lokavadvede 'pi anuvādakatā syāt /
etena vākyārthatātparyagrāhakānumānāt tātparyāvacchedakatayā tadupajīvino 'numānāt svātantreṇa vākyārthasiddherna śabdaḥ pramāṇamiti vaiśeṣikamatapāstam /
yathārthatātparyagrahasya vākyārthabodhāhetutvāt /
yattu jñāyamānakaraṇe iti, tanna, yathārthatātparyakatvādeḥ prathamaṃ jñātumaśakyatvenānumānasya bādhitatvāt vyāptyasiddheśca /
na hi vyāptiḥ śabdaśaktiśca kāraṇaṃ, kintu taddhīḥ, atīte 'numitidarśanāt /
apabhraṃśādau śaktibhramādanvayabodhācca /
na ca saivāpayujyata iti sādhyaṃ, prathamaṃ tadasambhavāt /
tasmāt yat arthāvyabhicāritvena jñātaṃ kāraṇaṃ tatra vyabhicārivailakṣaṇyajñānamupayujanyate anyathā śabdasyārthavyabhicāritayā jñātasya jñāpakatve liṅgatāpattervajjalepāyamānatvāt /
syādetadanāptokte bādhakenārthābhāvadarśanāt ākāṅkṣādimadvākyatvena sadarthakaṃ bādhitārthakaṃ veti saṃśayānna tāvanmātrādarthaniścayaḥ, na hi saṃśāyakameva niścāyakaṃ, ityadhikamapekṣaṇīyamiti cet /
children.translated_text:
Therefore, the quality of not being produced by error and the like, the quality of being spoken by a trustworthy person, the quality of having an un-sublated meaning, the quality of having a correct purport, the quality of having the suspicion of deviation removed, or any other [quality] distinguished from what deviates — whatever produces valid cognition, that [quality] exists in its own form but is not [previously] known.
Otherwise, since such [a quality], through its non-deviation from the sentence-meaning, serves as a mark through the recollection of such words, the connection [of word-meanings] would be established from the mark alone — thus the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> would triumph.
If [it is argued:] from the behavior [of the speaker] as inferred, the cognition endowed with action of the behaving agent, and through [the word-meanings] being presented [in that cognition], the words are grasped as causes [of knowledge] — hence they have the power of <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> (designating connected meanings) — [we respond:] at that time verbal testimony would not function as a separate [means of knowledge] since it would be subsumed under inference.
No.
Because through the very absence of the inferential mark, the arising of <s>anvita</s> (connected) cognition from verbal testimony is explained, and the causality of a sentence possessing expectancy and the like is preferred [over inference] due to parsimony. If [one argues:] the word's being an inferential mark, though possible, is not known by a child — [we respond:] that is the child's deficiency, not of reality itself — this will be stated [later].
Moreover, in this way, the <s>Veda</s> too, like ordinary usage, would become merely repetitive.
By this, the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> view that verbal testimony is not [an independent] means of knowledge — because the sentence-meaning is established either from the inference that grasps the purport, or from inference that is dependent upon that [purport-grasping inference] as the determinant of purport, or independently — is refuted.
Because the grasp of correct purport is not a cause of verbal understanding.
As for [the objection] "that which is being known as the instrument" — that is not correct, because the inference is sublated since the quality of having a correct purport and the like cannot be grasped first, and because the pervasion is not established.
For the cause is not the pervasion and the verbal power, but rather the cognition of these, as inference is observed [to function] even regarding past [events].
And because connected understanding arises from an erroneous [cognition of] verbal power, as in the case of corrupted words.
Nor is [the objection] "that very [verbal power] is what is to be proved" [valid], because that [i.e., the verbal power being inferred first] is impossible at the beginning.
Therefore, whatever is known as a cause through non-deviation from the meaning, there the knowledge of dissimilarity from what deviates is employed; otherwise, since verbal testimony known as deviating from meaning would [still] be informative, there would be the consequence of it being an inferential mark — and this would be nothing but idle talk.
[Objection:] This may be so — in the case of statements by untrustworthy persons, from seeing the absence of the meaning through a sublating cognition, there arises the doubt "does this sentence possessing expectancy and the like have a real meaning or a sublated meaning?" — and from that doubt alone there is no ascertainment of meaning. For what produces doubt does not produce certainty; hence something additional must be sought.

children.text:
na / arthasaṃśayasya tadbādhasaṃśayasya vā pramāṇāpratibandhakatvāt /
vahni-tadbādhayoḥ saṃśaye 'pi pratyakṣānumānādinā arthaniścayāt anyathā pramāṇamātrocchedaḥ, tatpūrvamartha-tadbādhasaṃśayāt /
vināpyarthaṃ vākyaracanā sambhatyata etasyāyamartho na vā, etatsadarthakaṃ na vā, etajjanyajñānaṃ sadviṣayakaṃ na veti saṃśayasyārthāvagamottarakālīnatvācca /
tasmādāptoktatvaṃ bhramādyajanyatvaṃ abādhitārthakatvaṃ yathārthavākyārthapratītiparatvaṃ vā jñātaṃ anugatamapi na hetuḥ prathamaṃ grahītumaśakyatvāt, kintu tātparyagrāhakatvenābhimatānāṃ nyāyajanyajñāna-prakaraṇādīnāmanyatarat tātparyavyāpyatvenānugataṃ, tathākāṅkṣāsattiniścayaḥ, tadviparyaye saṃśaye ca śābdajñānābhāvāt /
yogyatāyāśca jñānamatraṃ hetuḥ tatsaṃśaye viparyaye pramāyāñca vākyārthajñānāt , tathā vibhaktyādisamabhivyāharaḥ sambhūyoccāraṇañca śābdajñānamātre kāraṇāni nānārthe śrliṣṭe cānekopasthitāvapi prakaraṇādivaśādekamarthamādayānvayabodhaḥ /
lakṣaṇā ca na tātparyānupapattyā kintvanvayānupapattyaiva prakaraṇādbhojanaprajanakatvenāvagatapraveśanasya yaṣṭyanvayānupapatteḥ /
ajahatsvārthāyāṃ prakaraṇādeva chatri taditarasya yāntītyanena gamanakarttṛtvamavagataṃ tadanvayānupapatticchatrimātre, pacatītyasya kalāyamityanyoktena samaṃ nārthapratyākatvaṃ samabhivyāhārābhāvāt, tavāpi tasya tātparyagrāhakatvāt sahoccaritānāṃ sambhūyārthapratyāyakatvasya vyutpattisiddhatvāt /
children.translated_text:
No. Because the doubt about the meaning, or the doubt about its sublation, does not obstruct the means of valid knowledge.
Even when there is doubt about fire and its sublation, the meaning is ascertained through perception, inference, and the like. Otherwise, all means of knowledge would be destroyed, since there would be prior doubt about the meaning and its sublation.
And because a sentence-construction is possible even without [a corresponding real] meaning — "does this have this meaning or not," "is this meaningful or not," "is the cognition produced by this veridical or not" — such doubt arises only after the apprehension of the meaning.
Therefore, the quality of being spoken by a trustworthy person, or not being produced by error and the like, or having an un-sublated meaning, or the orientation toward true sentence-meaning cognition — even when known and common [to all cases], is not the cause [of verbal understanding], because it cannot be grasped first. Rather, one of the things held to be purport-revealers — cognition produced by reasoning, context, and the like — is what pervades the purport and is the common [cause]. Likewise, the ascertainment of expectancy, fitness, and contiguity [is a cause], because in their absence, or when there is doubt or the opposite, verbal cognition does not arise.
The knowledge of <s>yogyatā</s> (semantic fitness) alone is the cause, because when there is doubt, opposition, or even [the production of] valid cognition regarding it, there is [still] verbal understanding of the sentence-meaning. Likewise, the co-occurrence of case-endings and the like, and the simultaneous utterance [of words], are causes of verbal cognition in general. And when multiple [meanings] are presented even in the case of ambiguous or conjoined [words], the connected understanding (<s>anvayabodha</s>) takes one meaning based on context and the like.
And secondary signification (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>) [arises] not from the impossibility of purport but from the impossibility of syntactic connection — because when "entering" has been understood through context as having the purpose of feeding, the syntactic connection with "stick" is impossible.
In <s>ajahatsvārthā</s> [lakṣaṇā] (non-abandoning secondary signification), through context alone, by [the sentence] "the umbrellas go" — the agency of going is understood of the umbrella-bearers; the impossibility of syntactic connection is with respect to the umbrella alone. The sentence "he cooks" does not have the same capacity to convey meaning as [the word] "pulses" uttered by another, due to the absence of co-occurrence (<s>samabhivyāhāra</s>). Even for you, that [context] is a revealer of purport, since the capacity of co-uttered words to jointly convey meaning is established through linguistic convention.

children.text:
anye tu nānārthe lakṣaṇāyāñca niyatopasthityarthaṃ padārthe tātparyagrahāpekṣā tena vinā tadabhāvāt na vākyārthe, tadajñāne 'pi prakaraṇādinā saindhavapadaṃ turagaparaṃ kākapadaṃ upaghātakaparamiti hi pratiyanti /
anyatrānvayapratiyogyupasthitiḥ tātparyagrahaṃ vinaiveti na tadapekṣā /
vastutastu itarapadasya itarapadārthasaṃsargajñānaparatvaṃ tātparyaṃ tacca vede nyāyādavadhāryate loke nyāyāt prakaraṇādervā /
ata eva śābdabodhe nāniyatahetukatvaṃ taccetarapadārthasaṃsargajñānaṃ vākyarthajñānameveti sāmānyakāreṇa tatparatvagrahaḥ heturna tu viśiṣya, tacca svaparapadārthayoḥ saṃsargānubhavajananaṃ vinā anupapannamiti padāni sambhūya janayanti, ata eva nānārthe vinigamanā, tadanupapattireva lakṣaṇābījaṃ tadabhāvādeva pacatipade na smṛtakalāyānvayabodha iti siddhaṃ śabdasya pramāṇāntaratvaṃ /
tasya ca nirākāṅkṣādau saṃsargajñānājanakatvāt āṅkṣādikaṃ sahakārīti /
children.translated_text:
Others, however, [argue:] in the case of ambiguity and secondary signification, the expectation of purport-grasp is for the purpose of the presentation of the specific word-meaning; without that, there would be no [specific word-meaning presentation]; but not in the case of the sentence-meaning, because even without knowledge of that [purport], through context and the like, the word <s>saindhava</s> is understood as referring to a horse, and the word <s>kākapada</s> is understood as meaning "a harmful agent" — for people do understand [these meanings] thus.
Elsewhere, the presentation of the counterpart of the syntactic connection [occurs] without the grasp of purport — hence there is no dependence on it.
In truth, the purport is the orientation of one word toward the cognition of the connection of another word's meaning [with its own] — and that [purport] is ascertained in the <s>Veda</s> through reasoning, and in ordinary usage through reasoning or context and the like.
For this very reason, verbal understanding has no non-fixed cause. That [purport], being the cognition of the connection of one word's meaning with another, is indeed the sentence-meaning cognition itself. Hence the grasp of its orientation in a general way is the cause, not [the grasp of orientation] with respect to a specific [meaning]. And that [joint causation] is impossible without generating the experience of connection between one's own and the other word's meanings — hence words jointly produce [understanding]. For this very reason, there is resolution of ambiguity. The impossibility of that [syntactic connection] alone is the seed of secondary signification; due to the absence of that [impossibility alone], in the word "he cooks" there is no connected understanding with the remembered "pulses." Thus the independence of verbal testimony as a separate means of knowledge is established.
And since [the sentence] does not produce the cognition of connection when [there is] absence of expectancy and the like, expectancy and the like are the auxiliary causes.
