children.text: ucchanna-pracchannavādaḥ
children.translated_text: The doctrine of destroyed and concealed [Vedic branches] (<s>ucchanna-pracchannavāda</s>)

children.text:
tathāpi paratantrapuraṣaparamparādhīnatayā pravāhāvicchedameva nityatvaṃ brūmaḥ iti cet, na, smṛtyācārānumitānāṃ śākhānāmucchedadarśanāt /
syādetat, vivādapadamapūrvavodhikā smṛtiḥ smṛtyarthānubhavajanakavedamūlā avigīta-mahājanaparigṛhītasmṛtitvāt pratyakṣavedamūlakasmṛtivat, vedamūlakatvañca vedajanyānubhavajanyatvaṃ jñānādvārā jñāyamānasyaiva vedasya smṛtihetutayānumānaṃ, kuvindasyeva jñānādivyavahitasya paṭe, na tu kāraṇākāraṇatā, vede satyeva tatpratisandhāne smṛtipraṇayanāt, vedārthasmṛtitā ca prasiddhisiddhā, smṛtyarthaśca smṛtita eva upasthitaḥ /
na ca smṛtyarthabodhakavedānumāne smṛtyartharūpavedārthasya viṣayatvāt vedo 'nuvādakaḥ jñānāntaropanītasya viśeṣaṇatvena viśiṣṭabuddhisambhavāt, pākakṛtau mānasapratyakṣāyāṃ pākasya
children.translated_text:
[Objection:] 'Even so, we mean by eternality (<s>nityatva</s>) merely the unbroken continuity of the stream [of transmission], being dependent on a succession of persons who are themselves dependent [on others].' No — because we observe the destruction of [Vedic] branches (<s>śākhā</s>) that are inferred from <s>smṛti</s> texts and customary practices.
[Objection:] It may be argued thus: the point at issue is whether <s>smṛti</s> (traditional law), which produces cognition of something unprecedented (<s>apūrva</s>), has the <s>Veda</s> as its source — [specifically] the <s>Veda</s> that generates the experience of the meaning of <s>smṛti</s>. [We say yes,] because it is a <s>smṛti</s> accepted by undisputed great authorities, like a <s>smṛti</s> that has a directly known <s>Veda</s> as its source. And 'having the <s>Veda</s> as its source' means 'being produced by an experience produced by the <s>Veda</s>' — the inference [of a Vedic source] is possible because the <s>Veda</s> that is known through cognition serves as the cause of <s>smṛti</s>; just as a weaver [is the cause] of cloth even though separated [from it] by cognition and other [intermediate causes]. [This is] not [mere] non-causation-of-a-cause, because <s>smṛti</s> is composed only when the <s>Veda</s> exists and its content is recalled. And the character of [<s>smṛti</s>] as recollecting Vedic meaning is established through common knowledge; and the meaning of <s>smṛti</s> is presented through <s>smṛti</s> alone.

children.text:
saṃjñāsaṃjñijñāne saṃjñāyājñānayathārthatve tadanuvyavasāye bhramaviṣayasyeva, anyathā bhrānta-bhrāntijñasaṅkarāpattiḥ na tu śabdārtho 'numānasya viṣayaḥ tasyāsiddhatvenājanakatā smṛtyavyāpakatvāt /
sa ca vedo nityamanumeya evānumitādevārthamavadhārya smṛtipraṇayanasambhavāt /
nanvāsaṃsāramapaṭhitasya na vedatvaṃ utpattito 'bhivyaktito mauniśrlokavadabhiprāyato vānupūrvīhīnavarṇamātrasya nirarthakatvāt / jñānajanakasamabhivyāhārasyānekatve viśeṣānanumānāñceti cet /
na /
smṛtyarthajñāpakatvenaiva jñātasya vedasya smṛtyarthānubhāvakatvāt /
children.translated_text:
In the knowledge of the name (<s>saṃjñā</s>) and the named (<s>saṃjñin</s>), when there is error regarding the name, in the subsequent determination (<s>anuvyavasāya</s>) [of that cognition, the named is ascertained] just as in [the case of] the object of an erroneous cognition — otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of a confusion between the deluded person and the knower of the delusion. But the meaning of the word is not the object of inference, because due to its being unestablished [through inference alone], it is non-productive [of knowledge], since it does not pervade <s>smṛti</s>.
And that <s>Veda</s> is always inferable — because it is possible to compose <s>smṛti</s> after ascertaining [Vedic] meaning through inference alone.
[Objection:] But what has not been recited since beginningless <s>saṃsāra</s> does not have the character of being <s>Veda</s> — whether from the standpoint of origination, manifestation, or [the author's] intention — because mere phonemes lacking [proper] sequence are meaningless, like the verses of a sage who is silent (<s>mauni</s>). And because when the co-utterance (<s>samabhivyāhāra</s>) that produces knowledge is multiple, the specific [Vedic identity] cannot be inferred.
No.
Because the <s>Veda</s>, known precisely through its capacity to convey the meaning of <s>smṛti</s>, [thereby] has the capacity to produce experience of the meaning of <s>smṛti</s>.

children.text: (Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,1, p. 475)
children.translated_text: [page 475]

children.text:
na hi śābdabodhe niyatapadānupūrvī hetuḥ, vyabhicārāt /
padasya varṇāviśeṣānupūrvīniyame 'pi tattadvarṇānupūrvīkapadaviśeṣatvena hetutvaṃ hasta-karādipadānāṃ pratyekaṃ vyabhicārāt /
kintvavyabhicāritadarthajñāpakatvena jñātasya lāghavādāvaśyakatvācca, tadarthajñāpakatvajñānārthameva kvacidvarṇakramasvaraviśeṣāṇāmupayogaḥ /
ata eva varṇalopādau kuśamānayeti sakārasandehe lipāvuccāraṇe vā hasta-karasandehe 'pi vākyārthabodhaḥ /
nanu kramikapadavattvaṃ vākyatvam /
na cātra padakramaḥ, anuccāryamāṇatayoccāraṇādhīnasya yugapadanumīyamānatayā budyadhīnasya vā tasyābhāvāditi cet, na hi kramikapadavattvaṃ vākyatvaṃ, gaurava ityādāvabhāvāt kintu viśiṣṭārthaparaśabdatvaṃ taccātrāpyastyeva /
athānuccāryamāṇasya na vākyatvaṃ na vā arthānubhāvakatvamiti cet, na, lipyanumitānāmapi vākyatvāt arthabodhakatvācca, lipitulyā ca smṛtiḥ /
kiñca vākyamuccāryate na tūccāraṇādvākyatvaṃ, anyathā vākyamuccārayetyatrānanvayāpattiḥ, anuccāritamauniśrlokaśca vākyaṃ na syāduccāraṇadaśāyāñca vākyatve vākyasyāsattvameva syāt ekadā tāvatpadānāṃ uccāraṇābhāvāt /
children.translated_text:
A fixed word-order (<s>padānupūrvī</s>) is not the cause of verbal cognition (<s>śābdabodha</s>), because of deviation (<s>vyabhicāra</s>).
Even when there is a fixed order among the undifferentiated phonemes of a word, the causal efficacy belongs to [the word] as a particular word having the sequence of those particular phonemes — [but this is refuted] because of deviation in each of the words like <s>hasta</s> and <s>kara</s> [which are synonyms with different phoneme sequences].
Rather, [the cause is] the word as known through its invariable capacity to convey that meaning, and because of the necessity [of such knowledge] due to parsimony (<s>lāghava</s>). The usefulness of specific phoneme-sequences, accents (<s>svara</s>), etc. is only for the purpose of knowing [the word's] capacity to convey that meaning.
For this very reason, even when there is elision of phonemes (<s>varṇalopa</s>) etc. — as in [the command] 'bring <s>kuśa</s> [grass]' where there is doubt about the <s>sa</s>-phoneme in writing or pronunciation, or even when there is doubt between <s>hasta</s> and <s>kara</s> — verbal cognition of the sentence-meaning occurs.
[Objection:] Sentence-hood (<s>vākyatva</s>) consists in possessing words in sequence.
But here there is no word-order, because [the Veda], not being uttered, [has its sequence] dependent on utterance, or being simultaneously inferred, [has its sequence] dependent on cognition — [therefore] it is absent. No — 'possessing words in sequence' is not sentence-hood, because it is absent in [the single word] <s>gaurava</s> ('heaviness') and the like [which can express a complete meaning]. Rather, [sentence-hood is] being a word directed toward a qualified meaning (<s>viśiṣṭārtha</s>) — and that exists here as well.
[Objection:] What is not uttered has neither sentence-hood nor the capacity to produce cognition of meaning. No — because even [sentences] inferred from written script (<s>lipi</s>) have sentence-hood and the capacity to produce cognition of meaning; and <s>smṛti</s> (memory/recollection) is analogous to written script.
Furthermore, a sentence is uttered, but sentence-hood does not arise from utterance — otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of a failure of construal in [the expression] 'utter the sentence'; and the unspoken verse of a silent sage (<s>mauni</s>) would not be a sentence; and if sentence-hood [existed only] at the time of utterance, a sentence would never exist at all, because all the words are never uttered simultaneously.

children.text: (Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,1, p. 478)
children.translated_text: [page 478]

children.text:
na ca kṛta-kriyamāṇa-kariṣyamāṇoccāraṇasya vākyatvaṃ, samudāye pratyekasyābhāvāt /
tasmādarthaviśeṣajñāpakatvenaiva jñātādarthaviśeṣadhīḥ /
ata evāsti vahniliṅgamitiśabdāt pratīteḥ dhūme vahneranumānaṃ, na tu tadarthajñāpakatvena jñātāt padādarthajñānamātraṃ syāt na tu saṃsargadhīḥ, ghaṭaḥ karmatvamānayanaṃ bhāvanā tadbodhakamiti jñāne 'pi ghaṭamānayetivākyādivānvayabodhābhāvāt /
evañcānvayaprakārakarmatvādyupasthāpakavibhaktyādimatpadaviśeṣasya tadutthāpitākāṅkṣādeśca jñānaṃ vākyārthadīheturato na tairvinā jñāpakatvamātreṇa jñātādarthadhīḥ, hasta-karādisandehe kuśamānayetyādau vibhaktyādijñānādeva vākyārthānubhava iti, maivaṃ, na hi tattadvibhaktyādimatpadaviśeṣatvena vākyārthadhīhetutvaṃ, ananugamāt, kintu ghaṭaḥ karmatvamityādyanvayavirodhipadājanyapadārthopasthitistathā sā cehāpyasti /
vastutastu nānāpadāt padārthopasthityanantaraṃ vākyārthabodhe tathaiva sāmāgrī anumitavedādvākyārthānubhave vilakṣaṇaiva sā smṛtyarthajñāpakatvenaiva jñātasya smṛtyarthānubhāvakatvāt dharmigrāhakapramāṇena tasya tathaiva siddhatvāt /
taveśvarasyevāśarīrasya kartṛtve /
ata eva varṇapada vibhaktyādiviśeṣaghaṭitatvenājñātasyākhaṇḍasya sakhaṇḍasya vā vākyārthānubhāvakatvāt padārthasthanīyastasya vākyārthastatra varṇasamūhaḥ padaṃ padasamūhovākyamityatrāpi tato grahaḥ pramāṇaśabdatvamātreṇa tasya siddheḥ anyathā kḷptahetuṃ vinā so 'nubhāvaka ityādau tadasiddhāvāśrayāsiddhiḥ siddhau vā bādhaḥ tena vinaiva sarvānupapattiṃ paribhūya tadanubhāvakatvasya dharmigrāhakamānasiddhatvāt /
ata eva kvacit stuti-nindābhyāṃ kalpitavidhi-niṣedhakavedārthamadhigatya pravṛtti-nivṛttī /
anyathā vidhi-niṣedakānāṃ nānāprakārakatvena vibhaktyādiviśeṣavat padasyānumātumaśakyatvāt na tator'thadhīḥ syāt /
tathāpi vaktṛjñānānumānānantaramivānumitānumānādeva vākyārthasiddhalaukikavākyavadvedasyānuvādakatvaṃ syāditi cet, na, dharmigrāhakamānena smṛtyarthajñāpakatayā jñātāt sambhūtasāmagrīkatvenābhāvāt, anumānasya vyāptyādijñānāpekṣitatvena vilambitatvāt /
na ca vedasyāpi yogyatādijñānāpekṣitatayā vilambaḥ, tannirapekṣabodhakasyaiva dharmigrāhakamānasiddhatvāt yogyatādi viśiṣṭasyaivānumānādvā, evaṃ maṅgalācārasyāvigītaśiṣṭācāratvena kartavyatāmanumāya sā kartavyatā vedabodhitā alaukikāvigītaśiṣṭācārakartavyatātvāditi tadbodhakatvenānumitavedāt kartavyatādhīstataḥ pravṛttiḥ /
nanu sa ācārovedabodhitakartavyatākaḥ tādṛśācāratvādityanumitavedāt tatkartavyatādhīḥ, vibhaktyādikavinānumitavedāt tatkartavyatājñānābhāvāt maṅgalamācaredityevaṃrūpasya ca vedasya nānumānaṃ tathā vyāptyabhāvāt, tasmāt tasya kartavyatāmanumānaya tadbodhakavedānumānaṃ, prathamaṃ kartavyatājñāne 'pi vedānumānaṃ avinābhāvāt /
na ca tata eva pratyakṣavedānumānaṃ, pratyakṣatve ucchedānupapatteḥ śākhāntaravat /
children.translated_text: And it is not the case that sentence-hood belongs to what has been uttered, is being uttered, and will be uttered [taken together], because each is absent in the aggregate. Therefore, it is from being understood as a conveyor of a particular meaning that the cognition of a particular meaning [arises] from what is known. For this very reason, from the sentence 'there is the inferential mark of fire,' when smoke is cognized, there is inference of fire from smoke; but it is not the case that from a word known merely as conveying that meaning, there would be only cognition of the word-referent but not cognition of the connection—because even when there is knowledge of 'pot,' 'object-hood,' 'bringing,' 'injunction,' and 'what conveys those,' there is no co-occurrence cognition as from the sentence 'bring the pot.' Thus, the cognition of a specific word possessing case-endings and the like that present the co-occurrence-qualifier such as object-hood, and the cognition of <s>ākāṅkṣā</s> (expectancy) arising from that, are causes of sentence-meaning cognition; hence without those, there is no cognition of meaning merely from being a conveyor from what is known. In cases of doubt about hand versus arm and so on, sentence-meaning cognition arises from the sentence 'bring the <s>kuśa</s> grass' through the cognition of the case-ending alone. Do not say so—for it is not the case that being a specific word possessing particular case-endings is the cause of sentence-meaning cognition, because there is no uniformity; rather, it is the presentation of the word-referent not produced by a word opposing co-occurrence, such as 'pot,' 'object-hood,' and so on—and that exists here too. In reality, the causal complex for sentence-meaning cognition following the presentation of word-referents from various words is of one kind, while the causal complex for sentence-meaning cognition from an inferred Veda is of a different kind altogether—because it produces the experience of the meaning of a <s>smṛti</s> merely by being a conveyor of the meaning of the <s>smṛti</s> from which it is known, since that is established precisely so by the <s>pramāṇa</s> grasping the property-bearer—like the authorship of your God who is bodiless. For this very reason, because what is unknown—whether whole or partitioned—that is constituted by specific phonemes, words, case-endings, and the like, can produce sentence-meaning cognition, the word-referent-like entity's sentence-meaning is grasped from the aggregate of phonemes as a word, and the aggregate of words as a sentence—and from that too the grasp [occurs], since it is established merely by the fact of being a means of valid cognition. Otherwise, without an established cause, saying 'it is a producer' would involve the fallacy of unestablished substratum; or if established, there would be defeat. Without that [the specific Vedic text], by overriding all difficulties, the producer-hood is established by the <s>pramāṇa</s> grasping the property-bearer. For this very reason, in some cases, having understood the Vedic meaning consisting of injunctions and prohibitions postulated through praise and censure, [people] engage in action or refrain from action. Otherwise, since injunctions and prohibitions, being of diverse forms like specific case-endings, cannot be inferred as a specific word, there would be no cognition of their meaning. Even so, if [one says] just as after inferring the speaker's cognition, the sentence-meaning is established from the inferred inference itself—and so the Veda, like a worldly sentence, would be merely corroborative—no, because the causal complex that arises from what is known as a conveyor of the meaning of <s>smṛti</s> through the <s>pramāṇa</s> grasping the property-bearer is of this kind, and [such a causal complex] is absent [for mere inference], since inference requires knowledge of <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion) and so on and is therefore delayed. And it is not the case that the Veda too is delayed by requiring knowledge of <s>yogyatā</s> (fitness) and so on, because what produces cognition without depending on that is established by the <s>pramāṇa</s> grasping the property-bearer—or else it is inferred as qualified by <s>yogyatā</s> and the like. Similarly, having inferred through the uncontradicted practice of good people that auspicious conduct is obligatory, that obligatoriness is conveyed by the Veda—because it has the character of being uncontradicted good-people's obligatoriness that is extra-worldly—and from the Veda inferred as conveying that, the cognition of obligatoriness [arises], and from that, action. Objection: that practice has obligatoriness conveyed by the Veda; from the Veda inferred through being such a practice, the cognition of that obligatoriness [arises], since without case-endings and the like, from the inferred Veda alone there is no cognition of that obligatoriness; and a Veda of the form 'one should perform the auspicious rite' is not inferred—because there is no such <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion). Therefore, having inferred its obligatoriness, the inference of the Veda conveying it [follows]; even when there is prior cognition of obligatoriness, the Vedic inference [follows] due to invariable concomitance. And it is not the case that from that alone a directly perceived Veda is inferred, because if directly perceived, loss would be inexplicable—like [the loss of] other Vedic branches.

children.text: (Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,1, p. 487)

children.text: yattu aṣṭakāḥ kartavyāḥ kāryā aṣṭakā ityevaṃ rūpameva vākyamanumeyaṃ upasthitatvāt, evañca tatraivārthe pratipuruṣamanyānyavedānumānaṃ, pratyakṣatve ucchedanupapatteḥ śākhāntaravat /
children.translated_text: As for [the view] that the specific sentence-form 'the <s>aṣṭakā</s> rites are to be performed, the <s>aṣṭakā</s> rites are obligatory' is what is inferred—because it is what is presented [to the mind]; and thus for the very same meaning, different Vedic texts are inferred for each person; directly perceived [Veda] being impossible since loss [of a branch] would be inexplicable—like other [lost] Vedic branches.

children.text:
yattu aṣṭakāḥ kartavyāḥ kāryā aṣṭakā ityevaṃ rūpameva vākyamanumeyaṃ upasthitatvāt, tatraivārthe pratipuruṣamanyānyavedānumānaṃ na doṣāya ekārthānekapadopasthitau vānekavākyānumānameveti, tanna, ācārato vedānumāne maṅgalamācaredityādyanyataropasthitau niyamābhāvāt /
anekavedakalpane ca svānubhavavirodhaḥ, manusmṛtimūlañcānekaṃ vākyaṃ nāvaśyakamiti kathamādhuniko 'nekamanuminuyāt /
na ca smṛtyarthabodhakovedaḥ smṛtisadṛśa evānumeyaḥ niyamataḥ smṛterupasthitatvāt iti vācyam /
tadarthasmṛterapi nānāprakārakatvāt tasya ca pradoṣādau anuccaritavedasyeva vedatvaṃ śrotragrahāṇārhatayā ca śabdatvaṃ vākyatvamarthabodhakatvādityetadeva yuktaṃ smṛtyācāreṇa cānumitau vedor'thaṃ bodhayatīti pūrvapūrveṇānumitavedāt uttarottarasmṛtyācārāviti nāndhaparamparā śabdārthaśaktigrahavat svataḥ pramāṇamūlakatvāt /
tasmānnityānumeyatvaṃ vedasya na tūccheda iti / atrocyate /
ucchinnavedādarthaṃ pratītya smṛtyācārayorupapatteḥ na sāmagṣantarakalpanaṃ ata eva nāśrayāsiddhibodho vā smṛtyācārānumitavedasyāsmābhirabhyupagamāt /
idānīñca smṛterarthaṃ pratītyācārāñca kartavyatāmanumāya pravṛttiḥ /
na caivaṃ kiṃ vedeneti vācyam /
tulyatvāt avinābhāvācca tatkalpanaṃ tulyaṃ tathāca smṛtyācārayorvedajanyānubhavamūlakatvānumānādeva pakṣadharmatābalāt pratyakṣavedamūlakatvasiddhiḥ /
anyathā tasyānubhāvakatvābhāvena mūlatvānupapatteḥ /
tasmāt smṛtyācārānumito vedaḥ pratyakṣo 'dhyayanaviṣayaśca vedatvāt saṃmatavat, anyathā sāmagrayantarakalpane gauravaprasaṅgaḥ /
nanu stuti-nindārthavādena kalpitāt vidhi-niṣedhakavākyāt kathamarthamavagamya pravṛtti-nivṛttī, na hi tatra varṇa-pada-vibhakti-vidhipratyayakramaviśeṣāṇāmanumānaṃ sambhavati, vyabhicārāditi cet, na, stuti-nindāvākyābhyāṃ pravṛtti-nivṛttiheturartha eva kalpate /
lāghāvāt /
na tu vidhāyaka-niṣedhakavākyaṃ gauravāt uktadoṣācca, yatra cārthavādādeva tadarthāvagamaḥ ``tarati mṛtyumi''tyādau tatra na kalpanāpi /
atha tasyādhyayanaviṣayatve śākhāntaravat bahubhirmeghāvibhirādhyātmikaśaktisampannairghiyamāṇaśākhāyā ucchedāsambhava iti cet, na, ekasya na sakalaśākhādhyayane śaktirityekenevāparairapi tadanadhyayane śākhocchedasambhavādekānādhītāyā aparādhyayanaviṣayatvaniyame mānābhāvāt /
yadyapi vedasahasraśākhāvido vyasādayaḥ santyeva, tathāpyadhyayanābhāva eva śākhoccedaḥ /
nanu śākhocchede varṇa-padavākyahāniśaṅkayā pratyakṣavedādapi vākyārtha-prayogayoraniścaye vaidikavyavahāramātraṃ lupyeteti cet, na, śrūyamāṇamātrasyaiva mahānajaparigṛhītatvāt tanmātrabodhitāṅgatikartavyatayaiva śiṣṭairanuṣṭhīyamānatvācca tadarthaniścayāt /
na ca ucchinnaśākhābodhitekartavyatāśaṅkayā ekasminnapi karmaṇyanāśvasaprasaṅgaḥ, nānāśākhetikartavyatāpūraṇīyatvāt tasyeti sāmprataṃ, santi hi tattatkarmaṇi nānāśākhābodhitasakaletikartavyatābodhanāyainameva kālakramabhāvinamanāśvāsamaśaṅkamānairmarṣibhiḥ praṇītā mahājanaparigrahītāḥ smṛtayaiti nānāśvāsaḥ /
anyathā ekasya sakalaśākhānavagamāt śākhāntarabodhitetikartavyatāsaṃśayenaikaśākhāto nārthaniścayaḥ syāt /
children.translated_text: As for [the view] that the specific sentence-form 'the <s>aṣṭakā</s> rites are to be performed, the <s>aṣṭakā</s> rites are obligatory' is what is inferred—because it is what is presented [to the mind]; and different Vedic texts are inferred for each person regarding the same meaning, and this is not a fault because multiple words presenting one meaning entails the inference of multiple sentences. That is not so, because in inferring a Veda from traditional practice, there is no rule restricting it to the presentation of any particular one such as 'one should perform auspicious rites.' And the postulation of multiple Vedas contradicts one's own experience, and the statement that what has <s>Manu-smṛti</s> as its source need not be many sentences—how then would a modern person infer many? And it cannot be said that the Veda conveying the meaning of <s>smṛti</s> must necessarily be inferred as similar to the <s>smṛti</s> because of the <s>smṛti</s> being what is presented—because the <s>smṛti</s> about that meaning is also of diverse forms, and that [Veda], like an un-recited Veda at twilight, has the character of being Veda through worthiness to be grasped by the ear, and word-hood, sentence-hood, and meaning-conveying-hood. This alone is correct: through <s>smṛti</s> and practice, the inferred Veda conveys its meaning; thus from the Veda inferred by prior [evidence], the subsequent <s>smṛtis</s> and practices [follow]—and this is not a blind sequence, because like the grasping of the relation between word and meaning, it is grounded in a self-evident means of valid knowledge. Therefore, the Veda is always to be inferred as eternal, not as having been destroyed. Here it is said: since <s>smṛti</s> and practice are explicable by having understood the meaning from a destroyed Veda, there is no need to postulate another causal complex; for this very reason there is no fallacy of unestablished substratum or [contradictory] cognition, since we ourselves accept the Veda inferred from <s>smṛti</s> and practice. And now, having understood the meaning from <s>smṛti</s> and having inferred the obligatoriness from practice, action [follows]. And it cannot be said 'then what need is there for the Veda?'—because, being equal, due to invariable concomitance, the postulation of that [Veda] is equally [required]; and thus from the inference that <s>smṛti</s> and practice are grounded in experience born of the Veda, by the force of the property of the subject, the groundedness in a directly perceived Veda is established. Otherwise, without its capacity to produce [experience], its being the ground would be inexplicable. Therefore, the Veda inferred from <s>smṛti</s> and practice is directly perceived and is the object of study—because it is a Veda, like an accepted one; otherwise, the postulation of another causal complex would entail undue complexity. Objection: how can action or abstention from action [follow] from a sentence of injunction or prohibition postulated through praise and censure as <s>arthavāda</s>, since the inference of specific phonemes, words, case-endings, injunctive suffixes, and their sequence is not possible due to deviation? No—from the praise and censure sentences, only the meaning that is the cause of action or abstention is postulated, due to parsimony, not the injunctive or prohibitive sentence, due to complexity and the stated fault. And where the understanding of that meaning comes from the <s>arthavāda</s> alone, as in 'he crosses over death,' there is no need for postulation at all. Now, if [one says] since [the Veda] is the object of study, like other Vedic branches, many persons endowed with extraordinary mental powers, reciting a branch, make the destruction of that branch impossible—no, because one person does not have the capacity to study all branches, and since the destruction of a branch is possible when even one [person] does not study it and others also fail to study it, and there is no means of valid knowledge for the rule that what is not studied by one must be the object of study by another. Although there exist persons like <s>Vyāsa</s> who know thousands of Vedic branches, still the loss of a branch consists precisely in the absence of study. Objection: if a branch is lost, due to the fear of loss of phonemes, words, and sentences, even from a directly perceived Veda there would be uncertainty about sentence-meaning and application, and merely Vedic convention would be lost. No—because what is merely heard is not apprehended by the general public, and because the obligatoriness of subsidiary acts conveyed by that alone is what the learned practice, from that the meaning is certain. And it is not the case that the fear that a lost branch may convey a different obligatoriness leads to uncertainty about even a single rite—because that [rite's obligations] are to be fulfilled by the obligations taught by various branches, and this suffices for the present. For the <s>smṛtis</s> composed by sages—who, without fearing this future uncertainty, sought to teach the complete set of subsidiary obligations taught by various branches for each rite—are accepted by the general public; hence there is no uncertainty. Otherwise, since one person cannot know all branches, doubt about the subsidiary obligations taught by other branches would prevent certainty of meaning from even a single branch.

children.text:
yattu vibhaktyādimattatpadānāṃ tatsamudāyānāñca pratyakṣatvanteṣṭhapi kaścidvedaḥ tatrāyaṃ samudāyo veda ityaniścaya eva nityānumeyārthaḥ, vedatvaṃ vā tatrānumeyamiti, tanna pratyakṣavedātiriktavākye tadabhiyuktānāṃ mahājanānāṃ vedatvābhāvaniścayāt /
ata eva vedatvaṃ tatranānumeyaṃ bādhāt viśiṣya pakṣājñānāñca dharmavedanājanakatvañca vedatvaṃ nānumeyaṃ tajjanakatvasya pratyakṣatvāt, nādhyayanaviṣayatvaṃ tadabhāvāt, najātiranabhyugamāditi /
children.translated_text: As for [the claim that] even though the perceptibility of words possessing case-endings and the like and their collections is accepted, some [text] is a <s>Veda</s>, [but] the uncertainty 'is this collection the <s>Veda</s>?' is itself what is always to be inferred—or [that] <s>Veda</s>-hood is what is to be inferred regarding that—that is not so, because knowledgeable great persons have the certitude of the absence of <s>Veda</s>-hood in sentences other than the directly perceived <s>Veda</s>. For this very reason, <s>Veda</s>-hood is not to be inferred therein, due to contradiction and due to ignorance of the specific thesis-subject. Nor is <s>Veda</s>-hood to be inferred as 'the capacity to produce the cognition of <s>dharma</s>,' since that capacity is directly perceptible. Nor [is it] 'being the object of study (<s>adhyayana</s>),' due to its absence. Nor is it a universal (<s>jāti</s>), since that is not accepted.

smṛtyācārayorvedamūlatve tatrocchedādivivādastadeva tvasiddhaṃ, tathā hi vedasamānārthā mahājanaparigṛhītā ca smṛtiḥ svārthosthityanantaraṃ smṛtyarthānubhāvakavedānumāne liṅgaṃ tathāca prāthamyāt sādhyaprasidhyarthasupajīvyatvāñca smṛterevāpūrvādivākyārthajñānamastu kiṃ vedana tadarthasya smṛtita eva siddheḥ apūrvasyāpi śabdaikagamyatvena smṛtitojñātasya jñāpakatvenānuvādakatāpatteśca, sā ca smṛtyantarādityanādireva smṛtidhārāvaśyikī /
anyathā manusmṛteḥ pūrvantavāpi vedānumānaṃ na syāt /
sarvā ca smṛtiḥ smṛtijanyavākyārthapramājanyatvena mahājanaparigrahītatvena ca pramāṇamiti nāndhaparamparā, pratyakṣā ca smṛtiḥ smṛtimūlaṃ nānumitā anumitavedavattasyānanubhāvakatvāt /
vedārthasmṛtitāprasiddhistu pratyakṣavedamūlasmṛtisāhacaryeṇa bhramāt pratyakṣavedābodhitalobha-nyāyamūlasmṛtāviva tāntrikāṇāṃ liṅgābhāsajanyavedamūlakatvaṃ kalpayati /
atha smṛtiriva tadvedamūlakatvaprasiddhirapi mahājanaparigrahītā evañca sā vedamūlatvanibandhanā avigītamahājanaparigṛhītavedamūlatvaprasiddhitvāt pratyakṣavedamūlasmṛtau tatprasiddhivat, evaṃ vedārthatāprasiddhirapi /
anyathā mahājanaparigṛhītānādare veda-smṛtyorapi prāmāṇyaṃ na syāditi cet, na, yūpahastyādismṛtestatprasiddhau vyabhicārāt, kḷptalobhādita eva tatsambhavāt vicārakāṇāṃ vipratipatteśca tatra tatprasiddhau vigānaṃ mahājanānāmiti cet, na, atrāpi mūlāntarasambhavādviprattipatteśca
children.translated_text: One might say this: If <s>smṛti</s> (tradition) and <s>ācāra</s> (conduct) have the <s>Veda</s> as their source, the dispute concerning the interruption and the like therein is itself unestablished. For indeed, a <s>smṛti</s> that has the same meaning as the <s>Veda</s> and is accepted by great persons is, after establishing its own meaning, a logical mark (<s>liṅga</s>) in the inference of a <s>Veda</s> that conveys the meaning of the <s>smṛti</s>. And thus, since [the <s>smṛti</s>] has priority, and since the establishment of the probandum depends on it, let the knowledge of the sentence-meaning of unprecedented [injunctions] and the like come from the <s>smṛti</s> itself—what need is there for the <s>Veda</s>? Since the content [of the <s>Veda</s>] is already established from the <s>smṛti</s> alone. And even what is unprecedented (<s>apūrva</s>), since it is knowable only through verbal testimony, and since what is known from the <s>smṛti</s> merely indicates [it], there would follow the consequence of [the <s>Veda</s> being] merely reiterative. And that [<s>smṛti</s>] comes from another <s>smṛti</s> and so forth—thus the stream of <s>smṛti</s> is necessarily beginningless. Otherwise, even the inference of a <s>Veda</s> prior to the <s>Manu</s>-<s>smṛti</s> would not be possible. And all <s>smṛti</s> is a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge) by virtue of producing valid sentential cognition and by being accepted by great persons—thus there is no blind chain [of authority]. And the <s>smṛti</s> that is directly perceived is the root of [further] <s>smṛti</s>—it is not inferred, since like an inferred <s>Veda</s>, it would not be productive [of valid cognition]. The well-known status of 'being a <s>smṛti</s> of Vedic content,' however, is attributed through the association with <s>smṛtis</s> rooted in the directly perceived <s>Veda</s>, through error—just as the <s>Tāntrikas</s> attribute Vedic rootedness produced by a pseudo-logical mark to <s>smṛtis</s> rooted in desire for worldly gain, teaching obtained from the directly perceived <s>Veda</s>. Now if [it is argued that] just as with <s>smṛti</s>, the well-known status of being rooted in that <s>Veda</s> is also accepted by great persons, and thus that [status] is grounded in Vedic-rootedness, because of its being well-known as Vedic-rooted and accepted by undisputed great persons, just as the well-known status [exists] in <s>smṛtis</s> rooted in the directly perceived <s>Veda</s>—so too the well-known status of being of Vedic content. Otherwise, if the acceptance by great persons were disregarded, even the authority of the <s>Veda</s> and <s>smṛti</s> would not hold—if so objected, no, because there is deviation in the <s>smṛti</s> concerning sacrificial posts, elephants, and the like [where that well-known status exists but no Vedic source is found], since the possibility of that [well-known status] arises from the conventional use of established desire and the like, and because there is disagreement among the critically-minded. If [it is said that] the disagreement of great persons is a deviation regarding that well-known status therein—no, because here too there is the possibility of another root and disagreement.

vigānameva teṣāṃ /
ata eva smṛtīnāṃ nyāyamūlatve sambhavati vedamūlatvaprasiddhāvapi na vedamūlatvaṃ /
na ca vedamūle 'yamiti kṛtvā smṛtermahājanaparigrahāt tanmūlatvaṃ, vedamūleyamiti prathamaṃ jñātumaśakyatvāt śakyatve vā kimanumānena /

anyathā pramāṇe nairapekṣasya vaiyarthyāt /
na cācāre vedamūlatvaprasiddhestadanumānaṃ, asiddheḥ vyabhicārādanyathopapatteśca /

anyathā mūlābhāvenāndha-paramparāprasaṅgaḥ /
na ca manvādīnāmatīndriyārthadarśitvaṃ, tadupāyaśravaṇādestadānīmabhavāt /

nanvevaṃ smṛtirastu vedamūlāmaṅgalādyācārastvīśvarādeva bhaviṣyati ghaṭa-lipyādisamprādayavaditi cet, na, bahuvyāpāraghaṭitasya tattadācārasya gurutvena maṅgalamācaredityādivākyasyaiva lāghavena kalpanāt /
na ca maṅgalādipadaśaktigrahārthe tadupapatteḥ /
ata eva yatra vacanamātrāt parapratipattistatra nācāraḥ parīkṣakāṇāṃ, tasya ca vedatvaṃ neśvarapraṇītatvena śaktigrahaṇārthatadvacane vyabhicārāt, kintu tādṛśācārāsya vedamūlatvaniyamāditi /
syādet, pralaye satyevameva tat sa eva tu nāsti pramāṇābhāvat iti cet, na, kāla-kapālānyāvṛttighaṭaprāgabhāvaḥ kāryadravyānādhārādhāraḥ kāryadravyānadhikaraṇakāryādhikaraṇavṛttirvā abhāvatvāt ākāśavṛttyanyonyābhāvavaditi vṛttapralayasādhanāt /
evameva ghaṭadhvaṃsaṃ pakṣīkṛtyāgāmipralayasādhanam /
yadvā ghaṭaḥ kāryadravyānadhikaraṇakāryādhikaraṇavṛttidhvaṃsapratiyogī kāryatvācchabdavat /
yadvā kāryadravyatvaṃ kāryadravyānadhikaraṇakāryādhikaraṇavṛttidhvaṃsapratiyogivṛtti kāryamātravṛttitvāt śabdatvavat /
yadvā ekakālīnāḥ sarve paramāṇavaḥ samagrīpādeyaprabandhaśūnyā ārambhakatvāt naṣṭapavanārambhakaparamāṇuvat /
sarvatra pakṣatāvacchedakāvacchinnaṃ sādhyaṃ pratīyate iti ekakāle śūnyate labhyate /
na ca pavanaparamāṇūnāmapi pakṣatvenāṃśataḥ siddhasādhanaṃ, pakṣadharmatābalalabhyasādhyāpratīteḥ, abhedānumānavacca pakṣasya dṛṣṭāntatvāvirodhaḥ /
yadvā paramāṇavaḥ kāryadravyānadhikaraṇavṛttikāryavantaḥ nityadravyatvāt ākāśavat, bhūgolakasantāno 'yaṃ bhūgolakasantānānadhikaraṇavṛttidhvaṃsapratiyogī kāryatvāt ghaṭavat / yadvā etatkarmātiktāni karmāṇi etatpratibandhakapratibadhyāni karmatvāt etatkarmavat /
na cātra vyabhicāraśaṅkā, sarveṣāmevaṃrūpatvādanevambhāve ca svabhāvapracyavāt /
children.translated_text: Nor is there a suspicion of deviation (<s>vyabhicāra</s>) here, since all [cases] are of this very nature, and in the absence of this [nature], there would be a deviation from their own essential character (<s>svabhāva</s>).

children.text: anyathā niyame 'pi niyamāntarāpekṣāyāmanavasthiteḥ /
children.translated_text: Otherwise, even in the case of a rule (<s>niyama</s>), there would be an infinite regress due to the need for yet another rule.

children.text: āgamo 'pyamumevārthaṃ saṃvatadīti kṛtaṃ prasaktānuprasaktyā //
children.translated_text: The <s>Āgama</s> (scripture) also supports this very meaning — thus this [discussion] is concluded through the method of extended relevant elaboration (<s>prasaktānuprasakti</s>).

Their [understanding] is merely distinguishing.
Therefore, when <s>smṛtis</s> (traditional texts) being rooted in reason (<s>nyāyamūlatva</s>) is possible, even when their rootedness in the <s>Veda</s> is well-established, [we say] there is no rootedness in the <s>Veda</s>.
Nor [can one argue that] because this [<s>smṛti</s>] is rooted in the <s>Veda</s>, therefore from the acceptance by great persons (<s>mahājana</s>) its rootedness [in the <s>Veda</s> follows], since it is impossible to know first that 'this is rooted in the <s>Veda</s>,' and if it were possible, what need would there be for inference?
Nor is the acceptance by great persons qualified by the mode of being rooted in the <s>Veda</s>, because it is unestablished — since the acceptance by successive [generations of] great persons is explained by the prior acceptance of great persons [who regarded these] merely as <s>smṛtis</s> of <s>Manu</s> and others, and thus practice is accounted for. Similarly, even in the case of customs like <s>Holākā</s> (Holi festival) and others, since the knowledge of obligatoriness is explained by the <s>Vedic</s> indicative mark (<s>liṅga</s>) alone, what need is there for the <s>Veda</s> [itself], as the purpose [of the <s>Veda</s>] is established from the indicative mark alone?
Since the rootedness in the <s>Veda</s> is observed [only] for the conduct of the learned (<s>śiṣṭācāra</s>) that is not contradicted [by the <s>Veda</s>] and concerns non-worldly matters, in the inference of the <s>Veda</s>, even eating and other conduct would be rooted in the <s>Veda</s> by virtue of being uncontradicted conduct of the learned; and since the knowledge of its obligatoriness is possible even without the <s>Veda</s>, [the objection] 'there is no <s>Veda</s> for that purpose' applies equally here.
Since both the practice and the inference of obligatoriness are beginningless, and the obligatoriness of practices is rooted in inference, there is no blind succession (<s>andhaparamparā</s>).
Nor [can one say] that because the later inference depends on the prior inference, there is an absence of being rooted in an independent means of valid knowledge (<s>svatantrapramāṇa</s>), since all [inferences] are independent means of valid knowledge by virtue of possessing <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion) and <s>pakṣadharmatā</s> (the property of the subject).
Nor [is it the case] that the validity of everything depends on the validity of another, such that there is no independence, for that absurd consequence would apply to perception and other [means of knowledge] as well.
By this, the [argument] that 'the practice under dispute is rooted in an independent means of valid knowledge, because it is uncontradicted conduct of great persons, like practice rooted in perception or the <s>Veda</s>' is refuted,
since inference itself being an independent means of valid knowledge, the reason is accounted for merely by being rooted in a means of valid knowledge, and because independence, being superfluous due to its cumbersomeness, is ineffective [as a qualifier].
Nor [can one say] that there is no validity due to dependence, since <s>vyāpti</s> and other [conditions] are present.
Nor [can one say] that there is no validity due to dependence, since <s>vyāpti</s> and other [conditions] are present.
Otherwise, independence in a means of valid knowledge would be pointless.
Nor is there an inference of rootedness in the <s>Veda</s> for [every] practice, because it is unestablished, because of deviation (<s>vyabhicāra</s>), and because of alternative explanation.
Nor [does one say] that the acceptance by great persons is due to rootedness in the <s>Veda</s> alone, for the acceptance of great persons is not because 'this is rooted in the <s>Veda</s>,' since rootedness in the <s>Veda</s> cannot be known first, and if it could be, what need for inference?
Nor [can one say] that the acceptance by great persons [of a practice occurs] by knowing that 'this practice is accepted by great persons as rooted in the <s>Veda</s>,' due to the cumbersomeness and unestablishedness [of such a position].
Since the practice of successive [generations] is explained by the acceptance of prior great persons alone. If [it is argued] that the <s>Veda</s> is established through the pervasion of rootedness in the <s>Veda</s> for such <s>smṛtis</s> and practices — no, because having an alternative basis when [the stated one] is impossible serves as a limiting condition (<s>upādhi</s>).
Otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence that even <s>smṛtis</s> rooted in greed or <s>nyāya</s> (reasoning) would be rooted in the <s>Veda</s>.
Let there be beginninglessness of <s>smṛti</s> and practice.
Nor should it be said that [the sequence of] practice giving rise to <s>smṛti</s> and <s>smṛti</s> giving rise to practice constitutes a blind succession due to the absence of a foundational means of valid knowledge,
since both <s>smṛti</s> and practice are themselves means of valid knowledge.
Otherwise, there would be no inference of the <s>Veda</s> from them either.
It is replied: Since in the state of dissolution (<s>pralaya</s>), prior <s>smṛtis</s> and practices are destroyed, at the beginning of creation (<s>sarga</s>), the <s>smṛtis</s> and practices are rooted in the <s>Veda</s> composed by the eternal, omniscient Lord (<s>Īśvara</s>).
Otherwise, in the absence of a foundation, there would be the absurd consequence of a blind succession.
Nor do <s>Manu</s> and others have the capacity to perceive supersensory objects, since the means for that — hearing [the <s>Veda</s>] and so forth — did not exist at that time.
If [it is said that] <s>Manu</s> and others were omniscient beings established from a prior creation — no, due to the absence of a means of valid knowledge [for that claim].
If [it is said that] the very rootedness of <s>smṛtis</s> and practices in a means of valid knowledge is the ground for postulating that — no, because postulating their mutual [dependence] at each creation cycle would be cumbersome, and therefore postulating a single eternal omniscient being is [preferable]. Nor are the <s>smṛtis</s> themselves composed by Him, since the <s>smṛtis</s> reveal that their authors are <s>Manu</s> and others, and the <s>smṛtis</s> themselves record the rootedness of the <s>smṛtis</s> in the <s>Veda</s>.
Thus, the scripture (<s>Bhagavat</s>) is also a valid means for establishing rootedness in the <s>Veda</s> from the acceptance of <s>smṛtis</s> and practices by great persons.
For this very reason, the <s>Āgama</s> also [states]: 'At every <s>Manvantara</s>, a different <s>Śruti</s> is ordained.'
Thus, initially <s>smṛti</s> and practice were indeed rooted in perception, and subsequently, due to the gradual decline over time of the powers of longevity, health, strength, faith, comprehension, retention, and so forth, and due to the loss of <s>Vedic</s> branches (<s>śākhā</s>) through interruption of their study, people act by learning obligatoriness from <s>smṛti</s> and practice alone.
If [it is objected that] let <s>smṛti</s> be rooted in the <s>Veda</s>, but practices like auspicious rites (<s>maṅgala</s>) and the like will originate from the Lord alone, like traditions of pottery, writing, and so forth — no, because it is simpler to postulate a sentence like 'one should perform auspicious rites' and so forth, given the complexity of such practices involving many operations.
Nor [is there a need for such postulation] for the purpose of grasping the denotative power (<s>śakti</s>) of words like <s>maṅgala</s> and others, since that is accounted for by [the practice itself].
For this very reason, where the communication to others occurs from a mere statement alone, there is no [need for] practice for those who are critical examiners. And the <s>Vedic</s> status of that [statement] is not due to being composed by the Lord, because there is deviation (<s>vyabhicāra</s>) in [the claim that] a statement for grasping denotative power [must be Vedic]; rather, it is because such practice is invariably rooted in the <s>Veda</s>.
If [it is said:] granted, in the case of dissolution it is so, but that [dissolution] itself does not occur, due to the absence of a means of valid knowledge — no, because dissolution, past and future, is established [as follows]: the prior absence of a pot, [which ends in] a future period, is located in something that is not the substratum of the effect-substance, or abides in the locus of an effect that is not co-located with the effect-substance — [this is established] because it is an absence, like mutual absence residing in space.
In the same way, making the destruction of a pot the subject, future dissolution is established.
Alternatively: a pot is the counterpositive of a destruction that abides in a locus of an effect not co-located with the effect-substance, because it is an effect, like sound.
Alternatively: pot-ness resides in the counterpositive of a destruction that abides in a locus of an effect not co-located with the effect-substance, because it resides in effects only, like sound-ness.
Alternatively: all atoms at a single time are devoid of the series of causal aggregates (<s>sāmagrī</s>), because they are originators, like the atoms that originate the wind that has been destroyed.
In all cases, the <s>sādhya</s> (probandum) is cognized as delimited by the delimitor of the <s>pakṣatā</s> (subject-hood), thus the emptiness at one time is obtained.
Nor is there partial <s>siddhasādhana</s> (establishing what is already established) by making the atoms of wind also the subject, since the <s>sādhya</s> obtainable by the force of <s>pakṣadharmatā</s> is not cognized [in that way], and as in the case of inference of non-difference, there is no contradiction in the subject also being an example.
Alternatively: atoms possess effects that reside in loci not co-located with the effect-substance, because they are eternal substances, like space. This continuum of the earth-globe is the counterpositive of a destruction that resides in a locus not co-located with the continuum of the earth-globe, because it is an effect, like a pot. Alternatively: these actions are counteracted by things that counteract them, because they are actions, like those [other] actions.

children.text: vidhivādapūrvapakṣaḥ
children.translated_text: The prior objection (<s>pūrvapakṣa</s>) regarding injunction (<s>vidhivāda</s>)

children.text:
ācāramūlatvaṃ vedasya pravartakajñānajanakatvena bhavatīti pravartakajñānaṃ nirūpyate /
tatrābhidhā-saṅkalpāpūrva-bhāvanājñānaṃ na pravartakaṃ, tasmin satyapi apravṛtteḥ asatyapi pravṛtteśca /
kāryatvajñānaṃ pravartakamiti guravaḥ /
tathā hi jñānasya kṛtau janyāyāṃ cikīrṣātiriktaṃ na kartavyamasti tatsattve kṛtivilambohetvantarābhāvāt, cikīrṣā ca kṛtisādhyatvaprakārikā kṛtisādhyakriyāviṣayecchā pākaṃ kṛtyā sādhayāmīti tadanubhavāt, sā ca svakṛtisādhyatājñānasādhyā icchāyāḥ svaprakārakadhīsādhyatvaniyamāt /
ata eva svakṛtisādhye pāke pravartate, na tviṣṭasādhanatājñānasādhyā svakṛtyasadhye cikīrṣāpatteḥ, svakṛtyasādhyatvajñānaṃ pratibandhakamiti cet, na, tadabhāvakāraṇatve gauravāt /
athābhāva ubhayasiddhaḥ kṛtisādhyatādhīrasiddhetyato na lāghavāvasara iti cet, na, yatra śabdādanumānadvā daivāt sā tatra lāghavāvatārādicchāyāḥ svaprakārakajñānasādhyatvaniyamena kṛtisādhyatvajñānasyāvaśyakatvācca janakajñānaṃ vighaṭayata eva jñānasya pratibandhakatvācca /
vyāptijñānavighaṭanadvārā anumitipratibandhakānaikāntikajñānavat /
children.translated_text:
The rootedness of the <s>Veda</s> in practice (<s>ācāra</s>) consists in its being the generator of impelling knowledge (<s>pravartakajñāna</s>) — thus the impelling knowledge is examined.
In this regard, knowledge of denotation (<s>abhidhā</s>), volition (<s>saṅkalpa</s>), <s>apūrva</s> (unseen merit), and <s>bhāvanā</s> (productive operation) is not the impeller, because even when it is present, action does not [necessarily] occur, and even when it is absent, action [sometimes] does occur.
The teachers (<s>guravaḥ</s>) [hold that] knowledge of being-an-effect (<s>kāryatvajñāna</s>) is the impeller.
The explanation is as follows: in regard to knowledge about an action (<s>kṛti</s>) to be produced (<s>janyā</s>), there is nothing to be done beyond the desire to act (<s>cikīrṣā</s>), since in the presence of [<s>cikīrṣā</s>] there is no other cause for delay in action; and <s>cikīrṣā</s> is a desire (<s>icchā</s>) whose qualifier is accomplishability by one's own effort (<s>kṛtisādhyatva</s>), directed toward an action accomplishable by effort — as experienced in 'I shall accomplish cooking by effort' — and it is produced by the knowledge of accomplishability by one's own effort, since desire is invariably produced by cognition having its own qualifier [as content].
For this very reason, one acts toward cooking that is accomplishable by one's own effort, but [<s>cikīrṣā</s>] is not produced by knowledge of being a means to what is desired, since [otherwise] there would be the absurd consequence of <s>cikīrṣā</s> even toward what is not accomplishable by one's own effort. If [it is said that] knowledge of non-accomplishability by one's own effort is the obstructor — no, because there is cumbersomeness in [making] its absence a cause.
If [it is said that] the absence [of knowledge of non-accomplishability] is established on both sides, and [since] the cognition of accomplishability by effort is unestablished, there is no occasion for [the principle of] simplicity — no, because wherever that [cognition of accomplishability] arises from verbal testimony or inference or by chance, simplicity does apply there; and since the knowledge of accomplishability by effort is indispensable due to the rule that desire is produced by cognition having its own qualifier, [the opponent's] generative cognition is precluded by the very cognition [of accomplishability] that acts as an obstructor.
Just as knowledge of the fallacy of inconclusiveness (<s>anaikāntika</s>), which obstructs inferential cognition (<s>anumiti</s>), does so through precluding the knowledge of pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>).

children.text: anyathā svakṛtyasādhyatvāniṣṭasādhanatvopekṣaṇītvaniṣphalatvajñānaṃ pratibandhakaṃ kriyājñānameva pravartakaṃ kalpeta /
