children.text:
navyāstu svakṛtisādhyatājñānameva pravartakaṃ tena svakṛtyasādhye vṛṣṭyādau kārīryāñca kṛṣīvalasya na pravṛttiḥ /
na ca sañjātabādhasya viṣabhakṣaṇe pravṛttiprasaṅgaḥ, svakṛtisādhyatājñānaviṣaye iṣṭatvasya svarūpasataḥ pravṛttau sahakāritvāt /
na ca sañjātabādhasya viṣabhakṣaṇādāvicchāsti, iṣṭasādhanatvenājñānāt atītabhojane 'pyata eva na pravartate tṛpteḥ siddhatayā icchāviraheṇa bhojane tadupādhikeṣṭatvābhāvādatītatṛptāvicchā nāstīti tatsādhane 'pīṣṭatvābhāvādeva na pravṛttiḥ /
na caivaṃ pāke na pravarteta tasya svarasataiṣṭatvābhāvāditi vācyam /
iṣṭasādhanatvajñānena tasyāpīṣṭatvāt /
hantaivaṃ prāthamikatvādiṣṭatvārthamavaśyāpekṣaṇīyatvācca kṛtisādhyatve satīṣṭasādhanatājñānameva cikīrṣākāraṇamastviti cet, na, iṣṭāsādhanatvābhāve 'pi bhoge cikīrṣāsattvāt tasyāṃ svakṛtisādhanatvābhāve 'pi bhoge cikīrṣāsattvāt tasyāṃ svakṛtisādhyatvajñāne satīṣṭatvameva kāraṇaṃ na tviṣṭasādhanatvaṃ vyabhicārāt /
pākādau tadanvaya-vyatirekāvapīṣṭatvopakṣāṇau, evaṃ bhoge 'pi pravarteteti cet, na, iṣṭasādhanatāpakṣe 'pi muktirūpeṣṭasādhane sukhe pravarteteti tulyam /
sukhe cikīrṣā bhavatyeva kṛtistu na bhavati kṛteḥ /
children.translated_text: The newer [logicians] hold that the cognition of producibility by one's own <s>kṛti</s> alone is the impeller; therefore, with respect to rain and the like which are not producible by one's own <s>kṛti</s>, and with respect to the farming work [dependent on rain], the farmer does not engage volitionally. Nor is there the undesired consequence that one whose [desire] has been sublated would engage in consuming poison, because being desired (<s>iṣṭatva</s>), which exists in its own nature, is a cooperating condition (<s>sahakārin</s>) in volitional activity with respect to the object of the cognition of producibility by one's own <s>kṛti</s>. And one whose [desire] has been sublated has no desire for consuming poison, because there is no cognition of its being a means to the desired end. For the same reason, one does not engage in past eating — because, satisfaction being already accomplished, there is absence of desire, and there is no <s>iṣṭatva</s> (desirability) conditioned by satisfaction with respect to eating; there is no desire for past satisfaction, hence there is no volitional activity even toward its means, due to the very absence of <s>iṣṭatva</s>. Nor should one say that in that case one would not engage in cooking, because cooking lacks <s>iṣṭatva</s> in its own nature — for cooking too has <s>iṣṭatva</s> through the cognition of its being a means to the desired end. Well then, since <s>iṣṭatva</s> of a primary kind and the like must necessarily be presupposed, let the cognition of being a means to the desired end, given producibility by <s>kṛti</s>, be the cause of <s>cikīrṣā</s> — if so, no, because <s>cikīrṣā</s> exists even with respect to enjoyment where there is no being-a-means-to-the-desired-end; in that <s>cikīrṣā</s>, when the cognition of producibility by one's own <s>kṛti</s> is present, <s>iṣṭatva</s> alone is the cause, not being-a-means-to-the-desired-end, due to deviation. Even though the positive and negative concomitance of that [means-to-desired-end] are observed in cooking and the like, they are subsidiary to <s>iṣṭatva</s> — if one says that in that case one would engage volitionally even in mere enjoyment — no, because on the view that requires being-a-means-to-the-desired-end too, there would equally be the consequence of engaging in pleasure which is a means to the desired end in the form of liberation. There is indeed <s>cikīrṣā</s> toward pleasure, but <s>kṛti</s> does not arise, because of <s>kṛti</s>'s

children.text:
siddhavṛttyasiddhakriyāviṣayatvaniyamāditi cettulyam /
tasmāt svakṛtisādhyatvaṃ vidhiriṣṭatvaṃ sahakārīti, maivaṃ, iṣṭasādhanatājñānasyopāyecchāyāṃ hetutvāvadhāraṇāttasyāstajjanyatvaniyamādicchāyāḥ svaviṣayecchānutpādakatvaniyamācca /
nanu siddhaudanaḥ kutaḥ pāke na pravartate, odanamātrasya siddhatveneṣṭatvābhāvāt /
ata evātītabhojanādau na pravartate atītatṛṣṇādāvicchāvirahāt /
nanu sāmudrakavikhyāte bhāviyauvanarojye bhogasādhane svakṛtisādhyatve satīṣṭasādhanatvajñānāt kuto na pravartate, bhāvirājyasyāsiddhatvāt pravatteḥ siddhaviṣayatvaniyamāt rājyopāyāparicayācca /
tatparicaye ca pravartata eva devatārādhanādāviti cet, na, siddhe cikīrṣāviraheṇa yāgādāvapyapravṛttiprasaṅgāt devatārādhanāderapyasiddhatve na tatrāpyapravṛttiprasaṅgācca /
kiñca rājyopayāparicaye tatra mā pravarttiṣṭa svakṛtisādhyeṣṭasādhanatvena jñāne rājye pravṛttiprasaṅge kimāyātaṃ /
na hi kṛtisādhyeṣṭasādhanatvena jñāne 'pi tadupāyajñānaṃ tatra pravartakaṃ gauravāt bhinnaviṣayatvācceti cet maivaṃ yauvane hi yāvat pravartata eva rājye bālye tu rājyopāyamakṛtvā matkṛtyedānīṃ rājyaṃ na siddhyatīti svakṛtyasādhyatājñānādeva na pravartate yathā taṇḍulaṃ vinā pāke svakṛtyasādhyatājñānāt rājyopāye tu svakṛtisādhyeṣṭasādhanatvena jñāte devatārādhanādau pravartata eva /
ata eva vrīhyavaghātamakṛtvā puroḍāśastamakṛtvā yāgastamakṛtvāpavūrvaṃ sādhayituṃ na śakyata iti kramaśo 'vaghātādau pravartate na yugapat siddhavṛttyasiddhakriyāviṣayāviṣayasvabhāvatvāt pravṛtteḥ yāgānantarañca nāpūrve pravartate /
kṛtyantaraṃ vinaiva yāgakṛtitastatsambhavāt /
iṣṭasādhane ceṣṭotpattināntarīyakaduḥkhājanakatvaṃ viśeṣaṇaṃ na tu tajjñānābhāvaḥ kāraṇaṃ kintu tadeva viṣayatayā kāraṇatāvacchedakaṃ lāghavāt tena madhu-viṣasampṛktānnabhojane na pravṛttiḥ, pareṇāpi pravṛttipūrvaṃ liṅgaviśeṣaṇatvena anyathā vā tajjñānaviniyogasvīkārāt /
evañcālpāyāsasādhyādiṣṭotpattisambhave bahvāyāsasādhye na pravṛttiḥ /
ata eva śrutasvargaphalakatve 'pi bahuvittavyayāsasādhye jyotiṣṭomādau phalabhūmā kalpane anyathālpāyāsāsadhyādeva svargasiddhisambhave tatrāpravṛttau ananuṣṭhānalakṣaṇamaprāmāṇyaṃ tadvidheḥ syāt /
children.translated_text: nature of having as its object an unaccomplished action, not an accomplished state — if so, the same [objection applies] equally. Therefore, producibility by one's own <s>kṛti</s> is the injunction (<s>vidhi</s>), and <s>iṣṭatva</s> is the cooperating condition — let it not be so, because it is ascertained that the cognition of being a means to the desired end is the cause of desire for the means, and because of the rule that that [desire for means] is generated by it, and because of the rule that desire does not produce desire with respect to its own object. Objection: Why does one who has rice already available not engage in cooking? Because, since rice in general is already accomplished, there is no <s>iṣṭatva</s>. For this very reason one does not engage in past eating, due to the absence of desire for past thirst-quenching and the like. Objection: A young prince famous for his future kingdom — why does he not engage volitionally when he has the cognition that the kingdom, being producible by his own <s>kṛti</s>, is a means to the desired end? Because the future kingdom is not yet accomplished, and volitional activity is restricted to accomplished objects, and because the means to the kingdom are unfamiliar. And when those means become familiar, he does indeed engage in worshipping deities and the like — if so, no, because there would be the undesired consequence of non-engagement even in sacrificial rites due to the absence of <s>cikīrṣā</s> toward what is already accomplished; and if worshipping deities and the like are also unaccomplished, there would equally be non-engagement in those. Furthermore, even if one is unfamiliar with the means to the kingdom, so that one does not engage in those — what problem arises from the consequence of engaging in the kingdom itself when there is cognition of it as a means to the desired end producible by one's own <s>kṛti</s>? For even when there is cognition of being a means to the desired end producible by <s>kṛti</s>, the cognition of the means to that is not the impeller toward that [goal directly], due to complexity and difference of objects — let it not be so, for in youth one does indeed engage toward the kingdom, but in childhood, not having performed the means to the kingdom, one does not engage because of the cognition 'the kingdom is not accomplishable by my <s>kṛti</s> now,' just as one does not engage in cooking without rice due to cognition of non-producibility by one's own <s>kṛti</s>. But when the means to the kingdom — worshipping deities and the like — are cognized as means to the desired end producible by one's own <s>kṛti</s>, one does indeed engage. For this very reason, without threshing rice, one cannot make the sacrificial cake; without making that, one cannot perform the sacrifice; without that, one cannot accomplish the <s>apūrva</s> (unseen merit) — thus one engages sequentially in threshing and so on, not simultaneously, because volitional activity by its very nature has as its object an unaccomplished action, not an accomplished state. And after the sacrifice, one does not engage in <s>apūrva</s>, since it can arise from the <s>kṛti</s> of the sacrifice without any further <s>kṛti</s>. And the qualifier for a means to the desired end is that it does not produce suffering as a necessary concomitant of the arising of the desired result — it is not the case that the absence of such cognition is the cause; rather, that very [non-production of suffering] as the object is the delimitor of the causal condition, by parsimony. Therefore, one does not engage in eating food mixed with honey and poison. Even the opponent must employ this cognition as a qualifier of the inferential mark or in some other way, prior to volitional activity. Thus, when the arising of the desired result is possible through something achievable with little effort, there is no volitional activity toward something achievable with great effort. For this very reason, even though the <s>Jyotiṣṭoma</s> and similar [rituals] are heard to have heaven as their result, since they require expenditure of great wealth and effort, abundance of results must be postulated; otherwise, if heaven could be attained through something achievable with little effort, non-engagement in those [rituals] would amount to invalidity of the injunction prescribing them.

children.text:
balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitvañca na viśeṣaṇaṃ bahuvittavyayāyāsasādhyabahutaraduḥkhasyāpyabalavattvaṃ kvacidalpaduḥkhasyāpi balavattvaṃ /
tasyāpyuktātiriktasyānanugamāt /
āstikasya niṣiddhatvena jñāte 'pi pravṛttiḥ rāga-dveṣayorutkaṭatvena narakasādhanatvajñānatirodhānāt /
nanu na kalañjaṃ bhakṣayedityatra vidhyarthaniṣedhānupapattiḥ tadbhakṣaṇasya tṛptirūpeṣṭasādhanatvāt /
na cāsurāvidyādivat paryudāsalakṣaṇayā virodhyaniṣṭasādhanatvabodhanaṃ naño 'samastatvāt kriyāsaṅgatatvena pratiṣadhavācakatvavyutpatteśceti cet na viśeṣyavati viśiṣṭaniṣedhasya saviśeṣaṇe hīti nyāyena viśeṣaṇaniṣedhaparyavamāyitayā kalañjabhakṣaṇamiṣṭotpattināntarīyakaduḥkhātiriktaduḥkhasādhanamiti na kalañjaṃ bhakṣayedityanena bodhanāt /
iṣṭasādhanatāvācakasya siddheḥ sāmānyato niṣedhānupapatterbalavadaniṣṭānanubandhīṣṭasādhanatvaviśeṣaniṣedhatātparyaṃ tathācāśakyaviśeṣaniṣedhaparatvaṃ naña iti kaścit /
tanna /
yathā hyayogyatayā sacchidraṃ vihāya ghaṭatvena taditarānvayo na tu chidretaratvena yugapadvṛttidvayavirodhāt tathātrāpi balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitvenānupasthitau kathaṃ tanniṣedhaḥ /
śyenenābhicaran yajetetyatra kathaṃ vidhipravṛttiḥ hiṃsāyā balavadaniṣṭānubandhitvāt iti cet tatra kṛtisādhyatve satīṣṭasādhantvameva yogyatayānveti na tu balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitvamapi ayogyatvāt /
nindārthavādena prāyaścittopadeśena ca hiṃsāyā balavadaniṣṭānubandhitvāvagamāt /
ata eva vihite 'piśyene vigānānna tātvikapravṛttiḥ /
rāga-dveṣayorutkaṭatvenāniṣṭānubandhyaṃśasya tiraskārāt /
kasyacit pravṛttirityeke /
anye tvabhicārasya vairibadhaphalakatvena śrutatvāt badhasādhanatvena śyeno vidhīyate na tu badhasādhyanarakasādhanatvena narakasya phalatvenāśruteḥ /
na ca janakajanakasya janakatvaniyamaḥ kumbhakārapitṛparamparāyāḥ kumbhajanakatvāpatteḥ vidhinaiva śyenasya balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitvabodhanācca /
na ca śyenasya balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitvabodhanācca /
na ca śyenasya narakāhetutve apekṣitavairibadhahetutve vā avigānena pravṛttiḥ syāditi vācyam /
śyenādbadho badhāccāvaśyaṃ naraka iti pratisandhānena vigānāt /
children.translated_text:
And 'not being accompanied by a preponderant undesirable result' (<s>balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva</s>) is not a qualifier [of the impeller], since even greater suffering requiring much expenditure of wealth and effort may be non-preponderant, while sometimes even slight suffering may be preponderant.
Because there is no invariable concomitance of anything beyond what has been stated.
Even a believer (<s>āstika</s>) acts even when something is known to be prohibited, because the intensity of passion (<s>rāga</s>) and aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>) conceals the knowledge that it leads to hell (<s>naraka</s>).
[Objection:] In the prohibition 'one should not eat <s>kalañja</s> (a type of garlic),' a prohibition of the purpose of an injunction is untenable, since eating it is a means to the desired [result] in the form of satisfaction.
Nor [can one say] that the negative particle (<s>nañ</s>) conveys, through the figurative usage of exclusion (<s>paryudāsa</s>), that [the action] is a means to an undesirable result opposed [to the desired one], as in the case of <s>āsurī vidyā</s> and the like, because <s>nañ</s> is not a compound [with the verbal root] and its conventional meaning is established as expressing prohibition in connection with an action — [to this we say:] no, because by the principle that 'a qualified negation of a qualified [entity] amounts to a negation of the qualifier when the qualificand is present' (<s>saviśeṣaṇe hīti nyāya</s>), since the negation resolves into a negation of the qualifier, 'one should not eat <s>kalañja</s>' conveys that eating <s>kalañja</s> is a means to suffering beyond the suffering inevitably accompanying the production of the desired [result].
Some [say:] since the expression of being a means to the desired [result] is already established, and a general prohibition is untenable, the purport of the negative particle is the prohibition of the specific [qualification] of being a means to the desired [result] not accompanied by preponderant undesirable [consequences], and thus the negative particle has as its scope the prohibition of an impossible specification.
That is wrong.
Just as, due to unfitness, [the universal] pot-ness (<s>ghaṭatva</s>) is connected with [pots] other than a defective [pot with a] hole, setting aside the defective one — not by the property of being 'other than having a hole,' since two co-occurring [universal] properties would conflict — similarly here too, when 'not being accompanied by preponderant undesirable [consequences]' is not presented [to cognition], how can its negation [be effected]?
If [it is asked:] in 'one who practices sorcery should sacrifice with the <s>Śyena</s> [rite],' how does the injunction operate, since violence (<s>hiṃsā</s>) is accompanied by preponderant undesirable [consequences]? — [We reply:] there, what connects by fitness [to the injunctive meaning] is only being a means to the desired [result] when accomplishable by effort, but not also 'not being accompanied by preponderant undesirable [consequences],' due to [its] unfitness.
Because the accompaniment of violence by preponderant undesirable [consequences] is understood from censuring <s>arthavāda</s> (explanatory passages) and the prescription of expiatory rites (<s>prāyaścitta</s>).
For this very reason, even though the <s>Śyena</s> [rite] is enjoined, there is no genuine activity [toward it] due to the discernment [of its sinful nature].
[The activity of some] is due to the intensity of passion and aversion concealing the aspect of accompaniment by undesirable [consequences].
Some [hold that only] certain persons engage [in it].
Others, however, [say that] since sorcery (<s>abhicāra</s>) is heard [in scripture] as having the killing of an enemy as its result, the <s>Śyena</s> is enjoined as a means to killing, not as a means to hell through killing — since hell is not heard [in scripture] as the [direct] result.
Nor is there a rule that the producer of a producer is [itself] a producer, for [otherwise] the ancestral lineage of the potter would absurdly be the producer of the pot; and because the injunction itself conveys that the <s>Śyena</s> is not accompanied by preponderant undesirable [consequences].
Nor [is it correct that] the injunction conveys that the <s>Śyena</s> is not accompanied by preponderant undesirable [consequences].
Nor should it be said that activity [toward the <s>Śyena</s>] would occur without discernment, whether [it is held that] the <s>Śyena</s> does not cause hell, or that the desired killing of the enemy [follows],
because there is discernment [of the sinful nature] through the connected reasoning: 'from the <s>Śyena</s> comes killing, and from killing inevitably comes hell.'

nanu śyenomaraṇaphalakavyāpāratvena hiṃsā sā ca narakajaniketi cet na na hi sākṣāt paramparāsādhāraṇamaraṇaphalakavyāpāro hiṃsā kūpādau vinaṣṭe gavi tatkartturgobadhakarttutvāpatteḥ badhyasyāpi hanturmṛtyūtpādanadvāreṇātmahantṛtvaprasaṅgācca /
na hi anutpāditamanyuḥ kaścit kamapi vyāpādayati kintvanuniṣpādimaraṇaphalakovyāpāro hiṃsā yadanantaraṃ maraṇaṃ bhavatyeva /
na ca śyenastathā kintu khaṅgahananādikameva /
atha maraṇānuddeśena kṣiptanārācāddhatabrāhyaṇe ca hiṃsā na syāt /
kiñca hinastidhātvarthe avacchedakaṃ phalamavyavahitameva maraṇaṃ avyavahitaphalakasyaiva vyāpārasya dhātuvācyatvāt anyathā paramparayā vilkiptiphalakānnakāmeṣṭataṇḍulakrayādāvapi pacatītiprasaṅgāt /
evaṃ khaṅgābhighātānantaraṃ yatra vilambena maraṇaṃ vraṇapākaparamparayā vā anne viṣaprayogeṇa vā tatra hantṛtvaṃ prāyaścittādi ca na syāt iti cet na prāyaścittatulyatārthaṃ hi tatra hantṛvyadeśo gauṇaḥ vinigamakañca lāghavameva /
vastutastu maraṇoddeśena kṛto 'dṛṣṭādvārākastadanukūla vyāpāro hiṃsā /
kūpādau vinaṣṭe gavi tatkarturgobadhakartutvāpatteḥ badhyasyāpi hanturmutyūtpādanadvāreṇātmahantṛtvaprasaṅgācca /
na hi anutpāditamanyuḥ kaścit kamapi vyāpādayati kintvanuniṣpādimaraṇaphalakovyāparo hiṃsā yadanantaraṃ maraṇaṃ bhavatyeva /
na ca śyenastathā kintu khaṅgahananādikameva /
atha maraṇānukūlyavyāpāro maraṇoddaśenānuṣṭhīyamāno hiṃsā śyenaśca tathā kūpādau ca na maraṇoddeśenānuṣṭhīyamānatvamiti cet na evaṃ sati gauravāt maraṇānuddeśena kṣiptanārācāddhatabrāhmaṇe ca hiṃsā na syāt /
children.translated_text:
[Objection:] The <s>Śyena</s> [rite involves] violence (<s>hiṃsā</s>) because it is an activity whose result is death — and that [violence] produces hell. [Reply:] No. An activity whose result is death, whether directly or indirectly and exclusively, is not [what constitutes] violence, for [otherwise,] when a cow perishes in a well or the like, the one who made [the well] would absurdly be guilty of cow-slaughter; and even the slain person would absurdly be a self-slayer through producing the death of the slayer.
For no one kills another without having generated anger; rather, violence is an activity whose result is inevitably death, after which death certainly occurs.
But the <s>Śyena</s> is not like that; rather, it is only striking with a sword and the like.
Then, in the case of a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> killed by an arrow shot without the intention of killing, there would be no violence.
Furthermore, the delimiting result in the meaning of the verbal root 'to kill' (<s>hinasti</s>) is only immediate death, since only an activity with an immediate result is denoted by the verbal root; otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence that even purchasing rice for a sacrifice desired for food would be described as 'cooking,' since it remotely results in softening.
Similarly, where death occurs with delay after a sword-strike, through the succession of wound-festering, or through administering poison in food — in those cases there would be no killer-hood and no expiation (<s>prāyaścitta</s>) and the like. [Reply:] No, for the designation of 'killer' there is secondary (<s>gauṇa</s>), serving the purpose of equivalence in expiation, and the distinguishing criterion is simplicity alone.
In reality, violence is an activity favorable to death, performed with the intention of killing, operating through unseen merit (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>).
When a cow perishes in a well or the like, the maker [of the well] would absurdly be guilty of cow-slaughter; and even the slain person would absurdly be a self-slayer through producing the death of the slayer.
For no one kills another without having generated anger; rather, violence is an activity whose result is inevitably death, after which death certainly occurs.
But the <s>Śyena</s> is not like that; rather, it is only striking with a sword and the like.
[Objection:] If violence is an activity favorable to death performed with the intention of killing, and the <s>Śyena</s> is like that, while in the case of a well and the like it is not performed with the intention of killing — [Reply:] no, because in that case, due to cumbersomeness, there would be no violence in the case of a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> killed by an arrow shot without the intention of killing.

children.translated_text:
Furthermore, the delimiting result in the meaning of the verbal root 'to kill' (<s>hinasti</s>) is only immediate death, since only an activity with an immediate result is denoted by the verbal root; otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence that even purchasing rice for a sacrifice desired for food would be described as 'cooking,' since it remotely results in softening.
Similarly, where death occurs with delay after a sword-strike, through the succession of wound-festering, or through administering poison in food — in those cases there would be no killer-hood and no expiation and the like. [Reply:] The designation of 'killer' there is secondary (<s>gauṇa</s>), serving the purpose of equivalence in expiation, and the distinguishing criterion is simplicity alone.
In reality, violence (<s>hiṃsā</s>) is an activity favorable to death, performed with the intention of killing, operating through unseen merit (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>); and the <s>Śyena</s> is a means to death through <s>adṛṣṭa</s>, therefore it is not violence.
If violence were [defined as] any means to death even through <s>adṛṣṭa</s>, then since applying oil on the seventh [day] and the like is a cause of the death of a beloved wife through <s>adṛṣṭa</s>, the one who applies the oil would absurdly be a killer.
For this very reason, even when a cow dies in a well or the like, there is no guilt of cow-slaughter for the maker [of the well]; when one chokes to death on food stuck in the throat, there is no self-slayer-hood for the eater, nor killer-hood or <s>Brahmin</s>-slayer-hood for the server. Killer-hood in the case of death through the succession of wound-festering or through poison is primary, not [based on] the activity having death as its inevitable result, since [otherwise] there would be the absurd consequence of self-slayer-hood in the case of death from food stuck in the throat.
If [it is said that] there would be <s>Brahmin</s>-slayer-hood when a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> is killed by an arrow shot with a different intention — no, because that is the desired [conclusion]. The designation [of 'killer'] is secondary; it can also be justified by the figurative usage based on similarity of effect. In the alternative position, the over-extension cannot be prevented — this itself is the distinguishing criterion.
For this very reason,

apare tu anabhisaṃhitanarāntaravyāpāramadvārīkṛtyamaraṇasādhanaṃ hiṃsā khaṅgakārasyānabhisaṃhitanarāntaravyāpāradvārā maraṇasādhanatvaṃ tasya hi narāntaravyāpāradvārā maraṇasādhanatvaṃ tasya hi narāntaravyāpāro nābhisaṃhitaḥ kintu dhanalābha iti khaṅgakāro na ghātakaḥ /
viṣasyānne prakṣepeṇa narāntaravyāpāro bhojanamevābhisaṃhitaḥ anenedaṃ bhoktavyamityabhisandhāya viṣaprayogāditi hisaivānne viṣaprayoga iti /
tanna /
galalagnakavalādyatra maraṇaṃ tatra pariveṣayiturghātakatāpātāt anenedaṃ bhoktavyaṃ ityabhisandhāya parivaṣaṇādbhokturātmahantṛtvāpatteśca anabhisaṃhitanarāntaravyāpāramadvārīkṛtya maraṇānukūlānnaṃbhakṣaṇānuṣṭhānāt /
ata evāvyavahitaprāṇaviyogaphalako vyāpāro hiṃsā vraṇapākaparamparā mṛte tu hantṛtvaṃ vyāpārasyāvyavadhāyakatvāditi nirastam /
children.translated_text:
Others, however, [define violence as follows:] violence (<s>hiṃsā</s>) is a means to death that does not operate through the intermediary of an activity of another person that is not intended [by the agent]. The sword-maker's [activity] is a means to death through the intermediary of another person's activity; for his [concern is] another person's activity — not the intended [killing], but rather the acquisition of wealth — therefore the sword-maker is not a killer.
In the case of administering poison in food, the intermediary activity of another person — namely eating — is itself intended, since the poison is administered with the intention 'this person should eat this'; thus the administration of poison in food is itself violence.
[Reply:] That is wrong.
Because where death occurs from a morsel stuck in the throat, the server would absurdly be a killer, since the server serves with the intention 'this person should eat this'; and the eater would absurdly be a self-slayer, since [the eating] is an activity of consuming food favorable to death, performed without intermediation of an unintended activity of another person.
For this very reason, [the view that] violence is an activity whose immediate result is the separation of vital breath (<s>prāṇa</s>), and that killer-hood in the case of death through the succession of wound-festering is because the activity [of striking] does not intervene [between cause and death] — this has been refuted.

syādetat neṣṭasādhanatā vidhiḥ nitye sandhyopāsanādau phalābhāvāt /
atha nāstyeva tat nityaṃ yatrārthavādādikaṃ vidhivākye vā na phalaṃ śrutamasti ``sandhyāmupāsate ye tu satataṃ śaṃsitavratāḥ /
vidhūtapāpāste yānti brahmalokaṃ sanātanaṃ'' ityādyarthavādāt ``dadyādaharahaḥ śrāddhaṃ pitṛbhyaḥ prītimāvahan'' ityādividhivākyaśravaṇācca, kṛtvācintayātūcyate , yatra na phalaśrutistatra viśvajinnayāyāt svargaḥ phalamiti cet, na, kāmanopādhikāryatvena yāgavannityatābhaṅgaprasaṅgādaharahaḥ śrutyā hi tatkālajīvimātrakṛtisādhyaṃ sandhyāvandanamavagataṃ hi kāmanopādhikāryatve ca yadā phalakāmanā nāsti tadā tatsamaya eva tatkartavyatā na syāt na hi tatkāle phalakāmanāvaśyambhāvaḥ pramāṇabhāvāt /

na ca upāsanākaraṇaṃ pratyavāyaheturnopāsanābhāvaḥ tathāca duḥkhasādhanābhāvatvena kṛtiriṣṭā na tūpāsanamiti vācyam /
nindārthavādasyobhayatra sattvena ubhayasyāpi tathātvāditi tanna evamapi kāmyatve nityatākṣatiprasaṅgāt /

vastutastu kṛtisādhyatve satīṣṭasādhanatājñānaṃ pravartakatvena nirvyūḍhaṃ /
na ca kṛtau kṛtisādhyatvamastītyato na kiñcidetat /
children.translated_text: One might say: desired-instrument-hood is not the injunction for obligatory rites like <s>sandhyā-upāsanā</s> (twilight worship), because there is no fruit [mentioned]. But there is no obligatory rite at all where either in an <s>arthavāda</s> (explanatory passage) or in the injunctive sentence itself no fruit is heard—there exist [passages like] 'Those who constantly worship the twilight, being of laudable vows, their sins cleansed, they go to the eternal world of <s>Brahman</s>' and the like from <s>arthavāda</s>, and from hearing injunctive sentences like 'One should daily give <s>śrāddha</s> to the ancestors, bringing them delight.' Setting that aside, if [one says] where there is no mention of fruit, by the maxim of the <s>Viśvajit</s> sacrifice, heaven is the fruit—no, because since the effect-hood would be conditional upon desire, like a [kāmya] sacrifice, there would be the unwanted consequence of the loss of obligatoriness. For from the injunction 'daily,' <s>sandhyā-vandana</s> (twilight prayer) is understood as achievable through the effort of every living person at that time; and if effect-hood were conditional upon desire, then when there is no desire for the fruit, at that very time there would be no obligation—for there is no necessity that desire for the fruit exists at that time, there being no means of valid knowledge [for such necessity]. Moreover, from the 'daily' injunction independent of any subsequent motivation, the eligibility of every living person is understood; and thus one who has the desire for fruit introduced by the <s>arthavāda</s>, which pertains to the subsequent motivation, has no eligibility for that [obligatory rite]—because of contradiction with the initial 'daily' injunction. In obligatory rites, the mention of fruit and the <s>arthavāda</s> have their purport in praise. For this very reason, the avoidance of sin (<s>pratyavāya</s>) too is not the fruit—because if effect-hood were conditional upon the desire to avoid sin, obligatoriness would be lost. Moreover, prior to the understanding of obligation from the injunction, there is no means of valid knowledge for sin; the postulation of sin for non-performance after understanding obligation from the injunction would involve mutual dependence. Rather, from the censure-<s>arthavāda</s> and from the teaching of expiation (<s>prāyaścitta</s>), the absence of worship—that is, the absence of the very activity whose nature constitutes the primary act—is understood as the cause of sin. And thus the absence of <s>sandhyā-upāsanā</s>, through sin, is an instrument of suffering; its absence—namely, <s>sandhyā-upāsanā</s> [itself]—being the absence of an instrument of suffering, is the fruit, like the destruction of sin in expiation; and thus effort as an instrument of that is taught by the injunction. And it cannot be said that then avoidance of sin alone is the fruit—because avoidance, being of the form of prior absence, being beginningless, is not achievable. And it cannot be said that non-performance of worship is the cause of sin, not the absence of worship; and thus the effort desired is for the absence of an instrument of suffering, not the worship itself—because the censure-<s>arthavāda</s> being present for both, both are equally so. That is not so—even thus, if it were optional, there would be the unwanted consequence of loss of obligatoriness. Moreover, by [passages like] 'one who does not perform the enjoined act' and 'one who [neglects] the evening [twilight prayer],' it is taught that the non-performance alone is the cause of sin, not the absence of the object; otherwise, how could the sin be only for the non-performer and not for another, since the absence of the object is common [to all]? In reality, however, the knowledge of desired-instrument-hood, given achievability through effort, has been fully demonstrated to be the cause of action. And it is not the case that achievability through effort exists in effort itself—hence this [objection] amounts to nothing.

children.text: navyāstu nityāpūrvaprāgabhāvo duritadvārā duḥkhasādhanaṃ tadabhāvo 'pūrvaṃ duḥkhasādhanābhāvatveneṣṭaṃ tatsādhanatvena kṛtisādhyatvena ca sandhyopāsanaṃ vidhīyate iti tanna nindārthavādādinā sandhyopāsanābhāvastadakaraṇaṃ vā pratyavāyaheturavagato na tvapūrvābhāvaḥ prathamaṃ pramāṇābhāvena tadanupasthiteḥ vidheḥ iṣṭasādhanatvabodhakatvāt pariśeṣeṇāpūrvamiṣṭaṃ kalpyata iti cet tarhi viśvajinnayāyena svarga eva phalaṃ kalpyatāṃ kāmyatvasya tvayāpi svīkārāt kiñca vidhipravṛttāvapūrvajñānaṃ apūrvajñāne ca vidhipravṛttirityanyonyāśrayaḥ /
children.translated_text: The moderns, however, [hold that]: the prior absence of the <s>apūrva</s> (transcendent potency) of the obligatory rite, through demerit, is an instrument of suffering; its absence is the <s>apūrva</s>; being desired as the absence of an instrument of suffering; and <s>sandhyā-upāsanā</s> is enjoined as an instrument of that and as achievable through effort. That is not so—from the censure-<s>arthavāda</s> and so on, the absence of <s>sandhyā-upāsanā</s> or its non-performance is understood as the cause of sin, not the absence of <s>apūrva</s>, since initially, due to the absence of a means of valid knowledge, that [<s>apūrva</s>] is not presented. If [one says] since the injunction conveys desired-instrument-hood, by elimination, <s>apūrva</s> is postulated as the desired [end]—then by the <s>Viśvajit</s> maxim, heaven itself should be postulated as the fruit, since even you accept the optionality [that would follow]. Moreover, there is mutual dependence: knowledge of <s>apūrva</s> requires the operation of the injunction, and the operation of the injunction requires knowledge of <s>apūrva</s>.

children.translated_text: Some [say] that for the complete observance of obligatory and occasional rites, and for the proper maintenance of the prescribed actions of each life-stage, the attainment of the world of <s>Brahman</s> is heard as the fruit; thus the obligatory rite has a fruit. That is not so—because the operation of that injunction depends upon the obligatory injunction, and that [obligatory injunction], being without fruit, is initially mute; otherwise, each being dependent on the other, there is mutual dependence. Therefore, the injunction is merely of obligatoriness (<s>kāryatā</s>). Objection: even if the knowledge of obligation comes from the Veda in the case of obligatory rites, how can there be action without knowledge of a purpose? For even a foolish person acts for a purpose. No—because in obligatory rites, since there is defeat of the fruit, the knowledge of a purpose is not productive of mere action; even in optional rites, the knowledge of purpose is not directly the cause of action, because it pertains to the means, and because there is no action regarding the purpose [itself]; rather, it is exhausted in the knowledge of obligation through the knowledge of desired-instrument-hood. How is this certainty [possible]? Because the knowledge of desired-instrument-hood is impossible in the case of obligatory rites, and because the knowledge of obligation is possible even from the Veda. Objection: how can judicious persons engage in action that is fruitless or whose only fruit is suffering? Because the knowledge of obligation dependent on the Veda exists, and because even in action with fruit, that alone is the determining factor. As for [the fact that] in worldly matters one does not engage in what is fruitless or whose only fruit is suffering—that is because of the absence of the knowledge of obligation,

na ca /
nitye phalakāmanāyā asambhavaḥ trikālakamyastavapāṭhavat nitye phalakāmanāsambhavāt /

children.translated_text: whether based on the inferential mark of desired-instrument-hood or dependent on the Veda. And it is not the case that the knowledge of the only-suffering-fruit-hood is an obstruction to action, because when the knowledge of obligation exists, no obstruction by that is observed. Or alternatively, in optional rites, since the optative suffix (<s>liṅ</s>) conveys <s>apūrva</s>-hood, in obligatory rites too, the <s>apūrva</s> pertaining to the optative, worship, and other objects is conveyed; and that, even though fruitless, is a purpose in itself like pleasure—being eternal and being constantly sought after. It is said: in every obligatory rite, the eligibility is qualified by fruit-hearing and the desire for fruit of every living person. Just as in an eclipse, the occasional bath and <s>śrāddha</s> and so on are optional due to mention of fruit, and are also necessarily obligatory due to mention of expiation for non-performance; or just as the sixteen <s>śrāddhas</s>, due to hearing of desire for liberation from ghost-state as the fruit, are optional with a declaration aimed at the sixteen śrāddhas as causes of liberation from ghost-state, and through the general practice of great persons, are optional; and through the censure-<s>arthavāda</s> and mention of sin for non-performance, are necessarily obligatory—similarly, <s>sandhyā-upāsanā</s> too is optional due to mention of fruit, and necessarily obligatory due to mention of hell for non-performance and the teaching of expiation; [whereas] for the non-performance of that, there is no teaching of expiation. And it is not the case that the desire for fruit is impossible in obligatory rites—because, as in the recitation of the 'desire of three times' text, the desire for fruit is possible even in obligatory rites. As for [the objection] that from the initial 'daily' injunction, since the eligibility of every person living at that time is taught, one who desires the fruit has no eligibility—that is not so, because by the force of the single-sentence unity initially grasped between the 'daily' injunction and the <s>arthavāda</s>, [the daily injunction teaches obligation] without the co-occurrence with fruit for every living person at that time being separate from the single-sentence component. And it is not the case that the <s>arthavāda</s>, having praise as its purport, prevents single-sentence unity—because without a defeater, one does not abandon one's own meaning; since the fruit is presented by the injunctive sentence, the knowledge of obligation through the 'daily' injunction is by taking the fruit present in the injunctive sentence. Objection: if the eligibility is for those who at that time desire the fruit, when there is absence of desire for the fruit—like an impure person's absence of eligibility—there would be no obligatoriness; and sin [follows] non-performance by an eligible person, not mere non-performance. No—because even in occasional rites, for someone at that time who lacks desire, there would be the unwanted consequence of non-obligatoriness. Now, if [one says] in the absence of an exception, the naturally arising desire for fruit certainly exists, since the knowledge of fruit has the nature of producing desire regarding its own object; and for one who, due to the exception of desire for liberation, has no desire for other fruits, even non-performance entails no sin—hence such rites are not necessarily obligatory; similarly in obligatory rites, when desire for fruit is defeated by desire for liberation, non-performance entails no sin—the same applies. Moreover, when the obligation conditional upon the fruit introduced by the <s>arthavāda</s> is understood, from sentences like 'one who does not perform the enjoined act,' and from hearing of hell through censure-<s>arthavāda</s> for non-performance of <s>sandhyā-vandana</s> when pure, and from the teaching of expiation, sin is postulated; and even in the absence of desire for that fruit, one necessarily engages for the avoidance of sin—because sin is established by a means of valid knowledge following the operation of the injunction; and because the prior absence of sin, achievable by performance for one inclined toward non-performance, is achievable [through effort]—just as in occasional rites, when there is obligation conditional upon fruit and absence of desire, there is still necessarily obligatoriness.

children.translated_text: As for the [view] that one engages in obligatory [rites] even when they are fruitless, from Vedic cognition of obligatoriness without reference to any result — that is wrong, because when [an act] is cognized as having suffering alone as its result, persons of discernment have the rule of non-production of <s>kṛti</s> (effort), and because it is impossible to convey producibility by <s>kṛti</s> with respect to an obligatory [rite] due to its unsuitability. For this very reason, having raised the doubt that even the fruit of <s>sandhyā-upāsana</s> (twilight worship) is performed because of obligatoriness conveyed by the <s>Veda</s>, the <s>ācārya</s> (teacher) disregarded this with the intention 'this is the teacher's view, not mine.' As for the statement that <s>apūrva</s> (unseen merit) from a <s>pāṇḍa</s> rite is intrinsically its own purpose — that too is wrong, for in that case, even for you, if it were an object of desire (<s>kāmya</s>), the status of being obligatory (<s>nitya</s>) would be lost. Furthermore, pleasure and absence of suffering are the primary purpose, and their means is the secondary purpose; but the <s>apūrva</s> of an obligatory rite is [said to be] the purpose. If one says that in conformity with the impelling injunction (<s>vidhi</s>), that too is postulated as an impeller — no, because the people who are to be impelled do not know it as a purpose; even when the teacher says '<s>apūrva</s> of the obligatory rite is the purpose,' persons of discernment pay no heed. And liberation (<s>mukti</s>) and heaven (<s>svarga</s>), though supramundane, serve as purposes by being of the same kind as pleasure and absence of suffering — therefore a teacher who speaks thus is lightweight indeed. Here is the summary: since in obligatory [rites] volitional activity is inexplicable if suffering alone is the result, obligatoriness is conditioned by a result; and that result is either the absence of means to suffering or <s>apūrva</s> — and the desire for that must be resorted to daily for the sake of volitional activity, since without it volitional activity is inexplicable. And thus, let the result — whether stated in an <s>arthavāda</s> (laudatory passage) or heard in the injunctive sentence — suffice; enough with other [explanations]. Nor would it be the case that in the absence of desire there would be no fixed obligatoriness, because the same applies even in the absence of desire for <s>apūrva</s> and the like — the engagement invariably for the purpose of avoiding <s>pratyavāya</s> (sin of omission) is exactly the same. And where there is no statement of a result, the <s>Viśvajit</s> maxim applies. Objection: Since engagement is observed both from the cognition 'this is a means to the desired end' and from the cognition 'the desired end is producible by this,' what determines that only the first is the impeller? It is said: because in desire for the result, the cognition having one's own object as the qualificand is already established as the cause; desire for the means too, without a sublating cognition, is likewise. In reality, when the cognition from the word '<s>yajeta</s>' (one should sacrifice) first produces the cognition 'the sacrifice is producible by <s>kṛti</s>,' and then [produces] the cognition 'the desired end is the object to be produced by the sacrifice that is producible by <s>kṛti</s>' — since the cognition of the qualified requires prior cognition of the qualifier — you require two cognitions, whereas for me there is only one cognition: 'the sacrifice is producible by <s>kṛti</s> and is a means to the desired end.' Nor is it possible, having conveyed producibility by <s>kṛti</s> with respect to the sacrifice, then to convey through the inferential mark that 'the desired end is the object to be produced by the sacrifice producible by <s>kṛti</s>' — because, having conveyed the connection of one's own meaning with another word's meaning, there is no linguistic convention for conveying the connection of yet another meaning inclusive of that; and with respect to the word '<s>yaji</s>' (sacrifice), having conveyed the connection of sacrifice with <s>kṛti</s> and that being concluded, if it were again to produce cognition of connection with its own meaning, there would be the fault of infinite regress.

children.translated_text: consequent status of being not producible by it. For the same reason, it is not counter-positive-ness to the absence pervading the absence of that — because of the consequent producibility of taste by color. Nor is it the relation to a time-point pervaded by posteriority delimited by that — for being pervaded by posteriority means non-occurrence at a time that is not the locus of posteriority, and that is not established in the case of <s>ākāśa</s> (space), and is more complex. Therefore, being-a-cause-of-that is itself being-producible-by-that; and thus, by parsimony, the cognition of being-a-means-to-that alone is the impeller, not the cognition of being-caused-by-that. One might say: If the cognition of <s>iṣṭatva</s> (desirability) is the impeller, then even a satiated person would engage in eating, since there is cognition of the desirability of satisfaction through the mind. If one says that even though [desirability] exists in its own form, desire for the result is the cause, and that does not exist with respect to satisfaction since it is already accomplished — well then, since it is necessarily required, desire for the result alone is the cause, not its cognition, due to complexity. Furthermore, if cognition of desire were the cause, desire itself would not be a cause, since it would be destroyed by its own cognition; and to postulate a stream of desire and cognition-of-desire would lead to infinite regress. Moreover, the cognition 'pleasure is the object of desire' is not mental (<s>mānasa</s>) perception, because since pleasure is unaccomplished, direct perception having it as qualificand is impossible without perceptual contact with it; nor is cognition of <s>iṣṭatva</s> possible with respect to rice and the like through the mind, since the mind is not independent with respect to external [objects]. Nor is there cognition of <s>iṣṭatva</s> through the eye and other [senses] by means of contact with the qualificand there, as in 'it is known through the eye, it is done.' In reality, if the desired end is not specifically cognized through its pleasurableness and the like, then even when there is cognition that sacrifice or cooking is a means to the desired end, there would be non-engagement, because the desired end, varying in degree of more or less and being of many kinds, is not determinately grasped. Nor is <s>iṣṭatva</s> an indicator, with pleasurableness and the like — which delimit the object of desire — being the indicated property, because there is no unified indicated property in pleasure, absence of suffering, and their means, hence no unification. It is said: Where there is desire, the cognition of being-a-means-to-that alone is the impeller common to worldly and Vedic [contexts]; those objects of desire — pleasure, absence of suffering, and their means — though not unified [in themselves], are unified precisely by being objects of desire as real entities. Thus, when there is desire for pleasure and the like, and when there is the cognition 'this is a means to pleasure and the like, given producibility by one's own <s>kṛti</s>,' then one engages in cooking and the like. Objection: Since the object of the impelling cognition varies, the injunctive suffix, which has the capacity [to convey it], would have the fault of multiple meanings — no, because the sacrifice and the like, though not unified by pleasurableness and the like, convey through the inferential mark and the like their being means to a result unified by <s>iṣṭatva</s>; and thus, for the unification of results, desire for the result is possible [as what unifies], but not desire as a cause of cognition. If one says: The cognition that it is a means to pleasure and the like is the impeller — that is not possible, due to lack of unification; and what is possible — cognition of being a means to the desired end — is not the impeller; thus the injunction would have no impelling capacity — [reply:] Not directly so; rather, when 'the sacrifice is a means to the desired end' is conveyed through the inferential mark, and in the expectancy of what is desired, heaven, which is heard of as an object of desire, is understood as the desired end; thereupon, from the co-occurrence with the word '<s>svargakāma</s>' (desirer of heaven), the impelling cognition 'the sacrifice is a means to heaven' arises. Thus, the cognition that impels is generated by the cognition generated by the injunction.

children.translated_text: As for [the view] that no injunction directly impels, because producibility by one's own <s>kṛti</s> and the like cannot be ascertained from what conveys the injunction, and one's own being-a-means-to-the-desired-end — namely 'I am a performer of the sacrifice which is a means to the desired end, being a desirer of heaven, like the desirer of heaven understood from the <s>Darśa</s> passage' — is understood subsequently through implication — that is wrong, because since volitional activity is explicable from the verbal cognition alone that 'this is a means to that toward which there is desire,' that [additional] understanding is fruitless.

children.translated_text: Others hold that mere instrumentality (<s>sādhanatvamātra</s>) is the meaning of the injunction, and the obtaining of being-a-means-to-heaven-and-the-like is from co-occurrence, since even on the view that requires being-a-means-to-the-desired-end, that [co-occurrence] is relied upon. To elaborate: When the word '<s>yajeta</s>' conveys that the sacrifice is producible by <s>kṛti</s> and is an instrument, and in the expectancy of what the instrument's object-to-be-produced is, heaven — which is established through scripture as an object of desire — is understood as the object to be produced, since it is contextually present. And there is no expectancy of an object-to-be-produced for the sacrifice [separately], since it is already presented as producible by <s>kṛti</s>. For this very reason, in the <s>Viśvajit</s> and similar [rites], heaven alone is postulated as the object to be produced. Even on the view that being-a-means-to-the-desired-end is the content of the injunction, in <s>arthavāda</s> passages such as 'He crosses over death, he crosses over the sin of <s>brahmahatyā</s> (killing a brahmin), who sacrifices with the <s>Aśvamedha</s>' — an injunction would have to be postulated — if so, no, because of the invariable concomitance: being-a-means-of-that-nature is pervaded by being-enjoinable; or because there is no purpose for such postulation through the avenue of sublation by non-apprehension of the pervader — thus they also say.

children.text:
yattviṣṭasādhanatvābhidhāne karaṇe liṅgo 'nuśāsanāt darśa-paurṇamāsābhyāmityanabhihitādhikāravihitā tṛtīyā na syāditi /
tanna /
upāyatāmātrābhidhāne 'pi tadviśeṣakaraṇatvānabhidhānāt /
vastutastvabhihitānvayalabhyaṃ yāgeṣṭasādhanatvaṃ iṣṭasādhanatvamātrasya vidhyarthatvāt /
children.translated_text:
As for [the objection] that if the instrumental case (<s>karaṇa</s>) denotes being a means to the desired (<s>iṣṭasādhanatvābhidhāna</s>), then the third case-ending (<s>tṛtīyā</s>) in 'with the new-moon and full-moon [sacrifices]' (<s>darśa-paurṇamāsābhyām</s>), which is enjoined for the unexpressed eligible person (<s>anabhihitādhikāra</s>), would not obtain, since the indicative sign (<s>liṅga</s>) is [already accounted for] by grammatical instruction —
That is wrong.
Because even when mere means-hood (<s>upāyatā</s>) is expressed, the specific instrumental-hood (<s>karaṇatva</s>) thereof is not expressed.
In reality, the being-a-means-to-the-desired of the sacrifice (<s>yāga</s>) is obtained through the connection with what is expressed (<s>abhihitānvaya</s>), since only being-a-means-to-the-desired is the meaning of the injunction (<s>vidhi</s>).

children.text:
navyāstu cikīrṣādvārā jñānasya kṛtau hetutā cikīrṣā ca kṛtāvicchā sanaḥ prakṛtyarthagocarecchāvācitvāt pipakṣādivat /
na tu kṛtiviṣayapākādiviṣaye kṛtisādhyatvaprakārakecchābhidhāyakatvaṃ pākādeḥ prakṛtyanabhidheyatvāt /
na hi kṛtivācakasya tadviṣayavācakatvaṃ karotītyukte tadviṣayasaṃśayāt /
evañca kṛtāviccheṣṭasādhanatājñānāt tatsādhyeṣṭajñānādvā vṛṣṭyādau tathā kalpanāt /
yadā ca kṛtāvicchā tadā saiva cikīrṣā anyatrecchāmātraṃ na tu kṛtisādhyatājñānāt kṛtau kṛtisādhyatvābhāvāt /
atha pākaṃ kṛtyā sādhayāmītīcchānubhavasiddhā anubhavāpalāpe upekṣaṇīyatvāpatteḥ sā ca kṛtisādhyatājñānāt sā ca cikīrṣāpadāpratipādyāpi kṛtihetuḥ samānaviṣayatvāt na tu kṛtīcchā kṛtihetuḥ kṛtiviṣayāviṣayatvāditi cet asti tāvatpākakṛtāvicchā vṛṣṭīcchāvat asti ca kṛtisādhyatvaprakārikecchā pāke tathāpi kṛtīcchaiva kṛtikāraṇaṃ lāghavāt na tu kṛtisādhyatvaprakārikecchā gauravāt /
dhātvarthānuparakte kṛtisvarūpe icchaiva nodetīti cet na /
pākādikṛtīṣṭasādhanatājñānāt pākakṛtāvicchā tataḥ kṛtirityabhyupagamāt /
na cāvagati -pravṛttyoḥ samānaviṣayatvaṃ ubhayasiddhaṃ tasyaiva vicāryatvāt /
kathaṃ tarhi pākaṃ kṛtyā sādhayāmītīcchā yathā vahnisādhyatvena
children.translated_text:
The later [Naiyāyikas] (<s>navyāḥ</s>), however, [hold that] the causality of knowledge with respect to effort (<s>kṛti</s>) is through the desire to act (<s>cikīrṣā</s>), and <s>cikīrṣā</s> is a desire directed toward effort (<s>kṛtāvicchā</s>), since the desiderative suffix <s>san</s> denotes desire directed toward the object of the root-meaning, like <s>pipakṣā</s> (desire to cook) and the like.
But [the desiderative] does not denote a desire qualified by accomplishability-by-effort (<s>kṛtisādhyatvaprakārikā icchā</s>) directed toward cooking and the like, which are objects of effort, because cooking and the like are not denotable by the root [of the desiderative].
For a word denoting effort does not denote the object of that [effort], since when one says 'he does' (<s>karoti</s>), there is doubt about the object.
Thus, the desire toward effort [arises] from knowledge of its being a means to the desired, or from knowledge of the desired being accomplishable by that [effort], as is postulated in [cases like] rain and the like.
And when there is a desire toward effort, that alone is <s>cikīrṣā</s>; in other cases, it is merely a desire, but [<s>cikīrṣā</s>] does not [arise] from knowledge of accomplishability-by-effort with respect to effort itself, since effort does not have the property of being accomplishable by effort.
If [it is said:] the desire 'I shall accomplish cooking by effort' is established through experience, and denying experience would lead to the absurd consequence of [everything] being dismissible; and that [desire] arises from knowledge of accomplishability-by-effort; and that [desire], even though not conveyed by the word <s>cikīrṣā</s>, is the cause of effort due to having the same object; but the desire for effort is not the cause of effort, since [effort] is not the object of [the desire for] effort — [we reply:] there is indeed a desire toward the effort of cooking, like the desire for rain; and there is also a desire qualified by accomplishability-by-effort with respect to cooking; nevertheless, it is the desire for effort alone that is the cause of effort, due to simplicity (<s>lāghava</s>), and not the desire qualified by accomplishability-by-effort, due to cumbersomeness (<s>gaurava</s>).
If [it is said that] only the desire arises toward the essential nature of effort as colored by the meaning of the verbal root — no,
because it is accepted that from the knowledge of cooking-effort being a means to the desired, there arises a desire toward the effort of cooking, and from that, effort [itself arises].
Nor is the co-objectivity of cognition (<s>avagati</s>) and activity (<s>pravṛtti</s>) established on both sides, since that very [point] is under examination.
Then how [does one account for] the desire 'I shall accomplish cooking by effort'? Just as through accomplishability-by-fire,

children.text:
iṣṭasādhanatāvagamāt vahninā pākaṃ sādhayāmītīcchā tathā kṛtisādhyatvena iṣṭasādhanatvāt pākasya pākaṃ kṛtyā sādhayāmītīcchā anyathā tattadupāyasādhyatvena icchā pākādau tattadupāyasādhyatvaprakārakajñānāt syādityanantakāraṇakalpanā syāt /
mama tūpāyecchāyāmiṣṭasādhanatājñānameva hetuḥ kriyādvārā kṛteriṣṭasādhanatvajñāne kriyāyā apīṣṭasādhanatvaṃ viṣayaiti kṛtīcchā bhavantī kriyāviṣayāpi bhavatīti jñānecchāprayatnānāṃ samānaviṣayatāpi /
ata eva pākaṃ cikīrṣatīti cikīrṣāviṣayatayā pākaḥ pratīyate /
yadvā icchāviṣayaviṣayatayā pākaḥ pratīyate ita tasya karmatā grāmaṃ jigamiṣati śatruṃ jighāṃsatītyatra grāmāderiva, na hi grāmādāvicchā siddhatvāt /
ata eva bhoge sukhe ca cikīrṣā tadanukulakṛteriṣṭahetutvāt anyathā kṛtisādhyeṣṭasādhanatāpakṣe taccikīrṣāsāmagṣantaraṃ kalpyate /
evañca sandhyāvandanaṃ duḥkhasādhanāvandanābhāvarūpatveneṣṭaṃ tatsādhanaṃ kṛtiriti liṅgarthaḥ anyathā kṛtirna kṛtisādhyā sandhyāvandanañca neṣṭasādhanamiti kasya kṛtisādhyatve satīṣṭasādhanatvaṃ vidhyarthaḥ syāt /
ata evaikapratyayābhidheyatvapratyāsatterantaraṅgatayā vidhipratyayābhidheyeṣṭasādhanatvasya kṛtāvevānvayo na prakṛtyarthe tathaiva cikīrṣākāraṇajñānajanakatvāt prakṛtyarthasya ca kṛtau viṣayatvenānvaya iti /
children.translated_text:
from the cognition of being-a-means-to-the-desired through accomplishability-by-fire, the desire 'I shall accomplish cooking by fire' [arises]; similarly, since cooking is a means to the desired through accomplishability-by-effort, the desire 'I shall accomplish cooking by effort' [arises]. Otherwise, there would be a desire in cooking and the like qualified by accomplishability through each respective means, arising from knowledge qualified by accomplishability through each respective means — and this would lead to the postulation of infinite causes.
In my view, however, in the desire for a means, knowledge of being-a-means-to-the-desired alone is the cause. When the being-a-means-to-the-desired of effort is known through the action, and the action too is known as a means to the desired, then the desire for effort, while being [a desire for] effort, also has the action as its object — thus cognition, desire, and effort share the same object.
For this very reason, in 'he desires to cook' (<s>pākaṃ cikīrṣati</s>), cooking is cognized as the object of <s>cikīrṣā</s>.
Alternatively, cooking is cognized as the object of the object of desire, and thus its grammatical object-hood [is established], just as in 'he desires to go to the village' (<s>grāmaṃ jigamiṣati</s>) or 'he desires to kill the enemy' (<s>śatruṃ jighāṃsati</s>), where the village and the like [are the grammatical objects], since there is no desire directly toward the village and the like, [the relationship] being established [otherwise].
For this very reason, there is <s>cikīrṣā</s> even toward enjoyment (<s>bhoga</s>) and pleasure (<s>sukha</s>), since the effort favorable to them is a cause of the desired. Otherwise, on the view that the meaning of the injunction is being-a-means-to-the-desired-that-is-accomplishable-by-effort, another cause of that <s>cikīrṣā</s> would have to be postulated.
Thus, the <s>sandhyāvandana</s> (twilight prayer) is desired as having the nature of the absence of non-worship that is a means to suffering, and effort is its means — this is the meaning of the injunctive suffix (<s>liṅgartha</s>). Otherwise, [if] effort is not accomplishable by effort and <s>sandhyāvandana</s> is not a means to the desired, then for what would 'being a means to the desired when accomplishable by effort' be the meaning of the injunction?
For this very reason, due to the proximity of being denotable by a single suffix, being-a-means-to-the-desired, which is denoted by the injunctive suffix, is connected with effort alone as the more intimate [relation] (<s>antaraṅga</s>), not with the root-meaning, precisely because it generates the knowledge that causes <s>cikīrṣā</s>; and the root-meaning is connected with effort as its object.

children.text: (Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,2, p. 282)
children.translated_text: (Bibl. Ind. 98, IV,2, p. 282)

children.text:
ucyate /
vahnisādhyatvena kṛtisādhyatvena vā na pākasyaudanasādhanatā ityuktam /
kathaṃ tarhi vahninā pākaṃ sādhayāmītīcchā iti cet na iṣṭasādhanatvena jñāte yatra yatsādhyatvaṃ jñāyate tatra tatsādhyatvenecchā bhavatīti yatheṣṭasādhanatvena jñāte pāke vahnisādhyatvenāvagate iṣṭasya sādhanatājñānāt kṛtyā sādhayāmītīcchā tathāceṣṭāsādhanatvena kṛtisādhyatvena ca jñāte kṛtisādhyatvaprakārikecchā na tviṣṭasādhanatājñānamātrāditi /
children.translated_text:
It is replied:
It has been stated that cooking is not a means to [producing] boiled rice by virtue of accomplishability-by-fire or accomplishability-by-effort.
Then how [does one account for] the desire 'I shall accomplish cooking by fire'? [Reply:] No — when something is known as a means to the desired, wherever its accomplishability through something [else] is known, there the desire arises qualified by that accomplishability. Just as when cooking is known as a means to the desired and its accomplishability by fire is known, from the knowledge of the means-hood of the desired, the desire 'I shall accomplish it by effort' [arises]; similarly, when it is known as a means to the desired and as accomplishable by effort, a desire qualified by accomplishability-by-effort [arises] — but not from mere knowledge of being-a-means-to-the-desired alone.

children.text:
acāryāstu pravartakamiṣṭasādhanatājñānameva liṅgartastvāptabhiprāyo lāghavāt pākaṃ kuryāḥ kuryāmityatra vidhiliṅgaḥ sambodhya-svakartṛkakriyecchābhidhāyakatvenā jñā-prārthanāśaṃsanādiliṅgo vaktrādīcchābhidhāyakatvena liṅgamātrasyecchāvācakatvakalpanācca /
evañca svargakāmo yajetetyasya svargakāmasya kṛtisādhyatayā yāgo yāgayatno vā āpteṣṭa ityarthaḥ / tato yo vyāpāraḥ yasya kṛtisādhyatayā yadvyāpāraviṣayakaḥ prayatno vā yasyāpteneṣyate sa tasya balavadaniṣṭānanubandhīṣṭasādhanamiti vyāptigrahāt yāgasyeṣṭasādhanatvamanuminoti /
tathā hi yāgo madiṣṭasādhanaṃ matprayatnaviṣayatayā āpteneṣyamāṇatvāt yathā matpitrā matprayatnaviṣayatayeṣyamāṇaṃ madbhojanaṃ madiṣṭasādhanaṃ tathācedaṃ tasmāttathā /
evaṃ na kalañjaṃ bhakṣayedityasya mama kalañjabhākṣaprayatno nāptecchāviṣaya ityarthaḥ /
tataḥ kalañjabhakṣaṇaṃ mama balavadaniṣṭasādhanaṃ madiṣṭasādhanatve satyapyāptena matprayatnaviṣayatayā aniṣyamāṇatvāt yathā matpitrā matprayatnaviṣayatayā aniṣyamāṇaṇaṃ madhu-viṣasampṛktānnabhojanaṃ mama balavadaniṣṭasādhanaṃ tathācedaṃ tasmāttathā sa cāpto vedavyākhyātā bhagavānīśvara eva /
yastu vede pauruṣeyatvaṃ nopaiti taṃ prati vidhireva tāvaṅgarbha iva śrutikumāryāḥ puṃyoge pramāṇam /
na tarhi lāghavaṃ tātparyagauravādīśvarādyanantakalpanāditi cet na lāghavādinecchābodhakatvena loke liṅgaḥ pramāṇasiddhatvena phalamukhagauravasyādoṣatvāt /
children.translated_text: If [it is objected:] then there is no simplicity, due to the cumbersomeness of postulating the purport and the infinite postulation of the Lord and so forth — [we reply:] no, because the <s>liṅ</s> suffix is established by valid knowledge as denoting desire through [the principle of] simplicity and other [criteria] in ordinary usage, and cumbersomeness on the side of the result is not a fault.

children.text: na tu karturasmaraṇaṃ bādhakaṃ prāgeva nirāsāt tṛptikāmanayā viṣabhakṣaṇapravṛttasya viṣabhakṣaṇaṃ tat kṛtisādhyatayā neśvareṇeṣyate tato viṣabhakṣaṇasya īśvarecchāviṣayatve 'pi na tena vyabhicāraḥ /
children.translated_text: Nor is the non-remembering of the author an invalidating objection, since this has already been refuted. For one who has undertaken eating poison with the desire for satisfaction, the eating of poison is not desired by the Lord as accomplishable by [that person's] effort; therefore, even if the eating of poison is the object of the Lord's desire [in some other respect], there is no deviation (<s>vyabhicāra</s>).

children.text: yadvā ratkāmakṛtisādhyatvena yo vyāpāra āpteneṣyate sa tasyeṣṭasādhanaṃ viṣabhakṣaṇañca tṛptikāmakṛtisādhyatvena neśvarecchāviṣayaḥ mānābhāvāt /
children.translated_text: Alternatively: whatever activity is desired by a trustworthy person as accomplishable by the effort of one who has a [particular] desire — that is a means to the desired for that person. And eating poison is not the object of the Lord's desire as accomplishable by the effort of one desiring satisfaction, due to the absence of a means of valid knowledge [for that claim].

children.text: ata eva na kalañjaṃ bhakṣayedityatra kalañjabhakṣaṇaṃ tṛptikāmanayā bhakṣaṇapravṛttasya kṛtisādhyatvenāptecchāviṣayo neti tasyeśvarecchāviṣayatve 'pi viśiṣṭaniṣedha upapadyate abhiprāyavidhipakṣe balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitvamānumānikaṃ iṣṭasādhanatāvidhipakṣe tu tadapi śakyamiti gauravamiti //
children.translated_text: For this very reason, in 'one should not eat <s>kalañja</s>,' [the meaning is that] eating <s>kalañja</s>, as accomplishable by the effort of one who has undertaken eating out of desire for satisfaction, is not the object of the desire of a trustworthy person. Thus, even though it is the object of the Lord's desire [in some respect], the qualified prohibition (<s>viśiṣṭaniṣedha</s>) is justified. On the view that the meaning of the injunction is the intention [of the <s>āpta</s>] (<s>abhiprāyavidhipakṣa</s>), the 'not being accompanied by preponderant undesirable [consequences]' is inferential; on the view that the meaning of the injunction is being-a-means-to-the-desired (<s>iṣṭasādhanatāvidhipakṣa</s>), that too is possible — hence there is [only] cumbersomeness [as a disadvantage].

The teachers (<s>ācāryāḥ</s>), however, [hold that] the impelling [cognition] is knowledge of being-a-means-to-the-desired alone. The meaning of the injunctive suffix (<s>liṅgartha</s>) is the intention of a trustworthy person (<s>āpta</s>), due to simplicity. In 'you should cook' (<s>pākaṃ kuryāḥ</s>) and 'I should do' (<s>kuryām</s>), the injunctive suffix (<s>vidhiliṅ</s>) denotes desire for an action whose agent is the addressee; the potential and other suffixes (<s>liṅ</s>) in commands, requests, benedictions, and the like denote the desire of the speaker and others; and the suffix <s>liṅ</s> in general is postulated as denoting desire.
Thus, the meaning of 'one who desires heaven should sacrifice' (<s>svargakāmo yajeta</s>) is: the sacrifice (<s>yāga</s>), or the effort toward the sacrifice, as accomplishable by the effort of one who desires heaven, is desired by a trustworthy person (<s>āpta</s>). From that, through the grasping of the pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>) — 'whatever activity, or effort directed toward whatever activity, is desired by a trustworthy person as accomplishable by one's effort, that is a means to the desired not accompanied by preponderant undesirable [consequences] for that [person]' — one infers the being-a-means-to-the-desired of the sacrifice.
The explanation is as follows: the sacrifice is a means to my desired [end], because it is desired by a trustworthy person as being within the scope of my effort — just as food that my father desires as within the scope of my effort is a means to my desired [end]; so too is this, therefore it is likewise.
Similarly, the meaning of 'one should not eat <s>kalañja</s>' (<s>na kalañjaṃ bhakṣayet</s>) is: my effort toward eating <s>kalañja</s> is not the object of the desire of a trustworthy person.
From that: eating <s>kalañja</s> is a means to preponderant undesirable [consequences] for me, because, even though it is a means to the desired for me, it is not desired by a trustworthy person as within the scope of my effort — just as food mixed with honey and poison, which is not desired by my father as within the scope of my effort, is a means to preponderant undesirable [consequences] for me; so too is this, therefore it is likewise. And that trustworthy person (<s>āpta</s>) is none other than the blessed Lord (<s>Īśvara</s>), the expounder of the <s>Veda</s>.
As for one who does not accept the human authorship (<s>pauruṣeyatva</s>) of the <s>Veda</s>, the injunction itself, like the embryo within the womb of the virgin <s>Śruti</s>, is the means of valid knowledge when joined with the male [principle of authorship].
