children.text:
atrocyate ghaṭamānayeti vākyaśravaṇānantaraṃ prayojyasya dhaṭānayanagocarapravṛttyā ghaṭānayanakāryatājñānamanumitaṃ bālena na tu kāryānvitajñānaṃ pravṛttiviśeṣe tasyāhetutvādghaṭādipadaśaktigrahe tasyānupayogācca /
tatra tajjñānaviśeṣe ghaṭamānayetivākyaviśeṣasyānākalitapadavibhāgasya hetutvamavadhārya ghaṭapada-dvitīyā-dhātu-vidhipratyayānāṃ pratyekamāvāpodvāpadvāreṇa ghaṭakarmatvānayana -kāryatvajñāneṣu pratyekaṃ kāraṇatvamavagamya śaktiṃ kalpayati /
paścāt pravṛttisāmānyenānumitakāryānvitajñāna vākyamātrasyānyalabhyatvena kāryāṃśamapahāyānvitajñānamātre śaktiṃ kalpayati na tu prathamaṃ vākyamātrasya kāryānvitajñānamātrahetutvakalpanaṃ /
atha ghaṭānayanakriyāyāḥ prathamaṃ kriyātvajñānātpravṛttimātrānumānaṃ tena ca kāryānvitajñānamanumāya tatra vākyamātrasya hetutvaṃ kalpayitvā śaktiṃ kalpayati taduttaraṃ viśeṣayoḥ kārya-kāraṇabhāvadhīriti cet na prathamaṃ pravṛttimātra-kāryānvitajñānamātrayoranumānaṃ bālasya kramaśobhavatītyatra mānābhāvāt ghaṭādipadaśaktigrahasya tena vināpi sambhavāt /
na ca tadanumānasāmagrī tadāvṛtteti vācyam /
tadā vyāptyādismṛtau mānābhāvāt /
sāmānyayoḥ kārya-kāraṇabhāvagraho viśeṣayostathātvagrahe heturiti cet na viśeṣayoranvaya-vyatirekābhyāmeva tadgrahāt /
yathā dhūma-vahniviśeṣayoḥ kārya-kāraṇabhāvagrahe tatsāmānyayorapi hetu-hetumadbhāvo bhāsate anyathā na sakṛddarśanagamyā vyāptiḥ syāt tathātrāpi viśeṣayoḥ kārya-kāraṇabhāvavittivedya eva sāmānyayostathābhāva iti cet na pratyakṣeṇa viśeṣagrahe yogyatvāt sāmānyamapi bhāsate prakṛte ca kāryaviśeṣeṇa kāraṇaviśeṣānumitau na sāmānyamiti na yugapadupasthitiḥ /
atha viśeṣayoḥ kārya-kāraṇabhāvāt sāmānyayorapi tathātvamanumāpayatīti cet tarhi viśeṣayoḥ kārya-kāraṇabhāvāvagamaḥ prāthamika iti tanmūlakaḥ prathamaṃ padaviśeṣe śaktigraha eva syāt niṣprayojanakatvenāntarānumitau mānābhāvāt yaccoktaṃ pravṛttikāraṇatayopasthitaṃ kāryānvitajñānamapahāyānvitajñānaṃ kalpayitvā tatra śaktikalpanamayuktaṃ uyayathā gauravāditi tanna kāryānvitajñāne 'nvitajñānatvasya sattvāt tadviśeṣatvāt tasya atastatraiva śaktigraho na kāryatvāṃśe 'pi /
ata eva ghaṭavadbhūtalajñāne bhūtalajñānanatvamapīti tadbhinnaṃ tajjñānamabhāvavyavahāre kāraṇaṃ tvayāpi svīkṛtaṃ /
astyevaṃ kintu tadupasthitāvapyanvitajñānatvaṃ na viṣaya iti tasyaivopasthityantaraṃ kalpyamiti cet na kāryānvitajñāne anvitajñānaṃ viśeṣyamiti tadupasthitau tasyāpi viṣayatvāt viśiṣṭajñānasāmagrītoviśeṣyabhānāvaśyambhāvāt anyathā anyajjātijñānaṃ anyacca jātiviśiṣṭajñānamiti vyaktijñānamapahāya jātijñānaṃ kvāpi nopasthitamiti na tava jātireva padārthaḥ syāt jāteḥ kevalopasthitau ca vyaktisamānasaṃvit saṃvedyatvaṃ na syāt /
atha jātiviśiṣṭajñānopasthitervyavyaktijñānaviṣayatve 'pi gauravādvyakteranyalabhyatvācca jātiviśiṣṭajñānatvaṃ na śakyatāvacchedakaṃ kintu jātijñānatvaṃ lāghavāditi mataṃ tarhi tulyam / na ca yugapadupasthitau lāghavāvatārona cātra yugapadupasthitiriti vācyam /
viśiṣṭajñānasya viśeṣyaviṣayatvaniyamāt kiñca mamedaṃ kāryamiti jñānaṃ sākṣādupapādakaṃ pravṛttyā svakāraṇatvenānumitamatastatra śaktiṃ gṛhṇīyāt sākṣādupapādakaviṣayatvāt kalpanāyāḥ śaktiṃ gṛhṇīyāt sākṣādupapādakaviṣayatvāt kalpanāyāḥ /
na tvidaṃ kāryajñāne tasya sākṣādupapādakatvāt /
athedaṃ kāryamitijñāne śaktyaiva paramparayānumānadvārā mamedaṃ kāryamiti jñānasambhavāt anyalabhyatvena na śaktikalpanā tarhi itarānvitajñānaśaktyaiva kāryavācakapadasamabhivyāhārāreṇaiva kāryānvitajñānasambhavāt anyalabhyatvena na tatra śaktikalpanamiti tulyam /
children.translated_text: Here it is said: After hearing the sentence '<s>ghaṭam ānaya</s>' (bring the pot), the child infers the cognition of the obligatoriness of bringing the pot from the directed person's volitional activity pertaining to bringing the pot — but not a cognition of the connected-with-obligatoriness, since that is not the cause of the particular volitional activity, and since it is useless for grasping the capacity of words like '<s>ghaṭa</s>' (pot). There, having ascertained that the particular sentence '<s>ghaṭam ānaya</s>' — whose word-divisions have not yet been analyzed — is the cause of that particular cognition, and having understood through the method of agreement and difference (<s>āvāpa-udvāpa</s>) of the word '<s>ghaṭa</s>,' the accusative case-ending, the verbal root, and the injunctive suffix, that each individually is the cause of the cognitions of pot-as-object, bringing, and obligatoriness respectively, [the child] postulates the linguistic capacity. Subsequently, having inferred through volitional activity in general a cognition connected with obligatoriness, since only the sentence as a whole [produces this] and it is not obtainable otherwise, [the child] postulates the capacity for mere connected cognition, setting aside the obligatoriness component — but the initial postulation is not that the sentence as a whole is the cause merely of cognition connected with obligatoriness. If one says: First, from the cognition of the action-ness of the action of bringing the pot, mere volitional activity is inferred; then, having inferred through that the cognition connected with obligatoriness, and having postulated the causality of the sentence as a whole with respect to that, [the child] postulates the capacity, and subsequently there is cognition of the cause-effect relation between the particulars — no, because there is no evidence that the child first infers mere volitional activity and then mere cognition-connected-with-obligatoriness in sequence, since the grasping of the capacity of words like '<s>ghaṭa</s>' is possible even without that. Nor should one say that the inferential apparatus recurs at that time — because there is no evidence for the recollection of concomitance and the like at that time. If one says: The grasping of the cause-effect relation between the universals is the cause of grasping the same between the particulars — no, because the latter is grasped through positive and negative concomitance of the particulars alone. Just as when the cause-effect relation between particular smoke and particular fire is grasped, the causal relation between their universals also appears — otherwise, concomitance cognizable from a single observation would not be possible — so here too, the causal relation between universals is knowable only through the cognition of the cause-effect relation between particulars — if so, no, because when a particular is grasped by perception, the universal too appears due to suitability; but in the present case, when a particular effect is used to infer a particular cause, the universal does not [appear], so there is no simultaneous presentation. If one says: From the cause-effect relation between the particulars, the same between the universals is inferred — then, since the understanding of the cause-effect relation between the particulars is primary, the capacity-grasping should first be with respect to the particular word based on that alone, and there is no evidence for an intermediate inference, it being purposeless. As for the statement that, setting aside the cognition-connected-with-obligatoriness that is presented as the cause of volitional activity, one postulates the capacity with respect to mere connected cognition, and postulates the capacity there — this is unjustified, due to complexity — that is wrong, because connected-cognition-ness exists in cognition-connected-with-obligatoriness, it being a particular instance of that; therefore the capacity is grasped with respect to that alone, not also with respect to the obligatoriness component. For this very reason, in the cognition of a ground possessing a pot, the nature of ground-cognition is also present — and you too have accepted that a cognition different from that [i.e., ground-cognition without pot] is the cause of the usage of absence. If one says: Granted, but even when that is presented, connected-cognition-ness is not the content — so a separate presentation of that must be postulated — no, because in cognition-connected-with-obligatoriness, connected cognition is the qualificand, so in its presentation, that [connected-cognition-ness] too is a content, since in the apparatus of qualified cognition, the appearance of the qualificand is necessary; otherwise, [if] one cognition is of the universal and another is of the qualified-by-universal, and setting aside the cognition of the individual, the universal-cognition is never presented anywhere — then for you the universal alone could not be the word-meaning; and if the universal alone were presented, the perceptibility in the same cognition as the individual would not obtain. If one says: Even though the presentation of cognition-qualified-by-universal includes the individual-cognition as content, due to complexity and because the individual is obtainable otherwise, being-cognition-qualified-by-universal is not the delimitor of denotative capacity, but rather being-universal-cognition, by parsimony — then the same [applies here]. Nor should one say that parsimony enters [only] when there is simultaneous presentation, and here there is no simultaneous presentation — because of the rule that qualified cognition has the qualificand as its content. Furthermore, the cognition 'this is my obligation' is the direct explicator, inferred through volitional activity as its cause — therefore one should grasp the capacity with respect to that, since postulation has as its content what directly explains. But not 'this is an obligation' [without 'my'], since the former is the direct explicator of that. If one says: Through the capacity for the cognition 'this is an obligation,' the cognition 'this is my obligation' is possible through a further inference — so due to its being obtainable otherwise, there is no postulation of capacity [for the latter] — then equally, through the capacity for mere connected cognition, the cognition connected with obligatoriness is possible through co-occurrence with a word denoting obligatoriness — so due to its being obtainable otherwise, there is no postulation of capacity for that either — the parity is the same.

children.text:
nanvidaṃ kāryamiti jñānaṃ sākṣādeva pravartakaṃ kartavyatāprayojakayāvadekaviśeṣaṇasya svagatatvapratisandhānaṃ sahakāri tena nātiprasaṅgaḥ /
na ca sahakārivilambena kāryānutpāde sākṣātsādhanatvaṃ nivartata iti cet na lāghavena mamedaṃ kāryamiti jñānādeva pravṛtteḥ yathā ca bhaviṣyadviṣayā kāryatānumitistasthoktamadhastāt /
api ca yādṛśasya puruṣasyāvigītakṛtisādhyamidaṃ tādṛśo 'hamiti dhīrna pravṛttihetuḥ kṛtakriyamāṇaviṣayakakṛtisādhyatājñānasya siddhaviṣayasyāsiddhaviṣayecchānutpādakatvāt icchāyāḥ svaprakārakadhīsādhyatvena kṛtyā sādhayāmītīcchāyāḥ svaprakāradhīsādhyatvena kṛtyā sādhayāmītīcchāyāḥ svakṛtyanantarabhaviṣyattārūpakṛtisādhyatādhījanyatvācca /
api cāstu prathamaṃ kāryānvitajñāne vākyasya
children.translated_text: Objection: The cognition 'this is an obligation' is itself the direct impeller; the connecting of the single qualifier — its-belonging-to-oneself — with the obligatoriness that impels, is a cooperating condition; thereby there is no over-extension. Nor does the direct instrumentality cease when the effect is not produced due to the delay of the cooperating condition — no, because by parsimony, volitional activity arises from the very cognition 'this is my obligation.' And how the inference of obligatoriness pertains to a future object — that has been stated above. Moreover, the cognition 'I am such a person for whom this, whose producibility by <s>kṛti</s> is uncontested, [is to be done]' is not the cause of volitional activity, because the cognition of producibility by <s>kṛti</s> that has an already-accomplished-or-being-accomplished object does not produce desire with respect to an unaccomplished object; and because desire, being producible by a cognition having its own mode, and the desire 'I shall accomplish by means of <s>kṛti</s>' is produced by the cognition of producibility by <s>kṛti</s> having the form of what-will-exist-immediately-after-one's-own-<s>kṛti</s>. Moreover, let the sentence initially [have capacity] with respect to cognition connected with obligatoriness —

children.text:
sākṣātatkāraṇatābodhāttatra śaktigrahaḥ tathāpi paścādāvāpodvāreṇa padaviśeṣasyetarānvitasvārthajñāne śaktiṃ kalpayati lāghavāt /
na tu kāryatvāṃśe 'pi gauravāt anyalabhyācca /
na caivaṃ prathamapravṛttasya sākṣātkāraṇatābodhasya tanmūlakakāryānvitaśaktigrahasya ca bādhā syāditi vācyam /
iṣṭatvāt anyathāsiddhimapaśyato hi bālasya sa bhūta iti tasyābalavattvāt gauravānyalabhyatva-tarka-sahakṛtapramāṇajanyatvenottarasya balavattvāt /
na copajīvyabādhānna tathā pratyatīti vācyam /
upajīvyatve mānābhāvāt /
daivāddhi prathamaṃ tadvṛttaṃ na tu padaviśeṣaśaktigrahe tasya hetutvatena vināpi tatsambhavāt /
na ca prāthamikatvena balattvasya vyabhicārāt /
nāpi sarvaiḥ prathamaṃ pratīyamānatvena balavattvaṃ sarveṣā śarīrāhampratyaye candratārakādiparimāṇasya sarvairalpatvagrahe ca vyabhicārāt /
ata eva pūrvakalpanātaḥ kalpanāntaraprasaṅgaḥ syāditi /
nirastam /
yatrānanyathāsiddhatayopajīvyatayā vā balattvaṃ pūrvakalpanāyāstatra tathātvāt /
kiñca prathamaṃ kāryānvitajñāne vākyasya sākṣāt parampodāsīnaṃ kāraṇatvamātraṃ gṛhyate na tu viśeṣo 'pi upāyasyānvaya'vyatirekāderubhayaviśeṣasādhāraṇatvena tatsaṃśayakatvāt utsargo 'pi bādhakābhāvaniścayasahakṛto niścāyakaḥ /
na cānyalabhyatvasya bādhakasyābhāvamāpātataḥ svato darśanamātreṇa bālo niścetumarhati /
ata eva prāmāṇyasyautsargikatve 'pi bādhakābhāvasahakṛtaniścayādeva niścayaḥ anyathā pramāpramā vā sākṣātparamparāsādhanaṃ veti saṃśayaḥ kvāpi na syāt /
yacca harṣahetūnāṃ bahūnāṃ sambhavādityādi tanna svatohītaharṣahetustanapānāderbādhāvatāradanyasya harṣahetoragrahādupasthitatvādupapādakatvācca putrajanmajñānasyaiva harṣahetutvena kalpanāt /
anyapriyajñānaṃ harṣakāraṇaṃ bhaviṣyatīti śaṅkāyāḥ kathamevamiti cet na evaṃ hi kāryānvitajñāne 'pi śaktirna gṛhyate prayojyajñānahetūnāṃ bahutvādananyathāsiddhaśabdānuvidhānasya ca tulyatvāt anyapriyasyājñānācca jñāne 'pi vā tadā tadupasthitiniyame mānābhāvāt sandehābhāvopapatteḥ liṅgābhāsajanyakākatālīyasampannasaṃvādānumitivaddhaharṣeṇa liṅgena putrajanmajñānānumānasambhavācca /
na cāsāsajatvenānumiterbhramatve taddhetukaśaktigraho bhramaḥ viṣayasya tathābhāvena tayoryathārthatvāt /
yathā kaścit sūtrasañcārādhiṣṭhitaṃ dāruputrakaṃ ghaṭamānayeti niyuṅke sa ca tamānayati tadā cetanavyavahārādiva taddarśī bālo vyutpadyate /
iyaṃ kriyā kṛtijanyā sā jñānajanyā tat vākyajanyamityunumiti paramparāyā bhramatve 'pi taddhetuśaktigrahaḥ tajjanyaśābdabodhaśca yathārtha eva viṣayasya tathābhāvāditi siddhaṃ siddhārthe 'pi śaktigraha iti /
ata eva ``yanna duḥkhena sambhinnaṃ na ca grastamanantaraṃ /
abhilāṣopapanītañca tat sukhaṃ svaḥpadāspadaṃ'' /
ityarthavādopasthite sukhe vedādeva svargapadasya śaktigrahaḥ na tu candanādau sukhoparāgeṇa svargapadaprayogāddheyatādaśāyāñcāprayogāt sukhameva śakyaṃ bahuvittavyayāyāsasādhye tatkarmaṇi sukhamātrārthī na pravartata ityarthavādopasthite svargapadatātparyaṃ /
na cārthavādasyopajīvyatvāt tadunīte tata eva śaktigrahaḥ tasya svargapadatātparyaviṣayatvenāspadatvopapatterna atiśayitasukhatvaṃ vācyaṃ prayogopādhirvātiśayaḥ /
na cātiśayasya sāvadhitvena candanasukhe 'smādayaṃ svarga iti dhīḥ syāt rasādāvivātiśayasya jātitvenāvadhyanirūpyatvāt /
atiśayapadaprayogastu itarajñānāpekṣa iti cet na vicitrahetusādhyatayā vilakṣaṇātiśayasyānekatvenānanugamāt sukhatvāvāntarātiśayatvenāsyānugame 'pyanadhyavasāyena śaktyagrahādapravṛttyāpatteḥ /
sukhatvāvāntarajāteśca sukhamātrasādhāraṇatvāt prayogopādhernirākartavyatvāt loke ca lakṣaṇā /
nanu duḥkhāsambhinnasukhasya śakyatve candanādau svargapadaprayogolakṣaṇayāpi na syāt sātiśayasukhasya śakyatve tatsambandhitayā candanādau lakṣaṇā bhavati tasmāt duḥkhāsambhinnatvādinopalakṣitā sukhatvāvāntarajātireva vācyā ekajātisattve 'pi vilakṣaṇahetusādhyasvargeṣṭhakajātau mānābhāvāt /
vihitakarmajanyatā ca tattadviśeṣatvenaiva ananugatasyāpi janyatāvacchedakatvāt sambandhamātrañca lakṣaṇābījamiti vakṣyate /
evaṃ devatāyāmapi ``indramupāsītetyādau lāke prayogasyāniyamāt gauṇatayaiva vyavahārāccārthānadhyavasāye 'laukikasahasrākṣādāvindrādipadaśaktigrahaḥ pramāṇañca ``indraḥ sahasrākṣa ityādirvidhisabhabhivyāhṛtor'thavāda eva svargapadavat /
atha svargapade pravṛttyanyathānupapattyā ``tatsukhaṃ svaḥpadāspadamitiśruteścārthavādādeva śaktigrahaḥ na ceha tathārthavādaḥ kintu ``indraḥ sahasrākṣa ityādi stāvakatvena pravṛttiparamiti cet na indraḥ sahasrākṣaityādiprasiddhapadasāmānādhikaraṇyaśrutau bādhakaṃ vinā sahasrākṣasyaivendrādipadavācyatvāvadhāraṇāt prasiddhapadasamanvabalena pratīyamānamarthamabādhitamādāyaiva teṣāṃ pravartakatvāt /
mantraprakāśitaśaśiśekharādyupetamuddiśya havistyāgena tatraiva yājñikānāṃ devatāvyavahārāt /
api ca ``śivāya gāṃ dadyādityādinā devatāsampradānatvaśruteḥ śivādisahasranāmnāṃ paryāyatvena śrutermahājanaparigraheṇa pramāṇatvādārādhitadevatāyāṃ varadātṛtvaśruteśca bādhakaṃ vinā cetanaiva devatā /
atha devatācaitanyapakṣe
children.translated_text:
From the cognition of direct causality, the capacity [of words] is grasped there; even so, afterwards through the method of extraction and abstraction (<s>āvāpoddhāra</s>), [the learner] postulates the capacity of specific words to produce the cognition of their own meaning connected with other [words] — because of parsimony (<s>lāghava</s>).
But not in the obligation-aspect as well — because of prolixity, and because [that aspect] is obtainable from another [source].
Nor should it be said that in this way, there would be sublation of the first-arising cognition of direct causality and of the capacity-grasping grounded in obligation-connection —
because [the first cognition] was desired [at the time], and because for the child who does not see [that it is] otherwise established, it was [provisionally] valid. But [the first cognition] is weak; while the later [cognition] is strong, being produced by a means of valid knowledge assisted by the reasoning of prolixity and obtainability-from-another.
Nor should it be said that because of the sublation of what is depended upon (<s>upajīvya</s>), [the later cognition] is not so cognized —
because there is no means of valid knowledge for its being what is depended upon.
For it was by chance that [the first cognition] occurred first — it is not [the case that] it functions as a cause in the grasping of the capacity of a specific word, since that [capacity-grasping] is possible even without it.
Nor [is there] strength through primacy — because of deviation [from that rule].
Nor is there strength through being cognized first by all — because of deviation in the case of the body-ego cognition (<s>śarīrāhampratyaya</s>) [which is universal but erroneous], and in the grasping of the smallness of the moon, stars, etc. by all [which is also erroneous].
Precisely for this reason, [the concern that] from the prior postulation there would follow [the undesirable consequence of] another postulation — is set aside.
For where the prior postulation has strength through being not-otherwise-established or through being what is depended upon, there it is indeed so.
Furthermore, initially, in the obligation-connected cognition, only the mere causality of the sentence — indifferent to [whether it is] direct or indirect — is grasped, not even a particular [mode]. Because the method of agreement and difference (<s>anvayavyatireka</s>) etc., being common to both particular [modes], produces doubt about them. Even the general principle (<s>utsarga</s>) produces certainty only when assisted by the ascertainment of the absence of a sublating cognition.
Nor can the child determine, merely from his own casual observation, the absence of a sublating cognition [for the claim] of obtainability-from-another.
Precisely for this reason, even though the validity [of cognition] is a default (<s>autsargika</s>), certainty arises only from certainty assisted by the absence of a sublating cognition. Otherwise, nowhere would there be the doubt 'is this valid cognition or not?' or 'is this a direct or indirect means?'
As for [the objection] 'because of the possibility of many causes of joy' etc. — that is wrong: because the cause of joy that is beneficial by its own nature, such as suckling at the breast, has no occasion for sublation; because no other cause of joy is grasped; because [the knowledge of the son's birth] is readily available [as the cause]; and because of its supporting reasoning — [therefore] the knowledge of the son's birth alone is postulated as the cause of joy.
[Objection:] How [can it be said] that the suspicion 'knowledge of another pleasant [event] will be the cause of joy' [is not valid]? [Reply:] No — for in this way, even in obligation-connected cognition, no capacity would be grasped, because of the multiplicity of causes of the prompted person's knowledge, and because the conformity to the not-otherwise-established word is equally [applicable]. And because of ignorance of another pleasant [event]; or even if [there is] knowledge, because of the absence of a means of valid knowledge for the rule that its presentation would be [restricted to] that [time], it is compatible that there is no doubt. And because inference of the knowledge of the son's birth is possible through the inferential mark of that joy — like the coincidental correspondence-inference (<s>kākatālīyasampannasaṃvādānumiti</s>) produced from a pseudo-mark.
Nor [should it be said] that if the inference is erroneous due to [using] a non-genuine [mark], the capacity-grasping caused by it is also erroneous — because [both] are veridical, since the content is indeed so.
Just as someone commands a wooden puppet operated by strings, saying 'bring the pot,' and the puppet brings it — a child observing that learns the convention as if from the behavior of a sentient being. Even though the series of inferences — 'this action is produced by effort, that [effort] is produced by knowledge, that [knowledge] is produced by the sentence' — is erroneous, the capacity-grasping caused by it and the verbal cognition produced from it are veridical, because the content is indeed so. Thus it is established that capacity is grasped even regarding established [i.e. non-injunctive] meaning.
Precisely for this reason — [regarding the verse:] 'That which is not mixed with pain, not consumed immediately after [arising], and accompanied by longing — that pleasure is the referent of the word <s>svaḥ</s> (heaven)' — the capacity of the word <s>svarga</s> (heaven) is grasped from the <s>Veda</s> itself through the pleasure presented in this explanatory passage (<s>arthavāda</s>); not from the usage of the word <s>svarga</s> in connection with the pleasure accompanying sandalwood etc. [in worldly usage] — because there is no [such] usage in the state of [Vedic] instruction (<s>heyatā</s>). Pleasure alone is the denotation [of <s>svarga</s>]; [and] one who desires mere pleasure does not engage in rites requiring the expenditure of much wealth and effort — hence the purport of the word <s>svarga</s> [rests] in [the special pleasure] presented in the explanatory passage.
Nor should it be said that because the explanatory passage is what is depended upon, the capacity is grasped from that alone as elicited by it — because, since [the arthavāda] has its ground in being the content of the purport of the word <s>svarga</s>, [the denotation] need not be said to be 'surpassingly excellent pleasure.' Or the surpassing [excellence] is a condition of [worldly] usage.
Nor [can it be said] that since the surpassing [excellence] has a limit, [one might think] 'this pleasure from sandalwood is heaven' — because the surpassing [excellence], like the surpassing [excellence] in taste etc., is a universal (<s>jāti</s>) and hence cannot be determined by a limit.
[Objection:] The usage of the word 'surpassing' depends on knowledge of another [lesser pleasure]. [Reply:] No — because the variously-caused surpassing [excellences] are diverse and non-homogeneous; and even if this [surpassing quality] is homogeneous as a sub-universal of pleasure-ness, because of the undesirable consequence of non-engagement due to non-grasping of capacity through non-determination (<s>anadhyavasāya</s>).
And because the sub-universal of pleasure-ness is common to mere pleasure [in general], and because the condition of usage is to be excluded, there is secondary signification (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>) in worldly [usage].
[Objection:] If pleasure-not-mixed-with-pain is the denotation, then the usage of the word <s>svarga</s> for sandalwood etc. would not occur even through secondary signification. If surpassingly excellent pleasure is the denotation, then secondary signification can apply to sandalwood etc. through their connection [with that pleasure]. Therefore, the sub-universal of pleasure-ness indicated by [attributes like] 'not mixed with pain' etc. should be said to be the denotation — because even if there is a single universal, there is no means of valid knowledge for [a separate] universal of [specifically] heaven-pleasure characterized by being produced from variously different causes.
And the property of being produced by enjoined rites, being only in the form of this or that particular [rite], can serve as the delimiting condition of the [causal] relation even without homogeneity (<s>anugama</s>). And that mere connection is the seed of secondary signification — as will be stated.
Similarly, regarding deities too — in [injunctions like] 'one should meditate on <s>Indra</s>' etc., since the usage [of the word <s>Indra</s>] is not restricted in the world, and since the worldly usage is only figurative (<s>gauṇa</s>), and since the meaning is not [thereby] determined — the capacity of the word <s>Indra</s> etc. [to denote] the thousand-eyed [deity] (<s>sahasrākṣa</s>) etc., which is other-worldly, is grasped. And the means of valid knowledge is the explanatory passage co-uttered with the injunction — '<s>Indra</s> is thousand-eyed' etc. — just as with the word <s>svarga</s>.
[Objection:] In the case of the word <s>svarga</s>, the capacity is grasped from the explanatory passage alone through the impossibility of otherwise explaining the [prompted] activity, and through the <s>śruti</s> 'that pleasure is the referent of the word <s>svaḥ</s>.' But here there is no such explanatory passage; rather, '<s>Indra</s> is thousand-eyed' etc. is oriented toward praise (<s>stāvaka</s>) as the basis of activity. [Reply:] No — because when [the <s>śruti</s>] presents the co-referentiality of '<s>Indra</s> is thousand-eyed' with well-known words, in the absence of a sublating cognition, the denotation of the word <s>Indra</s> etc. is ascertained as being [the entity that is] thousand-eyed alone. Because [those texts] function as motivating factors only by taking the unsublated meaning cognized through the force of co-referentiality with the well-known word.
Because of the practice of ritualists (<s>yājñika</s>) who direct their oblation (<s>havis</s>) toward [an entity] described [in <s>mantras</s>] as having the moon-crescent and other [attributes], and apply the term 'deity' to that very [entity].
Furthermore, from the <s>śruti</s> '[one should give] a cow to <s>Śiva</s>' etc. which teaches that the deity is the recipient (<s>sampradāna</s>); from the <s>śruti</s> of <s>Śiva</s>'s thousand names etc. being synonyms; from the authority [of those texts] through their acceptance by great persons; and from the <s>śruti</s> of the worshipped deity being a granter of boons — in the absence of a sublating cognition, the deity is indeed sentient.
[Objection:] In the view that deities are sentient —

tatprītireva yāgavyāpāra iti nāpūrvasiddhiriti cet na prīteḥ sukhasya tadanubhavasya cāśutaravināśitvāt tajjanyasaṃskārasya svāviṣaye phalāhetutvāt phalahetusthāyikṛtivyāpārāpekṣāyāṃ lāghavena kṛtisamānāśrayasyaiva vyāpāratvakalpanāt /
nānāyāgeṣṭakadāhvāne caikadā sannidhānaṃ tadbaddhiviśeṣa eva pratiṣṭhāvidhinā pratimādāvahaṅkāravat /
atha rājasūyādiphalatvena śraterindrādiścetana eva devatātvantu tasya nāsti mānābhāvāt kintu deśanādeśikatacaturthyantapadanirddeśyatvaṃ devatātvamitīndrāyetyādipadameva devatā ata evāgniprakāśakamantreṇāgniprakāśanānantaraṃ agnaya iti niyamato havisastyāgo na paryāyāntareṇa /
na cendroddeśena havisastyāga indraniṣṭhakiñcijjanakaḥ tatsvarūpājanakatve sati taduddeśena kriyamāṇatvāt brāhmaṇāya dānavaditi vācyam /
aprayojakatvāt tadarthatvena kriyamāṇatvasyopādhitvācca /
indrāya svāhetyatra na tādarthye caturthī kintu svāhādipadayoge upapadavibhaktireva anyathā ``namaḥ-svasti-svāhetyādisūtravaiyarthyāt /
maivaṃ /
caturthyantapadasya devatātve mānābhāvāt caturthīṃ vināpi indro devateti vyavahārāt /
agraye kavyavāhanāyetyādau devatādvayaprasaṅgāt ``indraḥ sahasrakṣa ityarthavādasya ``indramupāsītetyādividhisamabhivyāhāreṇa ekavākyatayā tasyaivopāyasyatvāt ``śivasvannādadītetyatra mahādevamuddiśya tyakte 'pi śiṣṭānāṃ śivasvatvena vyavahārācca /
agnaya iti padena niyamatastyāgaśrutibodhitatvena tathā tyāgasya phalahetutvāt /
na ca bījākṣarāṇāṃ devatātvāt tatraiva śivādipadaśaktigraha iti vācyam / bījākṣarāṇāṃ caturthyantatvāniyamāt /
tadapratītāvapi mantraprakāśitaśaśiśekharādyupetamuddiśya havistyāgena tatraiva yājñikānāṃ vyavahāraḥ bījākṣarāṇāṃ havistyāgabhāgitvenānuddeśyatvāt śivasya pratimantraṃ bījākṣarāṇāṃ nānātvāt ananugamena śivapadaśaktigrahasyāśakyatvācca /
na ca mūrtibhedena śivaśarīrāṇāmananugatatvena tavāpi na śaktigraha iti vācyam /
bālyādinā bhinnaśarīreṣu caitratvavacchivatvajātedṛṣṭaviśeṣopagṛhītatvasya vānugatvāt adṛṣṭaśūnyasya ceśvarasya na devatātvaṃ īśānaśca tadbhinna eva tasmānmantrakaraṇakahavistyāgabhāgitvenoddeśyatvaṃ devatātvaṃ anyeṣāṃ haviḥsambandhe mantrasyāhetutvāditi /
children.translated_text:
If [it is said that] the satisfaction (<s>prīti</s>) of that [deity] itself is the intermediary operation (<s>vyāpāra</s>) of the sacrifice, and therefore <s>apūrva</s> is not established — no, because satisfaction, being pleasure (<s>sukha</s>), and the experience thereof are quickly destroyed; because the impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) produced by it is not a cause of the result in a domain other than its own; and because when a lasting intermediary operation of effort that is a cause of the result is required, by simplicity, the intermediary operation is postulated as residing in the same substratum as the effort (<s>kṛti</s>).
In the case of diverse sacrifices, the proximity [of the deity] at one time during the brick-laying ceremony is [to be understood as] a specific cognition connected with that [ceremony] alone, through the consecration injunction (<s>pratiṣṭhāvidhi</s>), like the ego-identification (<s>ahaṅkāra</s>) with images and the like.
Now, since <s>Indra</s> and other conscious beings are heard [in scripture] as recipients of the results of <s>Rājasūya</s> and other [sacrifices], [one might think] the deity-hood (<s>devatātva</s>) belongs to the conscious [being] itself; but that is not so, due to the absence of a means of valid knowledge. Rather, deity-hood consists in being denotable by a word in the dative case that is taught and taught [in the context of the sacrifice]; thus the word '<s>Indrāya</s>' (for <s>Indra</s>) and the like is itself the deity. For this very reason, after the manifestation of <s>Agni</s> by the <s>Agni</s>-manifesting <s>mantra</s>, the offering of the oblation (<s>havis</s>) is invariably made with [the words] '<s>Agnaye</s>' (for <s>Agni</s>), not by any other expression.
Nor should it be said that the offering made for the sake of <s>Indra</s> produces something in <s>Indra</s>, because it is performed for his sake while not producing his very form, like a gift to a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> —
because [the analogy] is non-conclusive, and because 'being performed for his sake' is a limiting condition (<s>upādhi</s>).
In '<s>Indrāya svāhā</s>' (for <s>Indra</s>, hail!), the dative is not in the sense of purpose, but is merely a secondary case-ending (<s>upapadavibhakti</s>) occurring in conjunction with words like <s>svāhā</s>; otherwise, the <s>sūtra</s> '<s>namaḥ-svasti-svāhā</s>' and the like would be purposeless.
Do not [say] so.
Because there is no means of valid knowledge for the deity-hood of the dative-ending word; because even without the dative, the usage '<s>Indra</s> is the deity' [exists]; because in [expressions like] '<s>Agraye kavyavāhanāya</s>' (for <s>Agni</s>, the carrier of offerings to the ancestors), there would be the absurd consequence of two deities; because the <s>arthavāda</s> '<s>Indra</s> is the thousand-eyed' is part of a single sentence with injunctions like 'one should worship <s>Indra</s>' and thus serves as a means [of knowing <s>Indra</s>]; and because in '<s>Śivasya annam ādadīta</s>' (one should take <s>Śiva</s>'s food), even though [the food] is offered to <s>Mahādeva</s>, the learned use the designation '<s>Śiva</s>'s' [for the food].
Because the offering is invariably made through the word '<s>Agnaye</s>,' as conveyed by the scriptural statement regarding offering, and because such offering is a cause of the result.
Nor should it be said that since the seed-syllables (<s>bījākṣara</s>) are the deities, the denotative power of words like <s>Śiva</s> and the like is grasped therein [i.e., in the seed-syllables] — because the seed-syllables are not invariably in the dative case.
Even when those [seed-syllables] are not cognized, the ritualists' practice consists in offering the oblation directed toward [the deity] endowed with the crescent-moon crest and other [attributes] revealed by the <s>mantra</s>, since the seed-syllables are not the intended recipient by virtue of being [merely] the share-holder in the offering of oblation; and because <s>Śiva</s>'s seed-syllables differ from <s>mantra</s> to <s>mantra</s>, there being no invariable concomitance, the grasping of the denotative power of the word <s>Śiva</s> [through the seed-syllables] is impossible.
Nor should it be said that since <s>Śiva</s>'s bodies lack invariable concomitance due to the difference of forms, even for you there is no grasping of the denotative power [of the word <s>Śiva</s>] —
because there is invariable concomitance of <s>Śiva</s>-hood as a universal (<s>jāti</s>), delimited by <s>Śivatva</s>, like <s>Caitratva</s> (being <s>Caitra</s>) in the different bodies [of <s>Caitra</s>] at childhood and other [stages], or because what is apprehended by a particular unseen [quality] is invariant. And for the Lord (<s>Īśvara</s>), who is devoid of the unseen (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>), there is no deity-hood; and <s>Īśāna</s> is indeed different from Him. Therefore, deity-hood consists in being the intended recipient in the offering of oblation that has the <s>mantra</s> as its instrument; for others, the <s>mantra</s> is not the cause of the connection with the oblation.

kvacicca vākyaśeṣācchaktigrahaḥ yathā yavamayaścarurbhavati vārāhī copānat vaitase kaṭe prājāpatyaṃ caruṃ cinotītyatra yava-varāha-vetasaśabdāḥ kiṃ kaṅga-vāyasajambūnāṃ vācakāḥ uta dīrghaśrūka-sūkara-vañjulānāmiti mlecchāryavyavahāradarśanādvipratipattau mukhyārthānadhyavasāyāt tatpade pramāṇyāniścaye vyavahārādvyutpattiḥ sa cāviśiṣṭaḥ pikādipadeṣu mlecchavyavahārādvyutpatteḥ sūkarasyeva carmaṇā kākasyāpyupānahoḥ sambhavāditi pūrvapakṣe vasante sarvasasyānāṃ jāyate patraśātanaṃ modanamānāḥ pradṛśyante yavāḥ kaṇiśaśalinaḥ /
''varāhaṃ gāvo 'nudhāvanti'' /
''ambujo vetasaḥ'' /
iti vākyāśeṣarūpavedavirodhinau mlecchaprasiddhaḥ smṛtiriva vedaviruddhā heyeti nirastāyāṃ mlecchaprasiddhau niṣpratipakṣāryavyavahārācchaktigrahaḥ / nanu vākyaśeṣāt śrūkarādiṣu tātparyaniścayo na śaktinirṇāyakaḥ kākādi sadṛśatayā śrūkarādau prayogasya gauṇyādināpi sambhavāditi cet na śrūkarādau tātparyavacchakterapi niścayāt /
tathā hi yadyapyanādiprayogayāgitā na śaktiniyatā vaidikagauṇyādinā vyabhicārāt tathāpi śaktiranādiprayoganiyatā ato varāhaśabdasyānādi /
prayogayogitā śaktiśca kāke kalpyeti gauravaṃ śrūkaratve 'nādivedasambandhāt prayogo 'nādisiddha eva śaktimātraṃ kalpyata iti lāghavamityanāditātparyāt śrakare śaktireva /
atha kākavat śrūkaro 'pyasadṛśa eva susadṛśasya gavayādeḥ sattvāt kathañcit sādṛśyaṃ kākasyāpyastīti cet na kāka-śrūkarayorvarāhaśabdād buddhisthatve 'nayoḥ ko vācya iti jijñāsamānasya smṛtiviṣaya iti tannirāsādanyathā tātparyagrāhakavākyaśeṣasyāpi niṣprayojanatvaṃ syāt kathañcit sādṛśyasya sarvatra sattvena tātparyānadhyavasāyāditi /
itarānvite śaktirityapi guḍajihvikā vastutonvaye 'pi na śaktiḥ /
nanu vyavahāreṇānumite itarānvitajñāne padaśakyatvagrahāt tatraiva śaktiṃ gṛhṇāti upasthitatvāt /
na cāgre tatyāgo hetvabhāvāt na tu padārthajñānamātre vyavahārāt tasyānupasthiteḥ upāyāntarāttadupasthityantarakalpane mānābhāvāt ata itarānvitasvārthajñānaśaktatvena jñātapadaṃ svārthānvayānubhāvakaṃ ityanvitābhidhānamiti cet na itarānvitapadārthajñānopasthitau padārthajñānaṃ viśeṣyamiti tadupasthitau tasyāpi viṣayatvāt viśiṣṭajñānasya viśeṣyaviṣayatvaniyamāditi tatraiva śaktiṃ kalpayati lāghavāt na tvanvayāṃśe 'pi gauravāt /
astu vā prathamamitarānvitajñāne śaktigrahe 'gre tatyāgaḥ anyalabhyatvapratisandhānāt ananyalabhyasyaiva śabdārthatvāt prathamagṛhītamātrañca na balamityuktameva tasmāt sarvaiḥ prathamagṛhītamātrañca na balamityuktameva tasmāt sarvaiḥ prathamavyavahārādupasthite kāryānvitajñāne 'nvitajñāne vā padakāraṇatvagrahāttatra śaktigraho 'gre 'pi gauravānyalabhyatvapratisandhāne 'pi na tatyāgaḥ
children.translated_text:
And in some cases, the grasping of denotative power [occurs] from the remainder of the sentence (<s>vākyaśeṣa</s>). For example, in 'the oblation-cake (<s>caru</s>) is made of barley (<s>yava</s>), and the sandal is of boar [skin] (<s>vārāhī</s>), and he arranges the <s>Prājāpatya</s> oblation-cake on a reed (<s>vetasa</s>) mat' — do the words <s>yava</s>, <s>varāha</s>, and <s>vetasa</s> denote <s>kaṅgu</s> (millet), <s>vāyasa</s> (crow), and <s>jambū</s> (rose-apple), or <s>dīrghaśūka</s> (long-awned [barley]), <s>sūkara</s> (boar), and <s>vañjula</s> (cane)? When there is disagreement due to observing both barbarian (<s>mleccha</s>) and noble (<s>ārya</s>) usage, since the primary meaning cannot be determined, and since the validity of those words is uncertain, the conventional learning is from usage [alone], and that is undifferentiated. In the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> [it is argued that] conventional learning from barbarian usage is [equally valid], since even a crow's [skin could serve for] a sandal, just as a boar's [skin does]. [Reply:] In spring, all crops undergo leaf-fall; the barley plants are seen rejoicing, bearing ears of grain.
'Cows chase after the boar (<s>varāha</s>).'
'The <s>vetasa</s> (reed) is aquatic.'
By these sentence-remainders, which are Vedic [in origin], the barbarian convention, contradicting the <s>Veda</s>, is rejected like a <s>smṛti</s> that contradicts the <s>Veda</s>, and is to be discarded. When the barbarian convention is thus eliminated, the grasping of denotative power [occurs] from the unopposed noble (<s>ārya</s>) usage. [Objection:] The determination of the intended meaning in <s>sūkara</s> (boar) and the like from the sentence-remainder does not settle the denotative power, since the usage for <s>sūkara</s> and the like could be through secondary meaning (<s>gauṇī</s>) and the like due to similarity with the crow and the like. [Reply:] No, because the denotative power determined by the intended meaning for <s>sūkara</s> and the like is also settled.
The explanation is as follows: although being connected with usage from beginningless [time] is not restricted to denotative power — due to deviation through Vedic secondary meaning and the like — nevertheless, denotative power is restricted to [what has] beginningless usage. Therefore, the beginningless usage-connection and the denotative power of the word <s>varāha</s> would have to be postulated for the crow too — this is cumbersome. For <s>sūkara</s> (boar), since the usage is already established from beginningless [time] due to its beginningless connection with the <s>Veda</s>, only the denotative power [needs to be] postulated — this is simpler. Therefore, from the beginningless intended meaning, the denotative power resides in <s>sūkara</s> (boar) itself.
If [it is said:] just as the boar, the crow too is entirely dissimilar, since highly similar [animals] like the <s>gavaya</s> (wild ox) exist, and even the crow has some similarity [to the boar] — no, because when both the crow and the boar are objects of cognition from the word <s>varāha</s>, one who inquires 'which of these two is the denotatum?' [finds that] they are objects of recollection (<s>smṛti</s>), and thus [the crow] is eliminated. Otherwise, even the sentence-remainder that determines the intended meaning would be purposeless, since some similarity exists everywhere, [and so] the intended meaning could never be determined.
That [the denotative power resides] in the connected [meaning] other [than being-an-effect] is also a sleight of hand (<s>guḍajihvikā</s>); in reality, even if there is connection, there is no denotative power [there].
[Objection:] When the knowledge of [the meaning] connected with the other [i.e., non-effect meaning] is inferred from behavior, since the capacity of the word to denote is grasped, one grasps the denotative power precisely therein, due to its being presented.
Nor is there later abandonment [of this postulation], due to the absence of a reason; but not in mere word-meaning knowledge [is the denotative power postulated], since from behavior that [mere word-meaning knowledge] is not presented, due to the absence of a means of valid knowledge for postulating another form of its presentation. Therefore, having a word known as having denotative power in cognition of its own meaning connected with the other [non-effect meaning], [that word] produces the experience of the connection of its own meaning — thus [the theory of] <s>anvitābhidhāna</s> (connected denotation). [Reply:] No, because when the knowledge of the word-meaning connected with the other is presented, the word-meaning knowledge is the qualificand (<s>viśeṣya</s>), and when that [qualificand] is presented, it too has the status of being an object [of the denotative power], since qualified knowledge invariably has the qualificand as its object. Therefore, by simplicity, the denotative power is postulated therein [i.e., in the word-meaning knowledge as qualificand] alone, not in the connection-aspect too, due to cumbersomeness.
Alternatively, even if the denotative power is first grasped in the cognition connected with the other [non-effect meaning], there is later abandonment [of that postulation] through the reflective reasoning of unobtainability-otherwise, since only what is unobtainable otherwise is the meaning of a word, and what is merely grasped first does not have [decisive] force — as has already been stated. Therefore, by all, when the knowledge connected with being-an-effect or the connected knowledge is presented from the initial behavior, and the causality of the word for that [knowledge] is grasped, the grasping of the denotative power is therein; and later too, even when the reflective reasoning of unobtainability-otherwise [is applied], there is no abandonment [of the effect-connected theory] due to cumbersomeness [of the alternative].

pūrvakalpanāyā viparītatvāditi svaśiṣyavyāmohanam /
atha kāryatvasyetarapadalabhyatvena tathā na tvevamanvaye tasyetarapadāśakyatvācchakyatve vā avivādāditi cet na ghaṭaśaktatvena jñātaṃ padaṃ svārthasmaraṇadvārā ākāṅkṣādisahakārivaśāt samabhivyāhṛtapadārthena saha svārthasyānvayamanubhāvayati svabhāvādityanyathaivānvayajñānalābhāt kiṃ śaktyā /
anvayamātraśaktāvapyanvayaviśeṣajñānārthamākāṅkṣāderavaśyamapekṣaṇāt kriyā-kārakapadayoḥ pratyekamitarānvitasvārthabodhakatve vākyarthadvayadhīprasaṅgāt /
na caikamevānvitābhidhāyakamitarattu pratiyogismārakamiti vācyam /
aviśeṣādaśakyānvayānubhave 'tiprasaṅgāt /
anvaye 'pi śaktiriti cet na aśakyamapi hi śakyānvayaṃ bodhayati nānyat śakyānvayatvasya svarūpatoniyāmakatvāt anyathā tavāpyapratīkārāt /
nanvevaṃ padānāmanvitajñānajanakatvāt tatra śaktirastyeva aśaktasyājanakatvāt tavāpi padādanvayabodha itīśvarecchāsattvāditi satyaṃ kintu anvayabodhe svarūpasatī sā vyāptiyate na tu jñātā ghaṭajñānaśaktatvena jñānādeva ghaṭānvayabodhopapatteḥ yathā tava jātiśaktapadasya ātmavyaktijñāne dṛṣṭañca jñātakaraṇe sāmānyasambandhitayā jñātasyāpi viśeṣabuddhyupāyatvaṃ yathā vahnisāmānyavyāptatayā gṛhītadhūmasya vahniviśeṣabuddhijanakatvam /
atha ghaṭajñānatvaṃ itarānvitaghaṭajñāne 'pyastīti tena rūpeṇānvitaghaṭajñāne 'pi jñātā śaktirvyāpriyata iti cet satyaṃ kintu ghaṭajñānatvaṃ śakyatāvacchekaṃ na tvanvitaghaṭajñānatvaṃ gauravāt anyalabhyatvācca /
evañca jātivācakapadasya vyaktāviva ekaiva śaktiranvayāṃśe svarūpasatī padārthāṃśe jñātā vyāptiyate /
jāti-vyakteyaḥ samānasaṃvitsaṃvedyatvāt tathā ghaṭajñānādikantu nānvayaviṣayatāniyataṃ smaraṇe vyabhicārāditi cet ghaṭānubhavaviśeṣaṃ prati ghaṭapadatvena kāraṇatā sa ca śabdānubhavo 'nvayaviṣayatāniyata eva kelalasya śabdenānanubhavāt smaraṇañca prati padatvena na janakatā vyabhicārāt kintu sambandhitayā jñātatvena /
syādetat anvayatātparyakatayā tatpratipādakaṃ padamityavivādaṃ tātparyanirvāhikā ca vṛttiḥ sā ceha na gauṇī na vā lakṣaṇeti śaktisiddhiḥ /
athānvaye lakṣaṇaiva svārthasambandhini tātparyāt padārthopasthityanantaraṃ tadanvayopapatteśca /
na ca vṛttidvayasya virodhaḥ anvayaviśeṣaṇatayā padārthopasthiteḥ /
na ca lākṣaṇikānāmananubhāvakatvādanvayānubhavaḥ kathamiti vācyam /
padārthasya smaraṇādanvaye śaktatvācca padānāṃ śaktyānanubhāvakatayā sarvatra lākṣaṇikasyaivānubhāvakatvaditi /
tanna /
vṛttirhi jñatopayujyate na svarūpasatyatiprasaṅgāt /
na ceha svārthasambandhitayānvayaḥ prāgavagataḥ vākyārthasyāpūrvatvāt /
kiñca śakyasambandhitayā anvaye lakṣaṇārtha padārthe śaktikalpanaṃ tadvaraṃ lāghavādanvaye 'pi śaktirastu kiṃ vṛttidvayakalpanā evaṃ sthite prayoge 'pi anvayaḥ padaśakyaḥ vṛttyatyantaraṃ vinā padapratipādyatvāt padārthavaditi /
ucyate /
vṛttiṃ vināpi tātparyanirvāhāt kiṃ vṛttyā padānāmuktakrameṇānvayabodhajanakatvasambhavādanyathā śaktyā tātparyanirvāhodṛṣṭa iti lakṣaṇocchedaḥ /
atha śaktiṃ vināpiśakyasambandhāt tannirvāha iti na tatra śaktiḥ tarhi vṛttiṃ vināpi tannirvāha iti kiṃ vṛttyā /
ata evānumānamaprayojakaṃ anyathā padapratipādyatvādeva śaktisādhane vṛttyantarocchedaḥ /
ata eva dhūmo 'stītyatra dhūmapadasya vahnibodhaparatve 'pi vahnau na lakṣaṇā śaktyā dhūmopasthitau anumānadvārā tatpratītisambhavāt /
tathā gaccha gacchati cet kānta panthānaḥ santu te śivāḥ /
mamāpi janma tatraiva bhūyādyatra gato bhavān iti /
vākyasya mā gacchetyatra tātparye 'pi na lakṣaṇā gamanasya priyāmaraṇahetutvaṃ hi vākyārthaḥ tena gamanaṃ mayā na kartavyaṃ priyāmaraṇahetutvādityanumānādeva gamane akartavyatābodhanena tātparyanirvāhāt /
children.translated_text: That it is the opposite of the previous postulation — this is merely bewildering one's own students. If one says: Obligatoriness is obtainable from the other word, so it is not so [that it must be part of the sentence's capacity]; but in the case of connection (<s>anvaya</s>), that [connection] is not expressible by the other word, or if it is, there is no dispute — no, because a word known as having the capacity for '<s>ghaṭa</s>' (pot), through the recollection of its own meaning and by the force of cooperating conditions such as expectancy (<s>ākāṅkṣā</s>), produces the experience of the connection of its own meaning with the meaning of co-occurring words, by its very nature — and so the connected cognition is obtainable otherwise; what need is there of a [separate] capacity? Even if the capacity is for mere connection, expectancy and the like must necessarily be resorted to for the cognition of particular connections; and if each of the action-word and case-word independently conveys its own meaning connected with the other, there would be the consequence of two sentence-meaning cognitions. Nor should one say that only one [word] denotes the connected meaning and the other merely reminds of the correlate — because in the absence of a distinguishing feature, there would be the over-extension that even what is incapable of [producing] the connection-experience would [do so]. If one says: There is capacity for the connection too — no, for even what is incapable [by itself] conveys the connection of what is within [the word's] capacity, and nothing else, since being-connected-with-what-is-within-capacity is a delimitor by its very nature; otherwise, you too would have no remedy. Objection: Since words produce connected cognition, there is indeed a capacity for that, since what lacks capacity does not produce [anything]; on your view too, the connection-cognition from words [requires] the existence of God's will — true, but that capacity, which exists in its own nature in the connection-cognition, operates [only]; it is not cognized [separately] — because the connection-cognition of pot is explicable from the very cognition that [the word] has capacity for pot-cognition. Just as on your view, a word having capacity for the universal [produces] cognition of the individual — and it is observed that what is known as a means of knowledge, being known as related to the universal, is also a means to particular cognition, just as smoke grasped as pervaded by fire in general produces cognition of particular fire. If one says: Pot-cognition-ness exists even in connected-pot-cognition, so the capacity known under that aspect operates even in connected-pot-cognition — true, but pot-cognition-ness is the delimitor of denotative capacity, not connected-pot-cognition-ness, due to complexity and obtainability otherwise. Thus, just as a word denoting the universal has one single capacity with respect to the individual, the capacity that exists in its own nature with respect to the connection-component operates when known with respect to the word-meaning component. If one says: The universal and individual are perceptible in the same cognition, whereas pot-cognition and the like are not restricted to having-connection-as-content, due to deviation in recollection — [reply:] The causality with respect to a particular experience of pot is by virtue of being a pot-word, and that verbal experience is indeed restricted to having-connection-as-content, since what is isolated is not experienced through the word; and with respect to recollection, the causality is not by virtue of being a word, due to deviation, but by virtue of being known as related. One might say: It is undisputed that the word conveys [meaning] as having connection as its purport (<s>tātparya</s>), and the function (<s>vṛtti</s>) that accomplishes the purport is neither figurative nor secondary — so the primary capacity is established. Or: With respect to the connection, there is secondary signification (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>) alone, since after the presentation of the word-meaning through purport directed at what is related to its own meaning, the connection is explicable. Nor is there a conflict between two functions, since the word-meaning is presented as a qualifier of the connection. Nor should one say: How is the connection-experience possible, since secondary meanings do not produce experience — because the capacity of words for connection is through recollection of word-meaning, and since words do not produce experience through their primary capacity alone, it is the secondary meaning everywhere that produces experience. That is wrong. For a function is useful [only when] known, not when merely existing in its own form — [the latter would lead to] over-extension. And here the connection through relation to one's own meaning is not previously known, since the sentence-meaning is unprecedented. Furthermore, if there is secondary signification for the word-meaning as related to the denotative capacity and also for the connection — then it is better, by parsimony, to simply have a capacity for the connection as well; why postulate two functions? This being so, even in usage, the connection is denoted by the word, since it is conveyed by the word without any other function, just like the word-meaning. It is said: Even without a function, the purport is accomplished — so what need is there of a function? Since words can produce connection-cognition in the stated order — otherwise, if the purport were accomplished by the [primary] capacity, secondary signification would be destroyed. If one says: Even without capacity, the purport is accomplished through the relation to what is within the denotative power — so there is no capacity there — then equally, even without a function, the purport is accomplished — so what need is there of a function? For this very reason, the inference is ineffective — otherwise, from the mere fact of being conveyed by words, establishing capacity would destroy all other functions. For this very reason, in '<s>dhūmo 'sti</s>' (there is smoke), even though the word '<s>dhūma</s>' (smoke) has the purport of conveying fire, there is no secondary signification with respect to fire, because since smoke is presented through the primary capacity, the cognition of fire is possible through inference. Similarly, in the verse: 'Go — if you must go, may the paths be auspicious for you; may my birth too be there where you have gone' — even though the purport of the passage is 'do not go,' there is no secondary signification, because the sentence-meaning is that going causes the death of the beloved, and through the inference 'going should not be done by me, since it causes the death of my beloved,' the purport is accomplished through the cognition of non-obligatoriness regarding going.

children.text:
yatra hi mukhyayā sākṣāt paramparayā vā na tātparyanirvāhaḥ tatra lakṣaṇā /
nanu ghaṭamānayetyatra pratyekamanvayaviśeṣe jijñāsā bhavati /
na ca sāmānyānavagame viśeṣe sa syāt ityanvayasāmānye śaktireveti cet na kāraṇena kiyāyā ca kriyākārakasāmānyākṣepāttadupapatteḥ dṛṣṭe phalādau rasaviśeṣajijñāsāvat /
etena yaduktamanvitapadārthe mama tvakaika śaktistava tvekā padārthe 'parā tvanvaya iti nirastam /
anvaye śaktyabhāvāt /
na caivamanyayānubhave padaviniyogo na syāditi vācyam /
anvayānubhavārthameva padārthe padānāṃ śaktikalpanāt /
tasmāt padaṃ karaṇaṃ padārthasmaraṇaṃ vyāpāraḥ ākāṅkṣādisahakārivaśāt smāritārthānvayānubhavaḥ phalaṃ padārthasmaraṇaṃ na vyadhāyakaṃ vyāparatvāt /
na ca smaraṇadvārā padārtha eva
children.translated_text: Where the purport cannot be accomplished through the primary meaning, whether directly or indirectly, there is secondary signification (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>). Objection: In '<s>ghaṭam ānaya</s>' (bring the pot), there is a desire to know the particular connection of each [word]. And that [desire] would not arise with respect to the particular without the cognition of the general — so there is indeed a capacity for connection in general — no, because it is explicable through the general implication of action and case-relations by the cause and the action, just as there is a desire to know the particular taste in observed fruits and the like. By this, the statement 'for me there is a single capacity for the connected word-meaning, whereas for you there is one for the word-meaning and another for the connection' is refuted — because there is no capacity for the connection. Nor should one say that in that case, the assignment of particular words to particular experiences would not be possible — because the capacity of words for the word-meaning is postulated precisely for the sake of the connection-experience. Therefore, the word is the instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>), the recollection of word-meaning is the operation (<s>vyāpāra</s>), and through the force of cooperating conditions such as expectancy, the experience of the connection of the recollected meanings is the result (<s>phala</s>). The recollection of word-meaning is not a separate instrument, being the operation.

children.text:
kāraṇaṃ tasyānāgatatvādinā svasmaraṇe anvayānabhave cānakatvāt /
tathapi padārthasmaraṇameva karaṇamastu āvaśayakatvāt ata eva cintāvaśopanītapadārthānāmanvayabodhanāt kāvyādiriti cet na smaraṇasya nirvyāratvenākaraṇatvāt ananyathāsiddhānvaya-vyatirekābhyāṃ ākāṅkṣādimatpadasyānvayānubhavaviśeṣe kāraṇatvāt padārthopasthiteḥ saṃsargadhīmātrahetutve 'pi śābdasaṃsargadhīviṣaye padasyaiva hetutvāt gauḥ karmatvamānayanamityatra padārthajñāne 'pi anvayajñānānudayāt padaviśeṣopasthitapadārthajñānasya hetutve padaviśeṣasyaivāvaśyakatvena hetutvācca /
kāvyasthale ca padārthajñānavyāpārakaṃ utprakṣādisahakṛtaṃ mana evānvayānubhavakaraṇam /
na caiva utprekṣayāḥ prathak pramāṇatvaṃ vyabhicārijātīyatayā liṅgādāviva pramākaraṇatāvacchedakānatiprasaktānugatarūpābhāvānnirvyāpāratvācca kintu pramāṇasahakāriṇī sā /
ata eva mānase liṅgaparāmarśe vyāptismṛtyādi na pṛthak pramāṇam /
atha padamantareṇāpi yogyatādijñāne 'nvayabodho bhavatyataḥ padārthasmaraṇa eva padānāmupakṣayaḥ /
taduktaṃ paśyataḥ śvetamā rūpaṃ heṣābdañca śṛṇvataḥ /
khuravikṣepaśabdañca śveto 'śvedhāvatīti dhīḥ /
iti cet satyaṃ prayojakavākyoccāraṇānantaraṃ prayojyavyāpāradarśanāt anvitajñānopapattyarthaṃ padasyaiva śaktiḥ kalpyate prathamastasyaiva kāraṇatvāvadhāraṇāt /
padārtheṣu śaktyantarakalpane gauravāt tadāhuḥ prāthabhyādibhidhātṛtvāttātparyopagamādapi /
padānāmeva sā śaktirvaramabhyupagamyatā /
iti śveto 'śvedhāvatīti dhīśca liṅgajā padasya kḷptakāraṇabhāvasyābhāvāditi /
children.translated_text: Nor is the word-meaning itself the cause, since being future and the like, in its own recollection, and in the absence of connection, it lacks causality. Still, if one says: Let the recollection of word-meaning itself be the instrument, since it is necessarily required — for this very reason, the connection-cognition of word-meanings brought to mind through reflection is [what constitutes] poetry (<s>kāvya</s>) and the like — no, because recollection lacks an operation and therefore is not an instrument; because through the invariable positive and negative concomitance that is not otherwise explicable, a word possessing expectancy and the like is the cause of the particular connection-experience; and because even though the presentation of word-meaning is the cause merely of relational cognition, only the word is the cause with respect to the content of verbal relational cognition; and because in the cognition 'cow,' 'objecthood,' 'bringing' — even with word-meaning cognition — connection-cognition does not arise [without the words]; and because when the causality of word-meaning-cognition presented by particular words is [established], the particular word itself is necessarily the cause. In the case of poetry, the mind itself — operating through word-meaning cognition and assisted by poetic fancy (<s>utprekṣā</s>) and the like — is the instrument of connection-experience. And poetic fancy is not a separate means of valid knowledge, since like the inferential mark which belongs to the class of deviating [things], it lacks a non-over-extended unified form that would delimit its being a means of valid cognition, and because it has no operation; rather, it is a cooperating condition of a [valid] means of knowledge. For this very reason, in mental inferential reasoning (<s>liṅga-parāmarśa</s>), the recollection of concomitance and the like is not a separate means of valid knowledge. If one says: Even without words, connection-cognition arises when there is cognition of suitability and the like — so words are useful only for the recollection of word-meaning — as stated: 'For one seeing a white form and hearing a neighing sound and the sound of hoof-beats, there arises the cognition: a white horse runs' — true, but after the utterance of the prompting sentence, from observing the prompted person's activity, the capacity is postulated for the word alone, for the sake of explaining the connected cognition, since the word alone is initially ascertained as the cause. Postulating a separate capacity for word-meanings would be overly complex. Hence they say: 'Due to primacy, due to being the speaker, and due to the acceptance of purport, let that capacity belong to the words alone — this is preferable.' And the cognition 'a white horse runs' is inferential, since the word's established causal status is absent [there].

children.text: jātiśaktivādaḥ
children.translated_text: The doctrine of the universal as the denotative capacity (<s>jātiśaktivāda</s>)

children.text:
evaṃ padārthamātre śaktau padārthonirūpyate /
tatra prabhākarāḥ /
yadyapyānayanādivyavahārādvyaktāveva śaktirucitā /
tathāpyānantya-vyabhicārābhyāṃ tatra na śaktigrahaḥ samuccayena śakyatve gāṃ dadyādityādau sarvopādānāsāmarthyaṃ ekasya śakyatve 'nadhyavasāyaḥ /
na ca govyaktimātramarthaḥ mātraśabdasya sarvārthatve uktadoṣāt sāmānyārthakatve vyakterapratīteḥ nānārthatve ca sarvāsāṃ pratyekaṃ jñātumaśakyaṃ śaktau śakye ca gauravaṃ apūrvagavi vyavahārābhāvācca /
nāpi gotvenopalakṣitā vyaktiḥ śakyā dhenupadavadato na śakyānantaraṃ na vyabhicāraḥ na sarvāsaṅgrahaḥ na nānārthatvaṃ gotvena tāsāmaikyāditi vācyam /
rūpāntareṇa vijñātamanyena rūpeṇa hi upalakṣyate yathā kākena gṛhaviśeṣogotvena dhāna karmavyaktiviśeṣaḥ svatovilakṣaṇaḥ na tu kākādyākāreṇaiva tatpratītiḥ /
na ca vyaktīnāṃ jātiṃ vinā rūpāntaramekamasti jñāyate vā gopadād gaurityeva pratīteḥ gotvaviśiṣṭe ca kāryānvayādgotvaṃ viśeṣaṇaṃ nopalakṣaṇaṃ tadanyena kāryānvaye upalakṣaṇarṃ yathāyaṃ vāsasvī devadattaśabdavācya ityatra vāsaḥ /
na ca gotvaikatvena vyaktīnāmaikyaṃ kriyate aśakyatvāt /
nāpi jñāpyate asattvāt /
na ca tadekatvameva vyakterekatvaṃ asambhavāt /
nāpi vyaktiḥ śakyā gotvamavacchedakaṃ kāraṇatve daṇḍavat evaṃ hi gopadāt na gotvaviśiṣṭabuddhiḥ syāt śaktigrahāhitasaṃskārasacivādgopadādeva dhenupadāviva gotvaviśiṣṭajñānaṃ tadudbodhaśca tadvadeva paramparāsambandhāditi cet na tatra hi dhānakarmavyaktiviśeṣasyāvaśyaśakyatve 'nugamāya gotvamavacchedakamātraṃ na tu vaiṣarītya gotvasya vṛṣabhe 'pi sattvāt iha tu vyaktiratiprasakteti jātiviśiṣṭaiva sā śakyā syāt /
children.translated_text:
Thus, when [it is established that] the capacity [of words] extends to word-meanings in general, the word-meaning (<s>padārtha</s>) is [now] examined.
Here, the <s>Prābhākara</s> [Mīmāṃsakas hold as follows]:
Although from usage such as 'bring [a cow]' etc., a capacity residing in the individual (<s>vyakti</s>) is appropriate,
nevertheless, because of [the problems of] infinity and deviation, capacity is not grasped there [in individuals]. If [all individuals] collectively were the denotation, in [the sentence] '<s>gāṃ dadyāt</s>' ('one should give a cow') etc., there would be incapacity to provide all [cows]. If a single [individual] were the denotation, there would be indeterminacy (<s>anadhyavasāya</s>).
Nor is a mere cow-individual the meaning — because if the word <s>mātra</s> ('mere') meant 'all,' the stated fault [would apply]; if it meant 'universal,' the individual would not be cognized; and if [the word 'cow'] were ambiguous (<s>nānārtha</s>), all [individuals] could not be known individually; there would be prolixity in [specifying both] the capacity and the denotable; and there would be no usage regarding a previously unseen cow.
Nor is the individual indicated (<s>upalakṣita</s>) by cow-ness the denotation — as in the word <s>dhenu</s> ('milch cow'). Therefore, [in that case] after [grasping] the denotation, there would be no deviation, no failure to include all, and no ambiguity — because of the unity of [all individuals] through cow-ness. [Reply:] This should not be said —
for what is known through one form is indicated (<s>upalakṣya</s>) through another form — just as a particular house [is indicated] by a crow [sitting on it], and the specific individual that is the object of a particular action [is indicated] through cow-ness — [this indicator is] different from [the indicated thing] itself; the cognition of that [house] is not through the form of the crow alone.
Nor is there, apart from the universal, a single other form common to [all] individuals — as it is known [or] as the cognition from the word 'cow' is simply 'a cow.' And since in [the cognition] qualified by cow-ness, the connection with the effect [i.e., the action] is through cow-ness, cow-ness is a qualifier (<s>viśeṣaṇa</s>), not an indicator (<s>upalakṣaṇa</s>); it would be an indicator [only] if the connection with the effect were through something other [than cow-ness] — as clothes [are the indicator] in 'the one wearing clothes is the denotation of the word <s>Devadatta</s>.'
Nor does the unity of cow-ness make the individuals into a unity — because this is impossible.
Nor does it make [their unity] known — because it is non-existent.
Nor is the unity of that [cow-ness] the unity of the individual — because this is impossible.
Nor is the individual the denotation with cow-ness as a delimiting condition (<s>avacchedaka</s>) [of the causal capacity], like a stick [is a delimiting condition of producing an effect]. For then, from the word 'cow,' there would be no cognition qualified by cow-ness. [Objection:] Through the assistance of a disposition deposited by capacity-grasping, the cognition qualified by cow-ness arises from the word 'cow' alone, just as in the word <s>dhenu</s>; and the arousal [of that disposition] too is the same, through an indirect connection. [Reply:] No — for there, the individual that is the specific object of the specific action must be the denotation; cow-ness is merely a delimiting condition for the sake of a common thread (<s>anugama</s>), but not conversely — because cow-ness is present even in a bull. But here, the individual is over-extended [as a denotation] — hence the denotation should be the individual qualified by the universal (<s>jātiviśiṣṭa</s>).

children.translated_text: [page 561]

children.text:
vastutastu jāteḥ śakyopalakṣaṇatve śakyavacchedakatve vāvaśyakatvāt lāghavācca jātireva śakyā syāt na tu vyaktiḥ dhenupade tu gotvaṃ na tathā atiprasaṅgāt /
astu tarhi jātiviśiṣṭaṃ śakyaṃ svavyavahāreṇa ca svahetutayā jātiviśiṣṭajñānasyānumitatvāditi cet na viśeṣyabhedādviśiṣṭānāmantatvena vyaktivācyatve uktadoṣagrāsāt /
viśeṣaṇasyaikyaikyena viśiṣṭanāmaikyasyopalakṣapakṣavadduṣyatvāt tasmādvyakterapadārthatve jātireva padārthaḥ /
vastutastu vyaktau jātiranugamikā viśeṣikā cāvaśyaṃ vācyeti nāgṛhītaviśeṣaṇānyāyena saiva vācyā /
atha jātāvapi vyaktireva viśeṣaḥ dharmāntarābhāvāt gavetarāvṛttitve sati sakalagovṛttitvāderūpādherapi vyaktighaṭitatvāt nāgṛhītaviśeṣaṇānyāyovyaktāvapītyubhayamapi vācyamiti na jāteḥ svata eva vyāvṛttatvāt /
anyathā jāti-vyaktorvyāvṛttatvajñānādanyonyavyāvṛttatvabuddhāvanyonyāśrayaḥ /
svatovyāvṛttatvañca na svayameva svavyāvartakatvaṃ svasmin svāvṛtteḥ /
nāpi vyāvartakaṃ vinaiva vyāvṛttatvaṃ asambhavāt /
kintu svāśrayavatsvātmani vyāvṛttadhījanakasvabhāvatvaṃ pareṣāmantyaviśeṣavat / vyāvartakadharme 'pi dharmāntarādeva vyāvṛttabuddhāvanavasthā syādata eva kiñciddhi vastu svata eva vilakṣaṇamityāhuḥ /
children.translated_text:
In truth, since the universal must necessarily serve either as an indicator of the denotable or as a delimiting condition of the denotable, and because of parsimony, the universal (<s>jāti</s>) alone should be the denotation, not the individual. In the word <s>dhenu</s>, however, cow-ness is not [the denotation] in the same way — because of over-extension.
[Objection:] Then let the denotation be the universal-qualified [individual] (<s>jātiviśiṣṭa</s>); and [this is confirmed] because the cognition qualified by the universal is inferred to be one's own cause through one's own usage. [Reply:] No — because since the qualificands are different, the universal-qualified [individuals] are infinite; and if [one says they are all] the denotation of the individual, the stated faults apply.
Because the unity of the qualifier does not make the qualified [individuals] into a unity — this is defective in the same way as the indicator-view. Therefore, when the individual is not the word-meaning, the universal alone is the word-meaning.
In truth, however, in [the cognition of] the individual, the universal is necessarily to be expressed (<s>vācya</s>) both as the common thread (<s>anugamikā</s>) and as the differentiator (<s>viśeṣikā</s>) — hence, by the principle that the qualifier that has not been [independently] grasped [must also be expressed], the universal itself is the denotation.
[Objection:] But in [the cognition of] the universal too, the individual alone is the differentiator, because there is no other differentiating property. [This is because] even [conditions like] 'being present in all cows while being absent from non-cows' etc. are constituted by individuals as adventitious conditions. [Hence] the principle of 'unapprehended qualifier' [applies] to the individual too — therefore both [universal and individual] must be expressed. [Reply:] No — because the universal is intrinsically differentiated (<s>svato vyāvṛtta</s>).
Otherwise, if the knowledge of the differentiation of the universal and the individual depended on each other's differentiation, there would be mutual dependence.
And intrinsic differentiation does not mean that [a thing] is itself its own differentiator — because [a thing] is not excluded from itself.
Nor is there differentiation without a differentiator — because that is impossible.
Rather, [intrinsic differentiation] is the natural capacity to produce the cognition of distinction in its own locus possessing its own substratum — like the ultimate particularities (<s>antyaviśeṣa</s>) for others. Even in the differentiating property, the cognition of distinction [would depend] on yet another property — [leading to] an infinite regress. Precisely for this reason, they say: 'Indeed, every entity is intrinsically unique.'

children.text:
astu vā vyaktyā vyāvṛttatayā bodhitā jātireva padārtholāghavāt na tu vaiparītyamubhayaṃ vā gauravāt kutastarhi vyaktidhīḥ jātiśaktādeva kathamanyaśaktādanyadhīḥ svabhāvāt tatsvabhāvatvameva vyaktiśaktiṃ vinā na nirvahatīti cet na gopadaṃ hi niyamatojātivyaktī bodhayati tatrāsya jātiśaktidhīreva sahakāriṇī kalpyate lāghavādāvaśyakatvācca na tu vyaktiśaktidhīrapi gauravāt /
jātiśaktijñāne sati tāṃ vinā vyaktibodhe vilambābhāvāt yathā tava padārthaśaktādevānvayadhīḥ /
yadvā jātiśaktameva padaṃ vyaktiṃ bodhayati aśakyatve 'pi jātyāśrayatvameva niyāmakaṃ yathā aśakyamapi svārthāntaraṃ bodhayati /
tatra prayojakatvena kḷptā śaktirevāstu jātyāśrayatvasya tathātvakalpane gauravāditi cet na anyalabhyasyāpadārthatvādanyathā anvayo 'pi śakyaḥ syāt lakṣaṇādyucchedaśca /
atha vā jātiśaktijñānājjātidhīrbhavantī vyaktimapi gocarayati /
vyaktiṃ vinā jāterabhāvāt yo yena vinā na bhāsate taddhīhetustamavabodhayati yathā jñānadhīhetustadviṣayaṃ yathā vā tavādhikaraṇasiddhānto jñānādinityatvaṃ anyathā padaṃ jātimapi na bodhayet kevalāyā apratīteḥ tathā ca jātiśaktikalpanāvaityarthaṃ tasmāt jātijñānārthaṃ kḷptā śaktirvyaktimapi bodhayati ekavittivedyatvaniyamāt /
etenaikavittivedyataiva vyaktiśaktiṃ vinā na syāt jñāpakābhāvāt /
na hi vyaktijñānamahetukaṃ jātihetukaṃ vā sadātanatvaprasaṅgāt /
nāpi jātidhīhetukaṃ saṃvidbhedāpatteriti nirastam /
jātiśaktereva vyaktijñāpakatvāt /
children.translated_text:
Or let the universal alone be the word-meaning, conveyed through the individual as [its] differentiator — because of parsimony. Not the reverse, nor both — because of prolixity. [Objection:] Whence then the cognition of the individual? From the capacity [of the word to denote] the universal alone. [Objection:] How can the cognition of something other [than the denotation] arise from a capacity for something else? [Reply:] By [its very] nature. [Objection:] That very 'being of such a nature' cannot be sustained without a capacity [of the word] for the individual. [Reply:] No — for the word 'cow' invariably conveys both the universal and the individual. Among those [two], only the knowledge of the capacity for the universal is postulated as the auxiliary cause — because of parsimony and because of necessity. But the knowledge of a capacity for the individual too [is] not [postulated] — because of prolixity.
Because when the knowledge of the capacity for the universal is present, there is no delay in the cognition of the individual without it — just as, for you, the cognition of connection arises from the capacity for the word-meaning [alone].
Alternatively, the word, having a capacity for the universal, conveys the individual [as well] — even without [the individual's] being the denotation, the property of being a substratum of the universal is the determining factor — just as [a word] conveys other [things] that are also not its denotation.
[Objection:] The capacity established as the motivating factor there should suffice [as the explanation]; postulating a separate capacity of substratum-of-universal-ness would be prolix. [Reply:] No — because what is obtainable from another [source] is not the word-meaning. Otherwise, even the connection [between word-meanings in a sentence] would be a denotation, and there would be the destruction of secondary signification (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>) etc.
Or rather, the cognition of the universal that arises from the knowledge of the capacity for the universal also encompasses the individual.
Because without the individual, the universal does not exist — and whatever does not appear without another [thing], the cause of its cognition also makes that [other thing] known. Just as the cause of the cognition of knowledge [makes known] the content of that knowledge; or just as, in your view, the topic-conclusion (<s>adhikaraṇasiddhānta</s>) [makes known] the eternality of cognition etc. Otherwise, the word would not convey even the universal, because the universal alone [without individuals] is never cognized. And thus, the postulation of a capacity for the universal would be purposeless. Therefore, the capacity postulated for the purpose of [conveying] the universal also conveys the individual — because of the rule of their being objects of a single cognition.
By this, [the objection] 'the being-objects-of-a-single-cognition would not exist without a capacity for the individual, because of the absence of something to make it known' [is answered] —
for it is not the case that the cognition of the individual is causeless or caused by the universal [alone, as a separate cause] — because that would lead to permanence. Nor is it caused by the cognition of the universal — because that would lead to a division of awareness. [All this is] set aside —
because the capacity for the universal itself makes the individual known.
